history_of_the_fire_nation.title: History of the Fire Nation
history_of_the_fire_nation.html:
From the first settlers of the Fire Islands to the Empire of Tajisaki: the origins, warlords, Sages, clans and Fire Lords of the Fire Nation before the Hundred Year War.

"Fire Nation" is the colloquial name used here for the state whose formal name is Tajisaki. For the modern industrial state and its government, see Empire of Tajisaki.
Formal nameTajisaki (the Realm, later the Empire, of Tajisaki)
Colloquial nameThe Fire Nation
HomelandThe Fire Islands, a volcanic archipelago on the equator in the western hemisphere
Main islandsCapital Island and Shuhon Island
Earliest traditionThe Tablets of the First Flame (c. 7000 BG, disputed)
Warring States EraSeveral millennia, ending in unification
UnificationAbout 4440 BG, under the first Fire Lord of the Tajisaki clan
Ruling houseThe Tajisaki clan (the Imperial family)
Noble housesThirteen, including the Imperial family
Major internal crisesThe age of Yosor and Szeto; the Camellia-Peony War (c. 312–295 BG)
Decline of the clans295 BG to the early reign of Sozin (Zoryu's project)
Industrial RevolutionFrom about 290 BG
Last clan revoltEarly reign of Sozin, crushed by General Oraso Eiko
Imperial era12 BG – 100 AG (the Empire of Tajisaki)

The history of the Fire Nation is that of a people of nomads, warriors and islanders who were gathered into one realm after thousands of years of warlord rule, and who built the most industrial state in the world. The realm they built was called Tajisaki, after the clan that won the Warring States Era and whose line supplied every Fire Lord for the next four and a half thousand years. Outsiders, and in time the islanders themselves, called it the Fire Nation, and the two names have been used side by side ever since.

It is a history of strong central government and of the nobles' resistance to it, of religious rule that gave way to autocracy, and of a long run of feuds, plagues, poisonings, purges and civil wars that the nation survived by reforming itself, and by becoming richer and better organized. Its fortunes were bound up with those of its neighbors at every stage: the Earth Kingdom's rebellions and secessions, the Water Tribes' isolation and decline, the pacifism of the Air Nomads and the shifting authority of the Avatar all shaped the road that led, through the Avatar Roku and Fire Lord Sozin, to the war. It is also a history with a hole in it. The earliest millennia are known mainly from traditions recorded long after the fact, because the Warring States Era destroyed much of the evidence, and because later rulers, most thoroughly Sozin, had reasons of their own to rewrite what survived. It ends, in the imperial era, with the Empire of Tajisaki and the Hundred Year War.

Names and etymology

Tajisaki

Tajisaki was the name of a clan before it was the name of a country. When the Tajisaki clan emerged victorious from the Warring States Era and its chief was raised as the first Fire Lord, the new realm took the clan's name, in the way that the realms of the mainland's early kings took the names of their capitals and dynasties. The state has been called Tajisaki in its laws, treaties, coinage and constitutions ever since, and the royal family's descent from the clan is the basis of every Fire Lord's claim to the throne. The formal title changed with the form of government, the Realm of Tajisaki in the age of the Sages and the clans, and the Empire of Tajisaki from the reign of Sozin, but the name never did.

The meaning of the word is disputed. The Fire Sages' scholars, who liked to find a sacred sense in everything, read it as an old island phrase for "the keepers of the hearth". Philologists of the Academy of Caldera argue that it is a place-name, the name of the harbor and valley where the clan first held land, and that the clan took its name from the place and not the reverse. No inscription settles the question, because the oldest uses of the name come from sources that do not survive in their original form.

The Fire Nation

"Fire Nation" is the name by which the realm is known everywhere else, and it is the name that most of its own people use in speech. It is a description and not a title: the Earth Kingdom and the Water Tribes named the people of the islands after the element that they bent, and the islanders adopted it, much as they adopted the habit of calling the other peoples "nations". The name does not appear in the Imperial Constitution, which uses Tajisaki throughout, but it is used in schoolbooks, in the press, in popular songs and by the Fire Lords themselves in speeches, where it carries a warmer note than the legal name. A person from the islands is a Fire Nation citizen in conversation and a subject or citizen of Tajisaki on a document. In this wiki "Fire Nation" is used for the country and its people in general, and "Tajisaki" and "the Empire" for the state and its government.

Names of persons

Names often have a hard "Z", like Zuko, Ozai, Azula, Sozin, Zhao, Azulon and Zoryu, a feature that has been traced to the speech of the old island chiefs. The thirteen noble houses use the clan name as a family name, and the Imperial family, as the Tajisaki clan, is the only one whose name is also the name of the realm.

Sources and the problem of the record

The history of the Fire Nation before about 4440 BG is known from a small and unreliable body of evidence. No authenticated document from the Era of Raava survives. The earliest accounts of that period were recorded thousands of years after the events they describe, from oral traditions, ritual recitations and fragments of older religious texts. The sources most often used are:

  • The Tablets of the First Flame, a set of fragments traditionally dated to about 7000 BG, said to have been recovered from a sealed chamber beneath an abandoned settlement on the western coast of the Fire Islands. Their text is incomplete, their language poorly understood and their dating disputed.
  • The Sages' recitations and murals, kept in the Dragonbone Catacombs beneath the capital, where the Fire Lords were buried with scrolls of histories and myths.
  • Coastal genealogies, which preserve the migration tradition that the imperial chroniclers later preferred.
  • Archaeology: pottery, metalwork and obsidian tools, which show contact with the mainland but cannot establish a political history.
  • Folklore, in which history and legend are mixed, as in the stories of Warlord Toz and the Kemurikage.

The gap in the record has an explanation, discussed below under the Warring States Era: for generations, rival houses burned each other's archives. It was made worse in the imperial era, when Sozin sealed the Dragonbone Catacombs so that the nation's history would appear to begin with him. Fire Nation historians have therefore worked as much by reconstruction as by reading, and a good deal of what follows is "traditional" or "conventional" in the sense that it is what the Sages and the chroniclers agreed on, and not what can be proved.

Origins (before 7000 BG)

The Fire Nation tells two stories about its beginnings, and its chroniclers have always allowed both. They are the spiritual tradition, which the Sages kept, and the migration tradition, which the later imperial historians preferred, and the evidence does not choose between them.

The spiritual tradition: the Era of Raava

In the Sages' account, the ancestors of the Fire Nationals lived in the Era of Raava, when dragons ruled the skies and the lion turtles sheltered humanity within their great cities. The ancestors were hunters, who received the gift of fire from the lion turtles through energybending whenever they went into the Spirit Wilds, to gather food and defend themselves against hostile spirits. The gift was lent and not given: a hunter carried the flame as long as he remained beyond the city's walls, and gave it back on his return.

When the lion turtles gave up their role as the protectors of mankind, after the events surrounding the first Avatar, the people left the lion-turtle cities and settled along the equator, on the islands that became the Fire Islands. They kept some habits from that time, such as raising hybrid pigs, and a desire to push out into the unknown, which a failed attempt to found a settlement in the Spirit Wilds already showed. Later Sage chronicles identified that expedition, remembered as the First Departure, with the stories of Yao and Jaya, whose descendants kept the belief that exploration and conquest were inseparable from the survival of their people.

The Tablets of the First Flame

The oldest surviving written account of these events is traditionally dated to about 7000 BG, more than two millennia before the Avatar cycle. The Tablets of the First Flame describe the age of the dragons and the lion turtles, the expeditions beyond the walls, and the departure from the cities. A passage translated by the Sages of Caldera in 183 BG reads:

Beyond the walls, the green world belongs to the spirits. We go with the flame upon our hands, and we return with the flesh of the earth. The flame is not ours to command, but ours to carry until we come home.

Scholars disagree over whether the Tablets are contemporary with the events they describe. Some believe that the text preserves fragments of a much older oral tradition. Others argue that its surviving form was compiled centuries later by Fire Sage scribes seeking to establish a sacred origin for the island communities, and perhaps for the families that later ruled them. The Tablets are further compromised by the fact that they are known only through fragments and later transcriptions, and not through a complete, independently authenticated original. Archaeological traditions associate the earliest settlements of the period with hybrid-pig husbandry, obsidian tools, communal hearths and the oldest known coastal fishing villages of the archipelago.

The migration tradition

In the migration tradition, the Fire Islands were settled over many centuries by nomadic warrior bands, island peoples who already lived on the archipelago, and migrants from the Earth Kingdom's western coast, who came by sea to escape its wars. These groups mingled. Their descendants were a warrior culture that depended on strong leaders, resourceful and used to living beside active volcanoes. The tradition does not contradict the Sages' account so much as ignore it, and the two were often reconciled by saying that the ancestors had carried the flame out of the lion-turtle cities and that others had joined them on the islands afterwards.

The Age of Migration (c. 7000–5000 BG)

The centuries after humanity's departure from the lion turtles are poorly understood. Later chronicles describe successive waves of migration toward the volcanic islands, but cannot establish whether the settlers arrived together or over thousands of years. The earliest communities were probably organized around fishing grounds, fertile valleys, volcanic resources and safe harbors, and their religion grew up around the sun, fire and the sacred status of dragons. By the end of the period permanent settlements had spread across parts of the archipelago, but nothing resembling a unified Fire Nation existed.

Trade and contact with the mainland

By about 6500 BG, several coastal settlements had grown into permanent trading communities. Their remains include pottery and metalwork like that found along the western Earth Kingdom coast, alongside distinctive local tools of volcanic stone. The evidence does not establish a unified trading network, but it shows that the islands were connected to the mainland long before the first kingdoms. Island merchants exchanged metals, volcanic minerals, dried fish and manufactured goods for livestock, textiles and commodities carried along the mainland's inland routes.

The confederation model

The most consequential influence came from the nomadic confederations of the central Earth Kingdom. These societies were organized around personal allegiance to powerful leaders, military service, negotiated tribute and the absorption of rival groups into larger coalitions. Envoys and mercenaries carried these methods to the islands, and returning warriors told of confederation armies whose strength came from a leader's ability to command followers from several communities, and not from the size of a single settlement. Some island chiefs began to copy the practice, rewarding service with fishing grounds, control of harbors and shares of tribute.

The islanders did not simply reproduce the mainland's structures. Where mainland confederations relied on mobile armies and overland routes, Fire Island leaders relied on boats, coastal settlements and networks of harbors. By about 5200 BG the most successful chiefs could assemble warriors from several islands, maintain fleets for raiding and trade, and compel weaker communities to supply provisions or fighters. These alliances were unstable. A chief's authority depended on his reputation, the distribution of plunder and his ability to protect the merchant routes, and when he died or lost a major battle, his subordinates tended to withdraw their allegiance or transfer it to a rival. The arrangements nevertheless established traditions that reappeared in the warlord states that followed.

The Warring States Era

The Warring States Era of the Fire Islands, known to the Sages as the Age of Ashes, was the long period in which the archipelago was divided among competing powers. Its dates are disputed. It is traditionally placed several thousand years before unification, and it was the most violent and the least documented period in the nation's history.

The warlords

For generations, rival warlords fought over islands, ports, farmland, mineral deposits and maritime trade routes. Political authority was split among competing houses, religious institutions, warrior clans and local rulers. Some controlled only a single settlement, while others commanded fleets, tributary communities and networks of allied warrior houses. Settlements were repeatedly conquered, abandoned, burned or absorbed into rival territories, and the fighting centered on harbors, valleys, fishing grounds and the volcanic mineral deposits of the larger islands.

Two features of the age shaped what followed. The first was the Sun Warriors, a civilization that learned the first firebending from the dragons, built cities that left a deep influence on the later Fire Nation, and later withdrew into isolation. They preserved the oldest religious teachings and kept contact with the wider archipelago only through limited trade. The second was the militarized chiefdom, in which a chief demanded tribute in exchange for protection and organized raids against his neighbors. Most of the houses that later became the noble clans began as chiefdoms of this kind.

The migrants from the steppe

The Warlord Age was not created from nothing by the islanders. Its roots lie on the mainland, in the centuries after Avatar Wan closed the spirit portals in about 9,829 BG, when humanity, cut off from the spirits that had guided and sheltered it, divided over land, grazing grounds, trade routes and allegiance. On the eastern steppes of the Earth Kingdom the horse peoples became the most prominent of the contending powers. Their herds moved between seasonal pastures, and a chief's authority rested on his ability to protect those pastures, secure livestock, distribute spoils and keep the loyalty of mounted followers. A chief who could no longer protect his people lost them, and a victorious chief grew by absorbing defeated bands and redistributing their wealth.

The steppe wars produced a steady stream of displaced families, defeated chiefs, mercenaries and exiles. Some fled east to the coast, where merchants and seafarers carried them across the sea. They could not carry the great herds, but they brought traditions of personal loyalty, martial service, tribute and the incorporation of defeated rivals into a victor's following. The Fire Islands were not an empty frontier. Established island communities, mixed bending populations and the Sun Warriors, whose ancient religion set them apart, already lived there. The Sun Warriors stayed out of the migrants' struggles, and their indifference let the newcomers expand without confronting the oldest surviving institution of the archipelago. The migrants introduced a new model of politics into a region that was already diverse, and over time the customs of the steppe chiefs were adapted to a world in which harbors, ships and sea tolls counted for more than pastures and herds.

The Warlord Age

Later tradition called the resulting order the Warlord Age. Authority was split among competing chiefs, harbor lords, military households and local rulers, and no regime could impose lasting control over the whole archipelago. The newcomers' most durable contribution was the system of personal allegiance: a chief's power rested on the oaths of warriors, retainers, subordinate chiefs and allied families, who were paid in captured wealth, land, offices and the right to collect tribute. Defeated rivals who submitted could be taken into the victor's following, which let a successful warlord expand quickly without destroying every institution he conquered. Island conditions changed the means: horses gave way to ships, and sheltered anchorages, fleets, fishing settlements, shipyards and maritime tolls became the sources of wealth.

The regimes varied from fortified ports governed by one household to networks of subordinate chiefs, tributary settlements and military dependants whose fleets could carry forces across several islands. War was a recurring part of political life, and it ran in a cycle: every conquest strengthened a warlord's following, and every redistribution of land and authority created new rivals among the people expected to stay loyal. A military defeat, a succession dispute or a failure to pay the rewards could dissolve an alliance almost as fast as it had formed. Fire Nation histories often portrayed the era as a contest between disorder and legitimate monarchy, but the warlords were not merely lawless raiders. They built the political relationships, military households, maritime networks and systems of landholding from which the later nobility grew, and their institutions outlived the wars that made them.

Warlord Toz and the Kemurikage

The best-known warlord of the age is Toz, a figure traditionally placed in the last centuries before unification. According to the account, he took an annual tribute from every village under his protection, and when one village refused to give up its children as extra hostages, his soldiers attacked it. The mothers who died resisting him returned as the dark spirits known as the Kemurikage and haunted his camp until his followers abandoned him and his regime fell. His success had shown the other warlords that the islands could be united, and they fought on, with the Kemurikage in the night, until one of them did unite them.

Toz's mistake, in the folktales, was one of method. He replaced the old bargain between a warlord and his followers, loyalty for protection and reward, with rule by fear: tribute under threat, and children taken as hostages from villages and subordinate households. Service no longer offered security, and submission no longer promised that a ruler would respect the lives of those under his protection. When a village refused his tribute and he seized its children, the mothers appealed to the spirits, and the Kemurikage answered by taking the children of his captains. The distinction the captains had relied on, that hostage-taking was something done to other people's households, collapsed overnight. Captains demanded their children back, warriors left their posts, subordinate chiefs withdrew, and the army deserted him.

The lesson was not universally learned. Many later warlords concluded that they needed more personal power, stronger guards and better control of their subordinates, and several tried to become the next Toz without understanding why he had failed. The story therefore did double duty. To commoners it was a tale of mothers whose grief brought down a tyrant; to subordinate chiefs, a warning that a lord who endangered their households forfeited their loyalty; and to later monarchists, an argument for replacing competing warlords with a single ruler able to restrain the abuses of lesser chiefs.

The story's accuracy is uncertain. No contemporary record of Toz has been found, and the earliest written version dates from the early period of the Sages' monarchy. Some historians read the Kemurikage as a supernatural account of a real revolt against hostage-taking, and others as a moral legend against rulers who mistook fear for loyalty.

The destruction of the record

The greatest break in the historical record occurred in this era. It was not the result of a single campaign, but of several overlapping processes:

  • The burning of archives. Palace records, genealogies, tax registers and local chronicles were destroyed whenever a rival stronghold fell.
  • The collapse of religious institutions. Temples and Sage establishments that kept ritual texts were looted or abandoned, and some records were lost when their custodians were killed or driven out.
  • The destruction of rival legitimacy. Warlords had every reason to destroy the inscriptions and genealogies that showed the ancient rights of their enemies.
  • The rewriting of history. Victorious houses commissioned new chronicles that presented their own ancestors as legitimate rulers and dismissed defeated dynasties as usurpers.
  • The loss of oral tradition. Whole communities were displaced or absorbed, and took their local histories with them. Some survived only as legends, ceremonies or regional folklore.

The result was a gap that later Fire Nation scholars struggled to close. The earliest centuries were not wholly forgotten, but the evidence was scattered, contradictory and difficult to authenticate. The same gap complicated the claims of the winners: no house could point to an uncontested ancient title, because the records that might have shown one no longer existed.

The Tajisaki clan and unification (about 4440 BG)

The rise of the Tajisaki

By about 4500 BG, several powerful houses controlled large parts of the archipelago. Their territories were not always continuous: a chief might hold a fortified island, keep allies across the sea and collect tribute from settlements that recognized him only when he was strong. No single warlord could permanently dominate the islands, and the repeated wars threatened the trade on which the strongest settlements depended.

The house that finally won was the Tajisaki clan. Its own tradition, preserved in the clan's chronicles and later in the imperial histories, held that it had begun as the lords of a harbor and valley on the main island, that it had grown rich on the harbor's trade, and that it had learned from the mainland confederations to bind other chiefs to it by oath and by reward and not only by force. It fought its rivals with a fleet and a coalition, took the surrender of some of them and the heads of others, and by the last generations of the era no other house could match its strength.

The Sages and the first Fire Lord

The Fire Sages, whose religious authority reached across several islands, had by then become the intermediaries in the disputes of the houses. They could negotiate settlements, sanctify oaths and command a respect that no warlord had. Their own chronicles credit the unification to the head of the Sages, who, they say, brought the houses under a common sovereign. The Tajisaki chronicles credit their chief. The two accounts were later reconciled by saying that the Sages anointed the Tajisaki chief, and the conventional history puts the emergence of the first Fire Lord around 4440 BG, with the Sages acting as the new ruler's priests and the Tajisaki as the ruler's house.

Unification did not create a centralized state at once. The first Fire Lord let some warlords keep their lands, and their families became the noble clans, which kept private armies and fiefs and for four thousand years were the main check on the Fire Lord's power. The new monarchy took its name from its ruling house, and the realm became Tajisaki. Every Fire Lord afterwards, whatever his or her personal name, belonged to the Tajisaki line, and the Imperial family and the Tajisaki clan were one and the same.

The harbor lords and the unification settlement

The Tajisaki came out of the maritime order as a lineage of harbor lords. Their strength rested on ports, fleets, coastal settlements and the networks of subordinate chiefs that depended on maritime trade and protection. Unlike warlords tied to one territory or one household army, they could move forces between islands and coordinate campaigns across the archipelago. Their victory was not a series of simple defeats. It took a coalition broad enough to overcome the other major warlords while keeping the allegiance of those who submitted before the end, and the clan used its fleets to carry allies, isolate hostile ports and concentrate against holdouts.

The downfall of Toz supplied the political lesson that tradition attached to the Tajisaki ascendancy. Where Toz had demanded obedience by terror and endangered the households of his own captains, the Tajisaki presented themselves as rulers who would bind chiefs by oaths, reciprocal obligations and rewards for service. The model did not abolish hierarchy or coercion; it made the relationship between ruler and elites predictable. Warlords who joined the coalition kept their lands and household troops in return for recognizing the new ruler's supremacy and furnishing military support, which lowered the cost of conquest and let the victors absorb much of the existing order. Chiefs who refused were defeated and executed. By preserving the compliant and killing the holdouts, the Tajisaki turned former enemies into stakeholders and showed what refusal cost.

Military victory alone could not make the coalition a monarchy. The Fire Sages supplied the religious legitimacy: by anointing the first Fire Lord they gave the new rule a sacred dimension that distinguished it from the dominion of an ordinary warlord, and the settlement turned the defeated and incorporated warlords into the noble clans of the emerging Fire Nation. Unification therefore ended not with the disappearance of the old warlords but with their transformation into a hereditary aristocracy. It rested on three foundations: the military supremacy of the Tajisaki, the reciprocal obligations binding the clans to the Fire Lord, and the Sages' religious recognition. It also kept the habits that had made the wars possible, personal loyalty, household power and inherited privilege, and for about four thousand years the Fire Lord's demand for obedience would be set against the entrenched power of the clans whose cooperation made the monarchy possible.

A monarchy built on a lost past

The new monarchy inherited the problem of the record. Much of the history that could have established the origins of its peoples and houses had already been lost, and the earliest royal chronicles were therefore not simple records of the past but attempts to reconstruct it, with all the temptations that went with the task. The first Fire Lord's court wrote a history in which the Tajisaki were the natural rulers of the islands, and this version, further revised by every succeeding dynasty of scribes, is the foundation of the conventional chronology. The Sages recorded the nation's history in murals in the Dragonbone Catacombs, where the Fire Lords were buried, with scrolls of histories and myths.

At some point one Fire Lord broke with the Sages, took political power for himself and turned the realm into a monarchy with a regular succession, while the Sages kept their spiritual role and some political influence.

The long strife (4440–300 BG)

The unification of about 4440 BG did not end the violence of the Fire Islands. It moved it. The Tajisaki Fire Lord had won the right to be called sovereign, but he had not won a monopoly on armed force, and for the next four thousand years the history of the realm is largely the history of what the crown, the clans and the Sages did to one another while sharing a country that none of them could rule alone. The Fire Nation was, in the same centuries, one of the strongest and one of the most unstable states in the world: it had a standing army, a literate bureaucracy and a rich agriculture, and it was repeatedly pulled to pieces from within.

The three-sided settlement

The settlement that followed unification rested on three powers, each of which depended on the others and distrusted them.

  • The Fire Lord and the Tajisaki house held the throne, the capital, the fleet and the right to name the realm's officers. They did not hold the land. Most of the islands' farmland, harbors and mines belonged to clans that had come to terms with the first Fire Lord and kept their estates as the price of their oath.
  • The noble clans, descended from the warlords of the old age, kept private armies, collected their own tribute and administered justice on their own lands. They owed the crown loyalty and service, but they remembered that their ancestors had been independent, and some of them never stopped hoping to take the central government for themselves.
  • The Fire Sages held the temples, the calendar, the rites of succession and the memory of the realm. They crowned the Fire Lords and buried them, and they were the only body that could confer sacred legitimacy on a ruler, which made them kingmakers whenever the throne was contested.

Every serious crisis of the era can be read as one of these three powers trying to take over the functions of another, or two of them combining against the third. The system had a strong tendency to produce civil war, and it also had a strong tendency to survive it, because the islands were small, the sea was a common enemy and the clans, however much they hated each other, needed a crown to arbitrate their quarrels.

Feud, hostage and private war

The clans' private armies were the main source of violence. Bloody feuds between clans were a common occurrence, and they bound up energy and resources that the realm might have spent on trade or defense. A feud could begin with a boundary dispute, a broken betrothal, an insult at court or a death at a duel, and once begun it was inherited, with the dead of each side demanding answer from the living. Chroniclers of later centuries describe burned granaries, drowned harbor towns and estates besieged for years over matters that outsiders would have thought trivial. Several recurring civil wars, they note with some bitterness, began over "pitiful issues".

The old customs of the warlord age survived in softened form. The practice of taking a rival's children as wards, which the story of Toz had made notorious, was kept by the clans as an exchange of hostages that guaranteed treaties, and the Fire Lords sometimes required the heirs of great houses to be raised in the capital. The practice kept the peace more often than it broke it, but it also meant that a clan whose child had died at court had a reason to remember the throne's debt.

The islands themselves resisted centralization. Many remained distinct and partly autonomous, with their own dialects, their own festivals and their own ideas of what was owed to the capital. They guarded their resources, and they were often unwilling to share them with other parts of the Fire Nation, let alone with the central government. A famine on one island did not necessarily bring grain from another, and a Fire Lord who wished to move rice or coal from a rich island to a poor one had first to persuade the lord of the rich one.

The thirteen houses

The known noble houses of the later period are the Sei'naka, Keohso, Rasuzo, Shirisa, Ziruyu, Shi-Wu, Zakai, Chozhu, Noyuno, Hineno and Kosihi clans and the Saowon, with the Imperial Tajisaki, thirteen in all. The Sei'naka dominated the ministries, although the clan itself was weak, and the Keohso held the capital's confidence for generations. The Saowon, whose fall in the purge of 295 BG is told below, were among the richest. The houses used the clan name as a family name, and only the Tajisaki had a name that was also the name of the realm.

Dynasties of one house

The Tajisaki line supplied every Fire Lord, but the line was not a single trunk. It was a clan with many branches, and the chronicles divide its rule into dynasties, each named for the branch or the era that held the throne. The names that survive include the Pei Zhi era, whose solar eclipse the chroniclers recorded as "the darkest day in Fire Nation history", and the Pho Zel dynasty, under which the komodo rhino was first domesticated, a development that changed farming and transport and that kept the animal as the nation's main beast of burden until industrialization after the Hundred Year War. A dynasty was usually founded when one branch of the clan defeated another, and it ended when the same thing happened to it.

The strife of these dynasties was a family quarrel with an army behind it. Members of the royal family feuded in their quest for power, and the court was marked by conspiracies, poisonings and the removal of rivals to remote temples. Because the clans were attached to different branches of the Tajisaki by marriage, a quarrel in the palace could become a war in the provinces within a season, and a regency or a disputed succession was the usual cause of the worst fighting.

The Sages and the throne

The Sages were not neutral. They had anointed the first Fire Lord, and they never forgot that the power of the crown came from them. At some point one Fire Lord broke with them, took political power into his own hands and made the monarchy a regular succession, and from then on the relationship was one of mutual suspicion: the Fire Lord needed the Sages' blessing, and the Sages needed the Fire Lord's protection, and each side tried to use the other. In times of crisis the Sages could tip the balance. They supported Chaejin against Zoryu in the Camellia-Peony War, and for that they were watched by every Fire Lord afterwards.

A strong state in a violent country

None of this made the Fire Nation weak. Despite its internal conflict, the nation became one of the most powerful and advanced countries in the world. Its people were resourceful and resilient, a trait that Iroh later put down to living on islands dominated by active volcanoes, where a village could be buried in a night and rebuilt by the next generation. The cities grew, the cultivation of the islands advanced, the bureaucracy developed its ranks of ministers and clerks, and the fleet kept the coasts. The state's offices were open to talent, and its violence was largely directed inward. Foreign wars were fewer than civil ones, and after the 4th century BG the Fire Nation enjoyed a relative peace in its dealings with other countries, even as its army kept contingency plans for everything from civil war to the invasion of the Earth Kingdom and the Water Tribes.

The age of Yosor and the reforms of Szeto

The worst crisis of the old order came in the reign of Fire Lord Yosor, when the Fire Nation came close to complete destruction. The chronicles tell of plagues and natural disasters that destabilized the country and left the common people struggling for survival, and of noble clans that took up arms and fought each other for what food and land remained. The central government, which had never controlled the clans' armies, was unable to bring the chaos under control. The realm fractured into semi-independent regimes, each ruled by a clan or a coalition of clans, and many people feared that the ancient warlord era was starting again.

Complete anarchy was averted by the Avatar. Szeto, a Fire Nation Avatar whom the Sages treat as the nation's own, stepped in and became a minister in the government. Working with Yosor and the other officials, he did several things at once:

  • He brokered peace between the clans, using the weight of the Avatar's office to make settlements that no Fire Lord could have enforced, and sometimes trading a clan's grievance for a place on the council.
  • He reformed the central government to make it more effective, strengthening the ministries and the chain of officials that carried the crown's orders to the provinces.
  • He reformed money, introducing monetary measures that gave the realm a more reliable coinage and made it easier for the crown to collect and spend revenue.
  • He set up relief for farmers in times of famine, a system of stored grain and remitted taxes that kept the worst harvests from turning into revolts.

The Fire Nation emerged from the crisis stronger, and Szeto is remembered in the Festival of Szeto, which the court held for centuries afterwards. But his reforms were double-edged, and the later history of the realm shows how. The ministries, the coinage and the grain stores were the instruments of a more effective crown, and the more effective the crown became, the more it could attempt against the clans. A Fire Lord who wished to reduce the nobility would find, centuries later, that Szeto's machinery was waiting for him. The precedent was also important: an Avatar had saved the nation by working inside its government, with a Fire Lord's consent. Roku, born in the same land, would later try to restrain the nation in a very different manner, and Sozin would remember that the Avatar had once been the crown's servant.

Isolation and the Platinum Affair (530 BG)

The Fire Nation's history cannot be separated from that of its neighbors, and nothing shows this better than the Platinum Affair. In the Earth Kingdom, the people had risen under General Nong against the Earth King Feishan, who was accused of tyranny and of being a puppet of the Fire Nation. The war was prolonged, and during the childhood of the Avatar Yangchen the Fire Nation and the Water Tribes secretly agreed to back the rebel with platinum ingots, in the hope of a friendlier government in Ba Sing Se. Feishan won. He kept the ingots, and he closed the Earth Kingdom's ports, in the diplomatic blunder known as the Platinum Affair (530 BG).

The consequences were lasting for all three countries.

  • The Fire Nation declared a state of isolation, as did the Water Tribes, after the Earth Kingdom's lead. Foreign trade was allowed only in a few "shang" cities, where merchants and officials met under supervision.
  • Jonduri, a Fire Nation island city, became one of the shang cities, and the zongdu (governor) Chaisee turned it into the jewel of the system. Fire Lord Gonryu enjoyed the revenue that flowed into the treasury from it, and he had Chaisee spied on, because he did not want any zongdu to linger past a term.
  • The Water Tribes routed their foreign trade through Port Tuugaq, where a few go-betweens handled ivory, hides and dried fish. Without native timber or a deep-water navy, the South was left poor and exposed, a fact the Fire Nation noted and, in time, exploited.
  • The Earth Kingdom was left angry and suspicious, with a government that had learned that other powers would buy its rebels and that it could cheat them without punishment.

For the Fire Nation, isolation had a curious effect. It cut the islands off from the mainland's markets but made the crown richer, since the shang cities' customs went to the treasury, and it reinforced the habit of settling foreign policy in secret. The Fire Nation had tried to buy a government and had been robbed of the price, and the lesson its ministers drew was not to avoid such schemes but to conduct them with more care. The same generation that closed its ports built the first steam engine, and a country that could not trade freely began to learn how to make what it could not buy.

The Saowon and the phoenix eels

The era also saw the first rise and fall of the Saowon clan, whose fortunes would decide the Camellia-Peony War. The Avatar Yangchen, who travelled to the Fire Nation as a young woman and came to be greatly respected there, made a new pact between the Saowon and the phoenix eel spirits that lived in the caverns under Ma'inka Island. The Saowon's people violated its terms by approaching the cenotes, and the children of Ma'inka were cursed to sleep and never wake. Yangchen, distracted from her investigations in the shang cities, negotiated with the eels again, and the children were released, on condition that the Saowon disgrace themselves for almost fifty years, with the promise that they might one day rise to prominence again. The humans of Ma'inka disrespected the terms of this agreement too, and the spirits turned dark. Years later, the Avatar Kuruk was forced to hunt and destroy them.

The story was kept in the Saowon's own tradition as a warning, and it explains why the clan, once it had risen again, was so tenacious. It also illustrates a theme of the age: the old pacts between the Fire Nation's families and the spirit world were failing, and the clans' relations with the spirits, once the basis of their authority, had become a source of danger.

The changing tide (312–255 BG)

The late fourth and the third centuries BG were a turning point in the balance of power in the world, and it is in these decades that the Fire Nation, without any single remarkable act, drew ahead of its rivals. The tide ran against the Earth Kingdom, and, for a time, against the Avatar's office itself.

The death of Kuruk and the crisis of the Avatar

The Avatar Kuruk was forced to deal with the Spirit World, and he left the four nations to solve their own problems. He died at 33, in 312 BG, and the Avatar's absence, followed by a failure to find his successor, emboldened those whom the Avatar would normally have opposed. For seven years the world had no Avatar that anyone could name, and the effect was felt everywhere: corrupt and ruthless people grew in power, and instability spread. The institution on which the whole international order rested, the Avatar's authority to mediate between nations, was, for the first time in a generation, absent.

The Yellow Neck Uprising and the Fire Nation's interest in lightning

In the Earth Kingdom the vacuum was filled by the daofei, the bandit armies of the interior. A charismatic and unbalanced man named Xu Ping An, who could generate lightning, a skill that had nearly died out, gathered them into the Yellow Necks, so called for the scarves they wore. They marauded through the heartland, killing officials, soldiers and civilians alike, and in some places stacking their victims in neat piles. The Earth Kingdom's army chose not to defend some of the remote hinterland, in part because the nobility's attention was consumed by the Wars of Secrets and Daggers, and the villages were left to be ransacked. The Earth Sage Jianzhu, who finally broke the rebels at Zhulu Pass in 304 BG, put an end to the uprising by an act of mass murder, burying thousands of the captured Yellow Necks alive and reporting a quite different story to the Earth King.

The Fire Nation took a practical interest. In 304 BG, its leadership struck a secret deal with Jianzhu: Xu Ping An would not be executed, so that the Fire Nation could study him and learn how he was able to generate lightning. This was one of the first documented occasions on which the Fire Nation treated a foreign phenomenon as a resource to be examined by the state, and it points toward the research institutions of the later empire. It also shows how closely the courts of Caldera and Ba Sing Se were bound together, even while their governments pretended to be isolated.

A succession crisis at home

While the Earth Kingdom burned, the Fire Nation was, for a few years, peaceful and prosperous. Under Fire Lord Chaeryu, in the time of Kuruk and the years after his death, harvests and fisheries were good, the economy thrived, and the country, in the chroniclers' phrase, "thrived". The family problems that would end this calm were already in place.

The Camellia-Peony War (c. 312–295 BG)

The Camellia-Peony War was the name given to the succession conflict between Fire Lord Zoryu and his illegitimate half-brother Chaejin. It was called a war in retrospect, and the word was a poetic exaggeration: open war was narrowly avoided, but the period was marked by enough violent clashes that the name stuck. It was the last major struggle between the throne and the great clans, and its outcome set the Fire Nation on a path that led directly to Sozin.

Chaeryu's two sons

Chaeryu had kept his teenage love, Lady Huazo of the Saowon clan, as his royal mistress, but was encouraged to end the relationship and marry Lady Sulan of the Keohso clan. Shortly after he committed to the marriage, Huazo revealed that she was pregnant, to Chaeryu's great embarrassment. To avoid dishonoring Huazo or her house, he acknowledged the child, Chaejin. Sulan died giving birth to her own son, Zoryu, and Zoryu's name made use of a character traditionally used only by the Saowon, which the Saowon took as an insult. Chaeryu eventually sent Chaejin to the Fire Sages and excluded him from the royal family, forbidding the matter to be discussed at court during his reign. His leading ministers supported the decision, which cleared the way for Zoryu to be the next Fire Lord.

Two houses, two crests

The feud took its name from the crests of the two families: the Keohso clan, which backed the Fire Lord, was represented by a winged peony, and the Saowon by a stone camellia. The Keohso were Zoryu's mother's people, and they supported him steadfastly, along with a number of other clans. The Saowon had behind them the memory of their disgrace and the energy of a family that expected to rise.

When Chaeryu died, Zoryu came to the throne, and the situation went against him. Contrary to the court's expectations, Huazo had turned out to be a highly capable politician and administrator, who gradually strengthened the Saowon, increased the clan's wealth and extended its power across the Fire Islands. Chaejin returned to court as a liaison for the High Temple. He was embittered by having been sent away, and he wanted the throne. He won the support of the Fire Sages, and Huazo and Chaejin used all their resources to delegitimize Zoryu.

Bad omens and the failing realm

Zoryu's rule was unstable. The good harvests of his father's reign came to an end, and the fisheries declined. Some of the older Sages began to say that the spirits themselves were unhappy with the Fire Lord, an accusation that in the Fire Nation was close to a declaration of rebellion. Many territories of the islands, apart from the capital and Huazo's lands, fell into poverty. Zoryu remained in power because of the unwavering support of the Keohso, and because of aid from the Earth Kingdom's Jianzhu, who, with the young man then believed to be the Avatar, Yun, skillfully mediated the conflict. The two advised Zoryu to recruit doubles, including a double of Yun, to maintain his position and protect himself from assassins, a stratagem that would later have terrible consequences.

The Festival of Szeto, 295 BG

In 295 BG, Zoryu invited the Avatar Kyoshi, who had been revealed as the true Avatar after a Fire Nation envoy to Yokoya had watched her bend all four elements and reported the new state of affairs, to celebrate the Festival of Szeto, hoping the occasion would settle some of the unrest at court. It did the opposite. Kyoshi mistook Chaejin for the Fire Lord, defied protocol by trying to dismiss him once her error was pointed out, and made Zoryu look weak by proposing to solve all his problems. The same night, Yun, now vengeful and false, raided the palace, held the gathered nobles hostage with earthbending and killed the loyal Chancellor Dairin and Lu Beifong. Many nobles were outraged, and some even wished for war against the Earth Kingdom, a notable sign of how quickly the court's anger could be turned outward.

North Chung-Ling and the purge

The tension between the Saowon and Keohso then broke into violence. The town of North Chung-Ling had become a frontier of their rivalry after Huazo bought several properties in Keohso territory, and when a message appeared in its melonyam fields championing Chaejin as Fire Lord, a crude scuffle broke out between the two clans' warriors. Kyoshi, assuming that Yun was working with the Saowon, kidnapped Huazo and Chaejin to make them confess, and found that they knew nothing. Zoryu, however, produced a double of Yun who confessed to conspiring in treason with the Saowon, and a purge of the clan began in the capital. The Fire Lord intended to kill every member of it, Chaejin and Huazo included. Kyoshi demanded clemency, and, after she killed the true Yun, Zoryu was intimidated into keeping his promise to her by the criminal Lao Ge.

Naming the war

Zoryu discussed the affair with his Chancellor Caoli, who suggested that it be called "The Camellia-Peony War". Zoryu liked the sound of it. It was pretty and poetic, and it was a war that, as he knew, he had managed to avoid. His real conclusion was less poetic. The war had shown, he decided, that the noble clans had too much power.

Zoryu's project and the end of the clans

Zoryu began what he intended to be a generational project: to break the strength of the noble clans, to make the Fire Nation's people loyal to the Fire Lord alone, and to have his descendants continue the work until the royal family ruled the country autocratically. The project had no single decree and no single battle. It was carried out in appointments, grants, marriages, taxes and the slow transfer of functions from the clans to the ministries, and it took about two centuries.

Methods

  • Selective favor. Zoryu promoted members of the loyal clans, but he took care to limit the Keohso's influence, and worked covertly to undermine it along with that of every other noble clan. The Keohso, who thought they had won, found that they had not greatly benefited from their victory.
  • The Fire Lord as judge. Common people who were unhappy with their clan's ruler began to look to the Fire Lord to resolve the situation, and the crown encouraged them to do so. A dispute that had been a private matter within a clan became a matter for the crown's officials.
  • Scrutiny of the Sages. Having supported Chaejin, the Sages were subject to new supervision by the government.
  • The Saowon as a lesson. The Saowon survived, but only just. Their lands were taken or reduced, and the clan struggled to survive in any capacity, as a visible warning of what the Fire Lord could do to a house that crossed him.

The clans' responses

Those who belonged to noble clans saw their families' influence slipping away, and had to adapt or fight the coming changes. Some clan leaders chose to become sycophants in the presence of the Fire Lord in order to maintain what little power they had, and others preferred to let their clans' power fade over degrading themselves by groveling before the throne. Both responses weakened the clans, and the first made them dependent on royal favor. The younger members of the great houses increasingly sought careers in the ministries, the army and the navy, where their loyalty was to the crown and not to the clan.

The new elites

By the reign of Fire Lord Taiso, the clans were still influential, but their might had been severely curtailed, and new elites were rising in their place: ministers who owed their posts to the Fire Lord, officers who were promoted on merit, merchants and industrialists who profited from the new economy and had no private armies. This was not a coincidence. The same years saw the Industrial Revolution, which replaced land with capital as the main source of wealth, and the families that had once drawn their strength from their estates found that the factories, the railways and the shipyards were beyond their control.

The last clash

The last real conflict between the crown and the clans occurred soon after Taiso's death, in the first years of his son Sozin's reign. The warring families, perhaps sensing that their last chance was passing, rose against the new Fire Lord, and General Oraso Eiko won a decisive victory in support of the government. After bringing the warring families to heel, Sozin was able to begin implementing policies to uplift his subjects, among them the poorest, and to strengthen the nation. The victory also had a darker consequence. With no internal power-brokers left to restrain him, the Fire Lord was able to act with impunity.

The effects of Zoryu's project were thus double. It ended the cycle of clan feuds and civil wars that had afflicted the nation for four thousand years, and it removed the only checks on the throne. A realm that had been strong and violent became strong and obedient, and the one remaining question was what its ruler would want.

A parallel in the Earth Kingdom

The subordination of the Fire Nation's nobility and Sages was part of a wider pattern. In the Earth Kingdom, the Earth Kings had in 66 BG massacred the sages who spoke out against them in the Night of Knives, abolished their order and taken the religious power for the crown. Both countries drew the same conclusion at about the same time: an independent priesthood was a rival to the throne. The Fire Nation's way was slower and less bloody, but its results were the same, and Sozin would later complete the task.

The changing balance of power (255–12 BG)

While the Fire Nation's government became stronger, the world around it shifted.

The fall of the Earth Kingdom's old order

In the Earth Kingdom, the southern lord Qin the Great had set out to reform the absolute authority of Ba Sing Se, with Kyoshi, the King of Omashu and the Lord of Yu Dao behind him. He was killed outside the walls of the city in 270 BG in a duel in which the Earth King cheated. His heirs claimed his realm as the Qin Dynasty, and the southern lands rose against them in the War of Liberation. In 255 BG the Qianchan Republic was recognized, and the Qin Dynasty collapsed in famine the same year. The Great Interregnum (255–230 BG) destroyed the continent's grain and administrative network and killed two to three million people. Ba Sing Se survived, and its garrison commander Bao Kun held the city and expanded outward.

The Fire Nation was a spectator, and a beneficiary. It had no part in the fighting, and its controlled trade profited from a continent whose disorders left its merchants and ministers with few rivals. The Earth Kingdom, once the world's dominant power, entered a long period in which it was corrupt, agrarian and incapable of reform. In about 215 BG its rulers founded the Dai Li to stop republican ideas from crossing the border with Qianchan.

Qianchan and the second industrial power

The new republic was a different kind of state. It had a system of representative government, a citizen-militia tradition and a belief in practical administration, and it industrialized quickly: coal engines appeared in Qianchan in 255 BG, and a repeating firearm in 130 BG. It would become the Fire Nation's rival in the technological race of the last decades before the war, and its existence meant that the Fire Nation's rise was never unchallenged. The two had opposite ideas of the relationship between the state and its citizens, and it is possible to read the later conflict as a contest between them, in which the republic's competence matched the empire's ambition.

The Water Tribes

The Water Tribes, meanwhile, remained poor and isolated. The South, left without a navy by its Platinum Affair isolation, was the main victim of the Fifth Nation, the confederation of pirates that had risen from the neglected coasts of the eastern sea and the southern Earth Kingdom (518–292 BG) and ravaged shipping for two centuries. The Fire Navy patrolled the Eastern Sea, with the Earth Kingdom's permission, after the pirate fleet was defeated in 296 BG, and so took, for the first time, a recognized role as a guardian of the world's sea lanes outside its home waters. This was a precedent that would later prove useful to Sozin.
