fire_nation_civil_war.title: Fire Nation Civil War
fire_nation_civil_war.html:
Also known as the Archipelago Civil War. Principal war 100–118 AG; Salvationist insurgency to 120 AG.

Date October 100 AG – 118 AG (Salvationist insurgency continued to 120 AG)
Location The Fire Nation archipelago and the Eastern Territories; the Western Air Temple island chain (Royalist supply and staging area)
Result Royalist victory. Azula killed by Zuko in a formal duel (118 AG). Zuko crowned Fire Lord. Imperial Court dissolved. The archipelago devastated. Salvationist remnants suppressed by 120 AG.
Belligerents Royalists (Restoration Government): Zuko; the Diet; about half the military; popular support. Foreign support: Qianchan Republic (supplies, via the south and the Western Air Temple island chain, which it occupied). Ozai loyalists (Court Government): Azula; the other half of the military; General Staff Directorate; Ministry of Truth; Flame Guard; fanatical cultists. Salvationists (Leftists): war veterans and radicals; a third party throughout, in control of most Court-side field armies from about 113 AG, and independent from 116 AG.
Commanders Royalists: Zuko; Iroh (killed by Salvationists, 101 AG). Ozai loyalists: Azula (killed by Zuko in a duel, 118 AG). Salvationists: Central Salvation Committee (members not identified in the sources).
Casualties Estimated 3.5 million dead (about 2% of the Empire's population), of whom about 2 million died in the fighting, about 1 million from famine and disease, and about 500,000 in massacres and reprisals; 7–10 million displaced. The 20 defining battles account for about 1.47 million of the dead. Together with the famine and warlord wars in the Earth Kingdom and the Yanakawan war, part of the Post-War Conflicts, the third most deadly war in history. All figures disputed.

The Fire Nation Civil War was an 18-year conflict that tore apart the Fire Nation archipelago after the death of Fire Lord Ozai in July 100 AG. It was more brutal than the ancient unification war, and was fought in cities and in the countryside with tanks, bombs and firebending. Three parties fought for power: the Royalists, loyal to Zuko; the Ozai loyalists, who wanted to restore the old order; and the Salvationists, who sought radical change. The Salvationists began as veterans' committees inside the Court's own army, took over most of its field formations in the middle years with the help of captured and prototype IRB weapons, and broke openly with the Court in 116 AG. The Royalists won, but the nation was devastated, and it took fifty years of Zuko's reign to rebuild it.

Background

The Empire had been polarizing since July 97 AG, when Ozai pardoned Rear Admiral Yueya and Captain Zhao of the Jasmine Island Mutiny and sent them to the Southern Water Tribe insurgency. The Diet and part of the military lost faith in the Fire Lord, and the opposition gathered around General Iroh, with bills for veterans, public provisions and the assimilation of the eastern colonies. See the Pardon Crisis of 97 AG.

Ozai was killed by the Avatar at Qinglan Port on 18 July 100 AG, in the middle of the Yanakawan War of Independence. The General Staff Directorate rigged the Privy Council's succession in favor of his daughter Azula by force over several days in late July, over the objection of the Diet, which had urged the confirmation of the popular Zuko. From then on both siblings claimed to be Fire Lord, Zuko with the backing of the Diet and the people, Azula with an equal right and the army; Ozai had planned to make Zuko the scapegoat while Azula terrorized the country, and his death at Qinglan ended that plan. Press outrage, and the Diet's confrontation with the military and the Court in August in which 31 people were killed, were the immediate trigger of the war. Details are in the article on the Battle of Qinglan Port.

The settlement that ended the Hundred Year War stripped the Fire Nation of all of its colonies, but some Imperial remnants rejected it and continued to fight, which overlapped with the first years of the civil war.

Parties

Party Composition Aims
Ozai loyalists About half the military; Azula; the General Staff Directorate; Ministry of Truth and Flame Guard; fanatical cultists who venerated Ozai as the Tentei Restoration of the old order under the Court
Royalists Zuko; Iroh; surviving members of the Diet; the other half of the military; the urban and rural population A restored throne under Zuko, with the Diet
Salvationists (Leftists) War veterans tired of the war, drawn heavily from the non-bender Kern infantry; radical movements Radical change of the political and social order

The military divided almost evenly between Azula and Zuko, unit by unit and often officer by officer, which produced a war without clear front lines in its early years.

Forces and equipment

Equipment was divided with the military. The IRB's 99 AG inventory gives the Empire's strength at the start of the war.[1]

Item Role Who held it in the war
Tessho-III armor, Type-3 Heiki rockets Standard infantry armor and anti-armor weapon All three parties
Breaker Mk II "Hagane no Oni" Power armor (about 60% of pre-Ba Sing Se strength by 99 AG) Court at first; many companies passed to the Salvationists from 109 AG
T-50 Koryuu, T-47 Tetsuzame, B-100 Ootori Fighters, fighter-bombers, strategic bombers The Court held most air bases; Salvationist units captured T-47 squadrons from 111 AG
Project Tetsuken systems (Kaen-Te gauntlet, Raijin lightning discharge, Kusari-Hi fire-chain) Systems that replicate firebending for non-benders Captured by the Salvationists in 109 AG; most of the veterans had served with the original Kern battalions
Ryuusei-B2 ballistic missile Prototype; 12 operational and 340 in production in 99 AG Captured by the Salvationists in 109 AG; first used in 113 AG
Qianchan QR-7 rifles, trucks, medical and anti-armor supplies Foreign aid The Royalists; some stocks captured by the Salvationists
Navy: 8 carriers, 94 submarines, Kaienha incendiary torpedoes Sea control Split by squadron in November 100 AG

Course of the war

Early stage (100–105 AG)

The first five years were marked by military defections and confusion. The Imperial Navy split by squadron in November 100 AG; garrisons changed sides by regiment, and units that had fought together fought each other. Regional Emergency Commands in the Eastern Territories acted as independent warlords. There were no clear boundaries, and the fighting consisted mostly of skirmishes and local feuds rather than campaigns. The first clashes were near the Shu Jing industrial center on 6 October 100 AG.

On 9 March 101 AG Iroh, the Royalists' Chief of Staff and a general who had been forced into retirement in 98 AG, was killed when a bomb exploded in the conference hall at Shu Jing where he was meeting delegates of two Regional Emergency Commands. Since joining Zuko in August 100 AG, Iroh had directed the Royalists' military organization and conducted the negotiations that brought defecting garrisons over to Zuko, travelling between commands that had split. He had also opened the first channel to the Qianchan military mission. The bomb killed him and ten others, including the senior officers of both delegations. Salvationist cells claimed the attack in a pamphlet, stating that Iroh, who had commanded the 96–97 AG siege of Ba Sing Se and been demoted for its failure, personified the war and the generals who would restore the army. The Royalists described the attack as an attempt to prevent negotiated defections. Zuko led the Royalists alone from that point.

The Royalists received international support from the beginning. Qianchan supplied Zuko's forces from the south and, in particular, through the Western Air Temple island chain, which Qianchan forces occupied, and which served as a transshipment point and staging area that the Court could not effectively interdict. The Yanakawan War of Independence, which ended on land in 105 AG (the Court's naval attempts on the coast continued until 110 AG), absorbed the remaining Imperial colonial forces during this period.

Middle stage (106–115 AG)

Most of the bloodshed took place in the middle stage. The lines hardened, and the Court and the Royalists fought set-piece battles in cities and in the countryside, using tanks, mechanized infantry, Breaker units, bombers and firebending. The Court held Caldera City and the western heartland, while the Royalists held Shu Jing's industry and relied on Qianchan supply. Millions died or were displaced during these ten years, and much of the archipelago's industry collapsed.

The middle stage was also when the Salvationists went from bombers and local committees to a major military force, by taking over the Court's army from within (see below), and by seizing the Court's prototype weapons. By 113 AG most of the Court's field army was under Salvationist committees, though it still fought in the Court's name.

Late stage (116–118 AG)

In 116 AG the Salvationists broke openly with the Court. They seized the western industrial belt from it, and then pushed outward against both of the other parties, seizing towns and supply lines. The Court and the Royalists were then fighting on two fronts, and the Court, deprived of most of its army, collapsed within two years.

The war ended in 118 AG with the death of Azula. With the Court's remaining forces broken, she made a last stand in the Imperial Palace. She blamed Zuko for everything that had befallen the Court and the Empire, and challenged him to a duel under the Fire Nation's tradition of the Way of the Warrior, which neither could refuse without dishonor. She said that it would end the matter once and for all, and that whoever lived would be the true inheritor of the lands. Zuko accepted. Azula broke the rules of the Agni Kai with lightning, which Zuko redirected, and he killed her in the duel on 9 May 118 AG, beheading her with a single stroke. See the Duel of the Palace. Royalist and most neutral sources treated the killing as consistent with the tradition, while Salvationist accounts condemned it. Zuko was crowned Fire Lord that year.

The Salvationist takeover of the Court side

The Salvationists were never a single organization. In 100 AG they were veterans' committees and radical cells in the Court's army and in the cities, with a following among the non-bender Kern infantry, who had borne most of the war's casualties. Their program was to end the war and to replace the system that had caused it, and they treated both Zuko and Azula as parts of it.

Takeover from within (107–113 AG). After the First Battle of Shu Jing in 107 AG, which destroyed much of the Court's strategic reserve, unpaid and ill-supplied units began forming "salvation committees" that displaced their officers or reduced them to figureheads. The pattern repeated after each Court defeat. In 111 AG the mutiny of the Court's Fourth Army at Tsurugi Bridge put about 60,000 troops under committee control. By 113 AG the Court's field army was largely Salvationist, but remained under the Court's flag, because the committees preferred to keep the Court's legitimacy and its supply system while the war lasted. The Court's own core was reduced to the Flame Guard, the Ministry of Truth and the cultists around Caldera City.

Captured and prototype weapons. The decisive step was the capture of the IRB's western complex in the Battle of the Ryuusei Facility (109 AG). The committees acquired the 12 operational Ryuusei-B2 ballistic missiles and the production line, and the Project Tetsuken systems. The Tetsuken gauntlets, lightning dischargers and fire-chain systems fit the Salvationist ideology, since they let non-benders match firebenders, and former Kern operators were trained to use them. The committees also acquired Breaker Mk II companies and T-47 squadrons from the units they controlled, and stocks of Qianchan rifles and trucks from captured Royalist convoys. They fielded all of it, though limited spare parts, trained operators and crystal supply kept the prototypes from being used in quantity. The Ryuusei missiles' 2,100-meter circular error made them useless against point targets, so they were used against city-scale targets, beginning with Shu Jing in 113 AG. The sect's later name, Thunderbolt, is traditionally linked to the Raijin discharge system.

The break (116 AG). The Salvationists declared themselves independent of the Court in 116 AG, when the Court's supply system collapsed and the committees no longer needed it. Their forces were by then the largest of the three on the Court side of the front, and the Court never recovered its field army.

Turning points

  1. The rigged succession and the Diet shooting (July–August 100 AG). These made a political crisis a military one and divided the army.
  2. The Navy split and the Western Air Temple chain (November 100 AG; 104 AG). The Royalists gained a sea lane, and Qianchan gained an occupied base from which to supply them. Without it the Royalists could not have survived the first five years.
  3. The death of Iroh (March 101 AG). It removed the Royalists' ablest organizer, made them dependent on Zuko alone and on Qianchan, and was the first major act of Salvationist violence.
  4. Iwakura Plain (110 AG). The Court's last major armored offensive was destroyed. After it, the Court could no longer take the strategic initiative.
  5. The Ryuusei Facility and the Tsurugi Bridge mutiny (109–111 AG). The Salvationists gained prototype weapons and most of the Court's army, which turned the war into a three-sided one.
  6. The Second Battle of Shu Jing (113 AG). The first use of ballistic missiles in the war, and the costliest city battle, which the Royalists survived with Qianchan-supplied air defenses and reinforcements.
  7. The Salvationist break (116 AG). The end of the two-sided war and the start of the Court's collapse.

Major battles

The war is conventionally defined by twenty battles. Names and dates follow the Royalist record; Court records use other designations. Casualty figures are estimated deaths.

# Battle Date Stage Outcome Est. killed
1 Clashes at Shu Jing Oct 100 – Jan 101 AG Early Royalists hold the industrial center 4,000
2 Phoenix Island Nov 100 AG Early Naval defectors give the Royalists the island complex 2,500
3 Hōryū Pass Mar – May 101 AG Early Court victory; the Royalists lose the pass and rail link 9,000
4 Kumo Straits Aug 102 AG Early Royalist and defector squadrons secure the southern sea lane 5,500
5 Seiryū Bay Mar – Jun 103 AG Early Court subdues the Eastern Regional Emergency Commands 11,000
6 Western Air Temple Landing 104 AG Early Qianchan holds the island chain; Court landing fails 3,000
7 First Shu Jing 107 AG Middle Royalists hold; the Court's strategic reserve destroyed 85,000
8 Ryuusei Facility 109 AG Middle Salvationist committees capture the IRB's western complex 14,000
9 Iwakura Plain 110 AG Middle Royalist victory in the war's largest tank battle 120,000
10 Tsurugi Bridge 111 AG Middle Court's Fourth Army mutinies and passes to the Salvationists 30,000
11 Siege of Hira 111–112 AG Middle Royalists take the Court port after a long siege 210,000
12 Second Shu Jing 113 AG Middle Royalists survive combined Court and Salvationist assault; first missile use 150,000
13 Kaien Straits 113 AG Middle Court submarines sink a Royalist convoy 14,000
14 Siege of Sakuragawa 114–115 AG Middle Royalists take the Court industrial city 190,000
15 The Black Rail 115 AG Middle Royalist offensive on Caldera is repulsed 95,000
16 Kuroshio Mills 116 AG Late Salvationists break with the Court and seize the western belt 60,000
17 Third Shu Jing 116–117 AG Late Royalists hold against attacks from both sides 110,000
18 Nagare River 117 AG Late Royalists defeat a Salvationist corps 75,000
19 Siege of Caldera 117–118 AG Late Three-sided siege; the Court's defenses collapse 260,000
20 The Palace 118 AG Late Azula's last stand; she blames Zuko, calls the duel, and is killed (9 May) 18,000

Selected battles

Clashes at Shu Jing (1, 100–101 AG). The first fighting of the war was a confused struggle between units of the same army over the industrial center's factories and rail yards. There were no front lines, and units changed sides in the middle of the fighting. The Royalists held the center and its industry, and it became their base.

Hōryū Pass (3, 101 AG). A Court offensive in the spring of 101 AG took the pass and cut the Royalist rail link to the south, in the weeks after Iroh's death. The Royalists were forced to rely on sea and Qianchan supply, which made the Navy split and the island chain decisive.

First Shu Jing (7, 107 AG). The Court's largest offensive of the early and middle war, with armor, Breaker companies and bombers, was stopped by the Royalists in the city's industrial districts. The Court's strategic reserve was destroyed, and the units that survived were the first to form salvation committees.

Ryuusei Facility (8, 109 AG). Committee-led units attacked the IRB's western complex from within, with defecting garrison troops, and captured it in a day of fighting. The facility's missiles, production line and Tetsuken program stock gave the Salvationists their weapons.

Iwakura Plain (9, 110 AG). The Court's last major armored offensive met the Royalists, with Qianchan anti-armor supplies, on open ground. The Court lost most of its armored strength and the Royalists gained the initiative, but at heavy cost.

Siege of Hira (11, 111–112 AG). The Royalists besieged the Court's main western port for eleven months. The garrison, now partly under Salvationist committees, ran out of food, and most of the dead were civilians.

Second Shu Jing (12, 113 AG). A combined assault by Court and Salvationist formations, with the first ballistic-missile strikes of the war, nearly took the city. The Royalists survived with Qianchan-supplied air defenses and reinforcements brought through the south. It was the war's costliest city battle.

Kuroshio Mills (16, 116 AG). The Salvationists declared their independence from the Court by seizing the western industrial belt, and turned the Court's own army against it.

Siege of Caldera (19, 117–118 AG). Royalist, Salvationist and Court forces fought across the capital for about nine months. Most of the dead were civilians, and the Court's defenses collapsed in the spring of 118 AG.

The Palace (20, 118 AG). Azula's last stand. After the collapse of the Court's defenses, she challenged her brother to a duel under the Way of the Warrior, and Zuko killed her in the Palace courtyard.

Casualties

The war killed an estimated 3.5 million people, about 2% of the Empire's population of about {{stat:pop_fn_100}}. It is the Fire Nation's part of the Post-War Conflicts (100–120 AG), which together are the third most deadly war in history, after the Hundred Year War and the Warring States wars. Most of the dead did not die in battle.

Cause Estimated dead
Fighting (including the 20 defining battles, which account for about 1,470,000) about 2,000,000 (about 1,300,000 military)
Famine and disease about 1,000,000
Massacres, purges and reprisals about 500,000
Total about 3,500,000

The war cut the islands' rice districts off from the cities, collapsed the rail net and the fuel supply, and was fought through the harvests, and both sides used scorched-earth tactics, which caused the famine deaths. The military dead were roughly split between the Court-side forces, including the Salvationist-led formations (about 55%), and the Royalists (about 45%). An estimated 7–10 million people were displaced. No authority tallied casualties, and the figures come from Qianchan archives and Royalist post-war surveys.

Aftermath

Zuko's reign (118–168 AG) began with a near-death experience: at his coronation an assassin in the crowd aimed a gun at his chest and was shot dead by a loyal guard before he could fire. It was not an isolated incident, and Zuko faced constant threats to his life and throne. The archipelago was in ruins, and he spent the next fifty years rebuilding it; the 140 AG economic recovery restored the Fire Nation to its prewar standing. Salvationist forces continued their insurgency until 120 AG, and some regional warlords, Fire Nation and Earth Kingdom alike, held out as stubbornly. In 169 AG a faction of the Salvationists broke away to form the Thunderbolt sect.

Historiography

The Royalists' account presents the war as the restoration of lawful government after a coup in the Privy Council. Court sources describe it as a defense of the Imperial order against traitors backed by a foreign power. Salvationist accounts present both as parts of the same system that caused the Hundred Year War, and describe the committees as the army's own revolt. Qianchan archives hold the most detailed record of foreign supply. Royalist propaganda later credited Zuko with the defeat of Ozai, which gave his claim legitimacy.

References

  1. Imperial Research Bureau, Consolidated Technology Status Report, 99 AG, Parts I–IV.

Royalist propaganda, continued by the state after 118 AG, credited Zuko with the defeat of Ozai, and the Avatar's part at Qinglan Port was played down in Fire Nation schools for decades.

yanakawan_war_of_independence.title: Yanakawan War of Independence
yanakawan_war_of_independence.html:
Also known as the War of the Twelve Battles (URN usage) and, in Imperial records, the Eastern Territories Rebellion. The war that produced the United Republic of Nations.

Date April 100 AG – 110 AG (land war to 28 April 105 AG; naval skirmishes 105–110 AG)
Location Yanakawa, the Earth Kingdom's western coastal province
Result Yanakawan independence. The Treaty of Qinglan (28 April 105 AG) was signed with the Fire Nation and the Earth Kingdom. The United Republic of Nations emerged. The Court faction's naval attempts failed by 110 AG.
Belligerents Yanakawan Liberation Front (YLF) and the Provisional Council, with the Earth Kingdom Reformed 2nd Army Corps and Qianchan surplus arms vs the Empire of Tajisaki: Regional Emergency Commands, and from 105 AG the Court faction under Azula
Commanders Yanakawa: Commander Lan Shuyi (YLF); the Provisional Council; Avatar Aang (Qinglan Port, later mediator); Lord Sokka (liaison, designer of the Republic's flag). Tajisaki: Governor-General Saitō Raizō (captured 18 July 100 AG); regional commanders; Azula (Court).
Casualties About 1,200,000 dead, mostly civilians and mostly from famine. All figures disputed.

The Yanakawan War of Independence was the war in which the Empire of Tajisaki's colonies in Yanakawa won their independence. It began as skirmishes in April 100 AG, became a full war after the Battle of Qinglan Port, and ended on land with the Treaty of Qinglan on 28 April 105 AG. The Court faction under Azula continued the war at sea until 110 AG, in naval skirmishes and landing attempts that never retook the coast. Twelve decisive battles gave the new state its symbol: the blue sun with twelve rays on the Republic's civil flag. The war killed about 1.2 million people and led to the United Republic of Nations.

Background

Yanakawa was the first province that the Empire took on the continent, in the ten-year campaign of 1–10 AG, and was the base of its Eastern Territories for ninety years. Its people were classified under the Imperial system of integration, and many were put to forced labor. In 98–99 AG the Diet's Eastern Colonies Assimilation Bill, which would have given them citizenship and representation, was shelved, and the moderates among the colonial leaders lost their argument. The rebellion began in April 100 AG, with raids on customs posts and depots. By June the raiders had joined as the Yanakawan Liberation Front.

Course

The first months (April–December 100 AG)

The YLF, with Earth Kingdom reformist units and Qianchan detachments operating under observer or volunteer status, took Qinglan Port after the Battle of Qinglan Port on 18 July, in which the Empire's forward Sōen array was captured and Fire Lord Ozai was killed. On 18 September the YLF formed a Provisional Council at the port. The Empire's Regional Emergency Commands, which had declared themselves independent of the capital, counter-attacked from the south and inland, and the war became a long struggle over the coast's ports and rail lines. The Earth Kingdom asserted its historic claim to the province. Qianchan gave the Provisional Council de facto recognition and supplied surplus weapons from the Hundred Year War.

The twelve decisive battles (100–105 AG)

# Battle Date Outcome
1 Qinglan Port 18 Jul 100 AG Port taken; the Sōen array captured
2 Lanxi Heights Oct 100 AG Counter-attack by Regional Commands repulsed
3 Relief of Yu Dao Mar 101 AG Garrison and city relieved
4 Hengli Crossing Aug 101 AG River line broken; the port of Hengli taken
5 Taigu Rising Jan 102 AG City rises, and the garrison surrenders
6 Shuangshan Ridge Oct 102 AG The ridge, an old site of Earth Kingdom losses, taken
7 Liangkou Apr 103 AG Gas stores captured and destroyed
8 Jinzhou Sep 103 – Feb 104 AG Provincial capital taken after a five-month siege
9 The Nine Bends Jun 104 AG Last Imperial defensive line broken
10 Seiran Bay Sep 104 AG Naval action; the Imperial squadron driven off
11 Anshan Dec 104 – Mar 105 AG Last Imperial stronghold falls
12 The Yuhe Landing Apr 105 AG Counter-landing defeated at the old Yu Dao beachhead

The Yanakawans fought with captured Imperial weapons, Qianchan surplus rifles and the Earth Kingdom corps' support, and the Regional Commands, which were warlords and not an army, fought each other as often as the rebels. Famine killed more people than the fighting did.

The Treaty of Qinglan (28 April 105 AG)

The war ended on land with the Treaty of Qinglan, which was signed with the Fire Nation and the Earth Kingdom. The Fire Nation agreed to withdraw from the province, and the Earth Kingdom recognized Yanakawa's independence. The Provisional Council became a council with representatives from each of the peoples of Yanakawa. The Court faction did not sign.

Naval skirmishes (105–110 AG)

Azula's Court, which still held much of the Imperial fleet, tried to retake the coast with naval raids and landing attempts until 110 AG. Yanakawa's coast guard and navy, which were built from captured Imperial ships and the Qianchan surplus, defeated them, and the attempts ended when the Court's fleet was committed to the civil war in the home islands.

Casualties

About 1.2 million people died in the war, about 1,000,000 of them civilians. Most of the dead were killed by famine, by the scorched-earth policy of the Regional Commands, and by massacres. The YLF and its allies lost about 150,000 fighters, and the Empire's forces about 50,000.

Aftermath

Yanakawa became the United Republic of Nations, whose council later gave way to a presidential system. Lord Sokka designed its first flag, a simple emblem for the army and protesters, and Avatar Aang helped the Republic rebuild. The Republic's charter, written in the shadow of the war, made the right to bear arms and the right to resist unamendable. Qianchan's surplus weapons became part of the Republic's founding story, and its relations with its neighbors rested on them for generations.

first_battle_of_agna_qela.title: First Battle of Agna Qel'a
first_battle_of_agna_qela.html:
Also known as the Week of Fire (Northern usage) and, in Imperial records, the Polar Operation (North). Part of the Subjugation of the Water Tribes.

Date 11–19 September 0 AG
Location Agna Qel'a and the northern ice shelf, North Pole
Result Northern defensive victory. The Imperial landing was repelled. The city was heavily damaged. The Empire established a forward base on the far eastern pole.
Belligerents Empire of Tajisaki: Northern Battlegroup, Polar Air Division. Northern Water Tribe: Agna Qel'a garrison, riflemen, waterbenders.
Strength Tajisaki: Northern Battlegroup of 38 warships (2 battleships, 9 cruisers, the rest escorts and 21 troop transports), about 24,000 landing troops, and a Polar Air Division of 46 zeppelins carrying about 180 early aircraft. Northern Water Tribe: about 28,000 trained riflemen and warriors, about 1,400 military waterbenders, and about 60,000 militia. No air force; navy already destroyed.
Casualties Tajisaki: approx. 9,000 killed, 11 zeppelins and 6 ships lost. Northern: approx. 52,000 killed, mostly civilians in the city. Both figures disputed.

The First Battle of Agna Qel'a was the Empire of Tajisaki's first attempt to take the Northern Water Tribe's capital. It took place a week after the assault on the Air Temples, when the Imperial Navy's Northern Battlegroup and a division of zeppelins attacked Agna Qel'a with bombs, shells and a new incendiary made specifically for use against ice. The Empire had overwhelming superiority in ships, aircraft, engineering and training. The Northern Water Tribe, which had a small, elite army equipped with bolt-action rifles and no navy or air force, defended the city with the environment and its waterbenders. The Imperial landing was thrown back after heavy losses. The Empire never tried again at the same scale. Instead it set up a forward air base on the far eastern pole and bombed Agna Qel'a periodically for the next hundred years, killing about 20% of the North's population by 40 AG.

Background

By 0 AG the Northern Water Tribe had been the stronger of the two Water Tribes for centuries, with a walled capital, a centralized government and a navy. The Empire had destroyed the combined Water Tribe fleets in the first weeks of the war and now controlled the sea approaches. Fire Lord Sozin's directive, issued before the war, was to subjugate the Water Tribes and work them to death, and he ordered the North taken a week after the assault on the Air Temples began. The comet had passed by then, so the Empire's firebenders no longer had its boost.

Forces

The Empire

The Empire had the largest industrial base in the world, with metal-hulled coal-powered warships, a precise and well-supplied army and the only air force. The Northern Battlegroup was assembled for the operation. The Polar Air Division consisted of 46 zeppelins, carrying bombs and flamethrower-equipped troops. For the operation, the Imperial Research Bureau (then a small department) had developed the Type 0 Hyōto ("ice-melter"), a thermite and napalm jelly with an adhesive base that stuck to ice and burned at very high temperatures. It was meant to cut trenches into the city's walls and melt the ice shelf under the defenders.

The Northern Water Tribe

The North had a small standing army of about 28,000, which was elite and well trained, and could conscript a militia of about 60,000. Its riflemen carried short bolt-action carbines, lubricated with seal oil and bone-handled so they would work at forty degrees below zero. About 1,400 waterbenders served in the military. The city sat on the ice shelf at the head of a fjord, behind walls and canals, and its defenders knew the ice, the weather and the sea.

The battle

Bombardment (11–12 September)

The Northern Battlegroup arrived in the fjord on 11 September and opened fire on the city. The zeppelins followed that night and dropped bombs and the Type 0 Hyōto. The incendiary burned through the outer wall in two places and melted large cisterns of ice, which flooded the lower streets. The first night killed about 11,000 people.

The defense (12–15 September)

The defenders adapted quickly. Waterbenders put out and froze the fires, drew the meltwater back into the walls and refroze the breaches within hours, and raised thick fog banks that blinded the zeppelins' bombsights. They threw up ice walls across the fjord and trapped several of the Imperial ships in ice. The cold hurt the Empire's machines: lubricants gelled, zeppelin gas cells and engines iced up, the napalm thickened and would not spread, and rifles jammed. Elite riflemen on the walls and on the ice shot at the gas cells of the zeppelins with incendiary ammunition. The hydrogen cells burned, and 11 airships were lost in four nights. Imperial bombing became inaccurate, as the zeppelins had to fly high above the fog.

The landing (16–18 September)

The Empire changed its plan and put 24,000 troops ashore on the ice shelf on 16 September, with flamethrowers and light guns. The defenders let the landing come inland, then cut the ice behind it with waterbenders and fought it on the shelf. Landing troops were cut off in groups, in blizzard and fog, and shot by riflemen on prepared positions. About 9,000 Imperial soldiers died, and the remainder were evacuated under cover of the fleet on 18 September, with the loss of six ships.

Withdrawal (19 September)

The Battlegroup withdrew on 19 September. Agna Qel'a was badly damaged, and about 52,000 people had been killed, mostly civilians in the lower city. The ice walls were refrozen within weeks.

Analysis

Historians give several reasons for the Imperial failure. The environment was the most important: the cold, storms, fog and ice neutralized the Empire's advantages in machines and precision, and the weapons designed against ice were hurt by the conditions they were designed for. Waterbending gave the defenders a way to repair the damage faster than the Empire could cause it. Logistics limited the Empire's ability to renew the attack, since the fleet and the troops were far from their bases. Coordination between the air division and the landing was poor. Finally, the Empire had underestimated the city's riflemen and the ability of a small, trained, well-equipped army to use ground and weather.

Aftermath

The Empire never again tried to take Agna Qel'a at this scale. It settled for a forward air base and forward operating base on the far eastern pole, and from there bombed the city periodically for the rest of the war. The Northern Water Tribe turned inward, and its population fell to about 80% of the pre-war number by 40 AG, mostly from the bombing. On 13 November 99 AG the Empire attacked it again by air and sea, and took it in December (the Second Battle of Agna Qel'a; see the Siege of the North).

See also

  • Subjugation of the Water Tribes
  • Air Nomad Genocide
  • Agna Qel'a
  • Siege of the North (99 AG), the Second Battle of Agna Qel'a

siege_of_ba_sing_se.title: Siege of Ba Sing Se
siege_of_ba_sing_se.html:
Also known as the Great Siege (Earth Kingdom), the Ba Sing Se Offensive (Imperial designation) and, in Qianchan archives, the Year of Streets. Part of the Hundred Year War.

Date 14 February 96 AG – 19 April 97 AG
Location Ba Sing Se, capital of the Earth Kingdom, and the approaches east of the Si Wong Desert (Hanxu, Babao)
Result Coalition victory. The Imperial armies breached the Outer Wall and Inner Wall, held the Palace and the Forbidden City for one week, and were driven out after a section of the Palace collapsed. Imperial withdrawal in April 97 AG.
Belligerents Empire of Tajisaki vs Earth Kingdom and Qianchan Republic
Commanders Tajisaki: Field Marshal Iroh (demoted to General after the siege); Lt. Col. Lu Ten (KIA, 25 November 96 AG); Fire Lord Azulon. Earth Kingdom: King Kuei; General Sung Yaowei. Qianchan: Lt. General Shen Yuwen.
Strength Tajisaki: approx. 1,000,000 committed over the siege, with Breaker Mk II companies, mechanized infantry and bomber fleets. Coalition: approx. 2,000,000, including civilian conscripts (Earth Kingdom approx. 1,750,000; Qianchan approx. 250,000).
Casualties Tajisaki: approx. 520,000 casualties; about 40% of Breaker Mk II strength lost. Coalition: approx. 1,300,000 military casualties (Earth Kingdom 1,200,000; Qianchan 100,000). Civilians: approx. 2.4–3.0 million dead (more than all military casualties combined), about half the pre-war population of the city's western section, including famine deaths during and after the siege. All figures disputed.

The Siege of Ba Sing Se was the Empire of Tajisaki's largest offensive of the Hundred Year War and its closest approach to taking the Earth Kingdom's capital. It lasted fourteen months, from February 96 to April 97 AG. Imperial bombers breached the Outer Wall in March 96, and the Imperial armies took much of the outer city and, in November, the Inner Wall and the Palace. They held the Palace and the surrounding Forbidden City for a week and pushed into the sublevels beneath it, until a charge detonated in the underground galleries and brought down one section of the Palace, killing Lu Ten, the Fire Lord's grandson and the most popular figure in the Imperial army. The Imperial troops that followed were more fanatical, and committed some of the war's worst atrocities. A Coalition counter-offensive and the collapse of the Imperial supply lines ended the offensive, and in December Fire Lord Azulon ordered the city razed and a fighting retreat, over the objection of General Iroh. The siege was the war's costliest single operation. It cost Iroh his son and his rank, and in the following months it led to the death of Azulon and the rise of Ozai.

Background

The Si Wong oil

The siege followed from the Si Wong Offensive (80–88 AG), which gave the Empire the Tongba oil basin. Oil production, about 140,000 barrels per day by 90 AG, paid for the late-war mechanization programs: mass production of the Breaker Mk II power armor, jet and bomber fleets, and armored and mechanized divisions.[1] The same planners who had designed Plan Yellow, with General Iroh as Planning Director, were the architects of the siege. Iroh was promoted to Field Marshal in 94 AG to lead it.

The Imperial plan

The Imperial General Staff Directorate wanted to end the war by taking the capital. The plan called for bombers to breach the walls, armor and Breaker units to enter through the breach and take the city ring by ring, and for the eastern flank, already secured in 95 AG, to hold the Coalition's armies apart. It assumed that the Earth Kingdom's fragmented command would fail under pressure, and that Qianchan's reserve would be tied down on the Omashu front.

The eastern flank (95 AG)

In 95 AG, a year before the siege, the Imperial eastern group took Hanxu and Babao, the road and rail junctions on the desert's eastern edge that linked the Earth Kingdom and Qianchan armies. It then reinforced the position by pushing toward Weidong and Shanhua. Shanhua is Qianchan territory, and the advance on it was limited: the General Staff Directorate had no plan to push south into Qianchan, and its priority was to hold the line and keep the Coalition's armies apart while the main force took the capital. The eastern line also carried the supply route from the Si Wong oil basin.

Lu Ten and the Diet

Lieutenant Colonel Lu Ten, Iroh's son and Azulon's grandson, was the most popular member of the Imperial family on the home front and in the colonies. He was known in the press as "the People's Prince" and was widely regarded as the next generation of the dynasty. He used that standing to press the Imperial Diet and Azulon directly for reforms: colonial representation in the Diet, civilian oversight of the General Staff, limits on conscription, and a negotiated end to the war once the capital was taken. These positions were vocal and public, and were considered radical in Imperial politics. They were opposed by Azulon's court and by the General Staff Directorate, and they deepened a political standoff between Azulon and Iroh, who was seen as Lu Ten's patron even though he rarely spoke publicly on the reforms. By 96 AG, Lu Ten commanded a Breaker battalion at the front, which made him a symbol of the war to the Imperial public as well as a political risk to the court.

The defense

The Earth Kingdom's defense was led by General Sung Yaowei, who organized earthbenders and non-benders into integrated units. These units could bring down buildings and use the city's terrain, and were particularly effective against Breaker units, which the IRB later admitted were vulnerable to heavy overhead collapse.[1] Qianchan, which is in effect the southern province that broke away from the Earth Kingdom in 255 BG, supplied munitions, demolition engineers and advisors from the start. It refused to commit combat troops to the city until the King had been evacuated, and it kept its whole air force on the Omashu front throughout. Its roughly 250,000 troops entered the city only after the evacuation of 17 November. The Coalition mined the sewers, the cellars and the underground galleries of the inner city so that they could be collapsed on Imperial troops.

Course of the siege

Leaflets and the air campaign (February–March 96 AG)

From the first day of the investment, on 14 February 96 AG, the Empire held complete air superiority over Ba Sing Se. The Earth Kingdom had no air force, and Qianchan's air force, the only one on the Coalition side, was committed to the Omashu front. Imperial jet fighters, which had been flying since 81 AG, controlled the sky and escorted turboprop bombers and fighter-bombers and the slower zeppelins, which flew over the city at will. In the first two weeks they dropped leaflets over all the rings of the city, urging the population and the garrison to surrender, and promising that those who did would be spared. Those who refused, the leaflets said, would face destruction. The Dai Li had kept the Hundred Year War from the people of the city for generations, and the leaflets could not be hidden: they fell in the streets and gardens, and in the Palace grounds.

King Kuei's eyes were opened in these first weeks. He read one of the leaflets, learned for the first time that his nation had been at war for ninety-six years, and demanded to know from the Grand Secretariat why he had not been told. The Council of Five, which met on 1 March, refused the Empire's demand, and Kuei, who for the first time sat in the council's debates, confirmed the refusal and put the city's defense in the hands of General Sung Yaowei.

When the deadline passed, the Imperial air arm carried out the threat. From March the zeppelins and aircraft dropped high explosives, incendiaries and chemical bombs across all the rings of the city, and not only on the walls and the garrison's positions. The bombs hit the dense residential districts of the Lower and Middle Rings hardest. Gas settled in cellars, courtyards and the narrow streets, where people sheltered, and the fires spread through wooden buildings. These raids killed civilians in large numbers, long before the first Imperial soldier entered the city.

Bombing and the breach (February–June 96 AG)

The Imperial investment of the city began on 14 February 96 AG. Around 20 March, Imperial heavy bombers dropped eleven Type-96 Kabeyaburi ("wall-breaker") bombs on the western and southwestern sections of the Outer Wall over three days. The Type-96 was a 10-tonne conventional penetrating bomb with a delay fuse that detonated inside the wall's earthen core. It was the largest conventional weapon in Imperial service, and each bomb was several orders of magnitude smaller in energy than the Sōen would be, but together they opened a breach about 1,200 meters wide. Imperial staff later regarded the Type-96 as the conventional forerunner of the Sōen's wall-breaking role. Imperial armor and mechanized infantry then went through the breach and, in the following months, took the Outer Ring and much of the Lower Ring. About half of the outer city's infrastructure was destroyed. Hundreds of thousands of civilians fled inward, and many more were trapped.

The push to the Inner Wall (July–October 96 AG)

By July 96 AG the Imperial armies were doing so well that Iroh ordered a push on the Inner Wall and the districts around it before the Coalition could re-form. The assault entered the Middle Ring, and civilians were drawn into the fighting. The offensive became a street-to-street battle in which Breaker units fought in narrow streets and in buildings, and Imperial infantry took heavy losses.

Close-quarters fighting in the Middle Ring followed a pattern. Imperial assault pioneers cleared buildings by "mouse-holing", blasting through party walls to move from house to house without entering the street, and then cleared each floor with flamethrowers, satchel charges and thermobaric hand charges, thrown in very large numbers into cellars, stairwells and tunnels, where the blast and the loss of oxygen were most lethal. Breaker companies led in the streets and were supported by infantry, but were vulnerable in the narrow lanes, where Coalition earthbenders brought down upper floors and façades on them. Coalition units in turn fought from the cellars and the sewers, and mined and collapsed the passages behind them as they fell back. Imperial forces also used chemical agents in the Middle Ring from the late summer of 96 AG, against positions that were still occupied by civilians. Civilians sheltering in the same cellars died in the same blasts and clouds, and the use of these weapons in residential areas was condemned after the war by Coalition, neutral and some Imperial sources. The fighting became a war of attrition in the rubble, block by block and cellar by cellar, with the sewers and ruined buildings changing hands daily.

Notable actions in this phase, as named in Imperial and Qianchan records, include the Battle of the Rail Terminal (August), in which a Breaker company lost nearly half its strength in a collapsed freight hall; the Granary Streets (September), a three-week fight over the Middle Ring's grain stores that the Imperial side won and the Coalition denied them by burning; and the Drum Yard (October), a series of attacks on a fortified block of workshops below the Inner Wall that served as the Coalition's main artillery position.

The Inner City and the Palace (November 96 AG)

On 17 November 96 AG, Imperial assault battalions, including Breaker companies, breached the Inner Wall, and on 18 November they captured the Palace. King Kuei had been evacuated on the first day of the assault, not to the shelters under the Upper Ring as the Imperial planners assumed, but to the eastern section of the city, where the Coalition's command had moved. This meant that the Imperial forces took the Palace without the King, and that the Coalition kept its government and most of its reserves intact on the far side of the city.

The Imperial forces held the Palace and the Forbidden City, the walled complex of courtyards, halls and administrative buildings around it, for one week. During that week they fought across the Forbidden City courtyard by courtyard, and Lu Ten's battalion, with engineers and infantry attached, pushed into the sublevels, the cellars, archives, guard galleries and passages that ran beneath the Palace and connected it to the Upper Ring. The fighting underground was close, in the dark, and at ranges of a few meters. Imperial troops used thermobaric charges and flamethrowers to clear the galleries, and Coalition units fought back with collapses, booby traps and counter-attacks from side passages.

On 25 November a large charge detonated in the galleries under the Palace's western wing, where Lu Ten had established his forward command post, and brought down one whole section of the Palace, the wing and the sublevels beneath it, on the Imperial troops inside. Lu Ten was killed with his staff and most of his battalion headquarters, along with several hundred soldiers. Imperial accounts attribute the charge to Coalition demolition engineers, who are said to have prepared it before the Palace fell. Coalition accounts credit it to Qianchan sappers and say that it was fired deliberately once the Imperial command post was identified. The question of who set it, and whether the Coalition had meant to sacrifice a section of the Palace, remains disputed. Over the following days, a counter-attack by civilian conscripts, with a small number of Zaofu-trained metalbenders attached to the Qianchan forces, drove the Imperial forces out of the rest of the Forbidden City, and by early December they were back at the Inner Wall.

After Lu Ten (November–December 96 AG)

Lu Ten's death had a strong effect on the Imperial troops. He had been popular in the ranks, and the news reached the front within a day. Over the following weeks, discipline in the assault units declined, and the units that fought on became more fanatical. Prisoners were shot, Coalition wounded were killed in captured aid stations, and shelters and cellars in the Upper Ring were burned or gassed without warning, with civilians inside. Several incidents in the Upper Ring and the northern Inner Ring were documented later by Qianchan and neutral observers, and some by Imperial military police, whose reports were suppressed. The Imperial Directorate treated the incidents as a result of the "intensity of operations", and Iroh issued orders against reprisals which were widely ignored. Historians disagree about how much control he and the senior commanders had at this point.

The fanatical assaults also gained ground. Between late November and mid-December, Imperial forces pushed through the northern Upper Ring and the districts along the Inner Wall's eastern face, and reached the edge of the eastern section, where Kuei and the Coalition command were. They were stopped there by the Coalition's reserves and by the collapse of the passes and bridges between the sections. The gain was the Imperial forces' last, and it could not be held without supplies.

The eastern line and the Ash Directive (December 96 – February 97 AG)

After the loss of the Palace, the Coalition tried to relieve the city by attacking the Imperial supply line where it passed through the eastern line. In December 96 AG a Qianchan-led force advancing from Shanhua struck Weidong, and by February 97 AG it had retaken Hanxu and Babao and cut the road and rail link to the Si Wong. This was the decisive blow to Imperial supply.

In the second half of December, as the supply situation became clear, the Imperial High Command, on Azulon's authority, issued the Ash Directive. It ordered the Imperial armies to raze the districts they held and the city's stores and infrastructure, and to withdraw by fighting retreat so that the Coalition would inherit a ruin. Iroh opposed the order in the High Command's sessions and in a written objection. The minutes of the Directorate record his argument in formal language: that razing the city would not shorten the war, would destroy the Empire's standing in the colonies and with neutral states, and would make a negotiated end impossible. Accounts from staff officers who attended give his language as much blunter, and the story that he told Azulon's envoy not to do it, in terms that could not be repeated in the Diet, was widely told in the ranks. Azulon overruled him.

Collapse and withdrawal (January–April 97 AG)

The siege was by then a stalemate in the ruins. Imperial supply lines, which ran from the Si Wong oil basin through the eastern line, began to fail in January 97 AG as the Coalition attacked them from the east and south. The Earth Kingdom's counter-attacks intensified, and the Imperial armies retreated from the city district by district. The Ash Directive was carried out only in part, because the units were short of fuel and explosives, because some commanders disobeyed it, and because the speed of the retreat did not allow it. It was carried out in full in the western section, the Lower Ring and the granary districts, where Imperial engineers burned the stores and demolished the water works and the rail yards. This worsened the famine. The last Imperial units left the outer districts on 19 April 97 AG.

Casualties

The siege's casualties were the highest of any operation in the war, and were far heavier on the Earth Kingdom side. Civilian deaths outnumbered Coalition military deaths by about four and a half to one, mostly from the air campaign, whose high explosives, incendiaries and chemical bombs fell across all the rings of the city and not only on its defenses. Imperial losses included about 40% of Breaker Mk II strength, which the IRB later put at 60% of its pre-siege level, and heavy losses in the bomber fleets.[1] The collapse under the Palace accounted for several hundred Imperial dead in a single event, including Lu Ten. Civilian deaths were the largest category: from combat, bombing, and Imperial chemical, thermobaric and incendiary weapons in the city, from the reprisals after Lu Ten's death, from the destruction carried out under the Ash Directive, and from the famine that began during the siege and continued after it. The Earth Kingdom's record does not give a figure. The civilian deaths were concentrated in the western section, which the Imperial breach opened first, where the fighting lasted longest, and where the razing of the retreat was most complete. About half of that section's pre-war population, an estimated 2.4–3.0 million people, died, which is more than the military casualties of both sides together.

Aftermath

Iroh. After the siege General Iroh was demoted from Field Marshal to General. The formal reason was the failure of the offensive and the loss of the supply line. The political reason was widely understood to be different. Azulon blamed Iroh for the failure, for the death of Lu Ten and the reform movement that had formed around him, and for the public opposition to the Ash Directive, and the demotion came at a time when the Fire Lord and his heir were already in a standoff. It had the opposite effect to the one intended. The troops, who had learned of Iroh's argument against razing the city and who had seen him lose his son at the front, and the public at home and in the colonies, who had loved Lu Ten, turned in favor of Iroh. He was more popular after the demotion than he had been before the siege. Iroh remained a general until he was forced to retire in 98 AG (see the Pardon Crisis of 97 AG), and later joined his nephew Zuko in the civil war.

Lu Ten. Lu Ten's funeral in the capital was the largest of the war, and drew crowds in the colonies as well. The Diet reformers lost their leader, but the cause did not die with him. His proposals, which Azulon's court had treated as radical, were taken up again by colonial delegates in the following years, and the memory of "the People's Prince" remained a political force that the court was unable to suppress. The atrocities committed by the troops who fought on after his death were later cited by the Imperial public as a betrayal of what he had stood for.

Azulon and Ozai. On the night of 10 June 97 AG, Fire Lord Azulon was poisoned at his dinner, went to bed, and died in his sleep. The Court physicians identified poison, and the Ministry of Imperial Order announced that Qianchan agents had infiltrated the palace kitchens. A steward and two cooks were executed, and Qianchan's denial was dismissed. The poisoning was in fact arranged by his younger son, Ozai, who had presented himself during the siege as the war's firmest advocate and used Azulon's break with Iroh as his opening. Ozai took the throne days later, and Iroh, demoted and in mourning, did not contest it. Ozai's authorship was established only after the civil war, from palace records seized by the Royalists. As Fire Lord, Ozai radically escalated the war effort.

Imperial reforms. The Empire reformed its doctrine in 96–99 AG: expanded mechanized warfare, jet aircraft programs, a centralized military command, and intensified ideological indoctrination.

Earth Kingdom. The city was devastated, and the collapsed section of the Palace was left as a ruin. The siege famine, which began when the Imperial armies cut the plains approaches in 96 AG and was made worse by the destruction of the city's stores in the retreat, continued after the siege and through 99 AG, because the ruined city and the surrounding plains could not feed their population. King Kuei attempted military reform and centralization, but met resistance from established institutions, which culminated in the Dai Li coup attempt of 98 AG. The walls were about 60% rebuilt by December 99 AG and repairs continued into 100 AG, and the depopulated western districts were resettled with refugees. The rebuilt western sections were destroyed again in the Sōen strike of 17 July 100 AG.

Historiography

Imperial records present the siege as a nearly decisive operation that failed because of supply, and tend to give the loss at the Palace as the work of Coalition sappers, and to leave out the Ash Directive or to attribute it to the High Command as a whole. Earth Kingdom authorized histories present it as a victory of the city's population, and give no casualty figures. Qianchan archives document the Imperial use of chemical and thermobaric weapons, the atrocities after 25 November, and the Hanxu–Babao fighting in the most detail. Iroh's opposition to the Ash Directive is known mainly from staff memoirs and from the Directorate's minutes, which were opened after the civil war.

References

  1. Imperial Research Bureau, Consolidated Technology Status Report, 99 AG, Parts I, III–IV.

siege_of_the_north.title: Siege of the North
siege_of_the_north.html:
Also known as the Second Battle of Agna Qel'a, the Fall of Agna Qel'a and, in Northern usage, the Long Night. Imperial designation: the Northern Operation. Part of the Hundred Year War.

Date 13 November – 19 December 99 AG (occupation of the North: December 99 AG – September 100 AG)
Location Agna Qel'a and the northern ice shelf, North Pole
Result Tajisaki victory. Agna Qel'a fell. The Chief and most of the Council fled. The Empire occupied the North until after the death of Fire Lord Ozai.
Belligerents Empire of Tajisaki vs Northern Water Tribe
Commanders Tajisaki: Rear Admiral Mori Takeshi (Northern Fleet); Air Commander Ishida Ren; Colonel Daigo Kenji (Special Landing Force). Northern Water Tribe: the Chief and the Council of Elders (evacuated 18 December); Marshal of the Walls (killed in the last defense).
Strength Tajisaki: Northern Fleet of 96 ships (3 carriers, 9 icebreakers, 40 transports); an air group of about 180 jets (T-50 Koryuu and T-47 Tetsuzame) and 60 B-100 Ootori bombers; a Special Landing Force of about 9,000 elite winter troops in Arctic Breaker armor, with about 4,000 flamethrower specialists, and 24,000 line infantry following. Northern Water Tribe: about 22,000 riflemen, about 900 military waterbenders, about 60,000 militia; no navy or air force. About 1,600,000 people in the city (1,200,000 residents and about 400,000 refugees).
Casualties Tajisaki: approx. 14,000 killed. Northern: approx. 800,000 killed in the siege, about half the people in the city, and about fifteen times the toll of the First Battle of Agna Qel'a; mostly civilians. Occupation deaths below. All figures disputed.

The Siege of the North was the Empire of Tajisaki's successful attack on Agna Qel'a, the capital of the Northern Water Tribe, between 13 November and 19 December 99 AG, as part of a combined operation against both poles. It was the Empire's second attempt, after the failure of the First Battle of Agna Qel'a in 0 AG, and it was fought as a massacre. The Empire used jet aircraft carrying chemical, napalm and ice-specific incendiary bombs, a fleet of icebreakers, and a landing force of elite winter troops, many of them veterans of the Southern Pole, in a new cold-weather power armor, with flamethrowers firing napalm. The Northern Water Tribe's defenders were elite waterbenders and riflemen with bolt-action rifles, who had won in 0 AG with the weather and the ice and could not do so again. Both sides fought without mercy. About 800,000 people died in five weeks, in a city that held about 1.6 million. The Avatar did not intervene. Agna Qel'a fell on 19 December, the Chief and the Council fled by submarine, and the Empire occupied the North.

Background

After the failure of 0 AG, the Empire built a forward air and operating base on the far eastern pole and bombed Agna Qel'a from it for the rest of the century. The Northern Water Tribe turned inward. It had no navy, kept its small elite army, and lost about 20% of its people to the bombing by 40 AG. Meanwhile the Empire occupied the South, where it perfected a system of forced labor, reprisals and terror, and fought the Southern uprising of 99 AG. On 13 November 99 AG the Empire launched a combined operation against both poles at once. Its aim, planned by Sozin long before, was to eradicate the Water Tribes so that no new Avatar could rise from them, and to scorch both poles clear for a new Fire Nation colony. The siege of Agna Qel'a was the northern half. The southern half was the final assault on the Southern Uprising, and the siege was under way while the Avatar was found in the South.

Forces

The Empire

The Northern Fleet included icebreakers that could cut the ice boom the Northern waterbenders raised across the fjord. The air group consisted of jets that flew above or through the weather and were not vulnerable to riflemen, with heavy bombers. They carried bombs, chemical munitions, napalm, and the Type 9 Hyōto, an improved ice-melting incendiary developed from the one used in 0 AG. Over the five weeks the Empire dropped or fired about 21,000 tonnes of munitions on the city, of which about 5,500 tonnes were chemical agent (mustard and phosgene mixtures, and a persistent blister agent that stayed in the ice) and about 3,800 tonnes were napalm and Type 9 incendiary.

The Special Landing Force was made up of elite winter and Arctic troops: the 1st Arctic Assault Division, whose soldiers called themselves the "Ice Demons," the Winter Warfare Brigade, and the Southern Veterans Brigade, which was made up of battalions of the Southern Garrison with experience of the Southern Pole. These veterans had taken the glacier tunnels at Taluqqriaq and the ice towns of the South, and had brought the methods with them: bombardment of the ice above the defenders, armored troops sent into tunnels, napalm in confined spaces. The troops wore the Arctic Breaker (Mk II-N), a cold-weather version of the Breaker Mk II power armor: a bulky riveted frame with hydraulic legs, heated joints and a fixed visor, resistant to rifle fire and cold, with an integral flamethrower. They carried Type-4 assault rifles. About 4,000 flamethrower specialists went in with the assault companies, carrying backpack flamethrowers with napalm, and these were used extensively for clearing buildings and tunnels.

The Northern Water Tribe

The North's army was small and elite, equipped with bolt-action rifles and incendiary ammunition. Its waterbenders were its best weapon, and its defenses were the ice walls, canals, fog and the fjord. All of these had worked in 0 AG. The city had about 1.2 million residents, and about 400,000 more had come in from the countryside during the bombing. Most took shelter in the ice cellars and tunnels under the city, which turned out to be traps.

The siege

Air offensive (13 November – 3 December)

The jets attacked on 13 November and kept up the bombing for three weeks. They flew too fast and too high for the riflemen, and their incendiaries were designed for ice. The Type 9 burned through the outer wall and into the lower city, and the chemical munitions, which waterbenders could not freeze or put out, forced the defenders from the walls and killed people in the shelters, where the heavier gases settled in the cellars. Napalm fires burned through whole districts, and the meltwater refroze into sheets of ice that trapped people. Pathfinder aircraft dropped flares and marker bombs that penetrated the fog. The defenders could raise the weather but could not hide from bombers that did not need to see. About 380,000 people died in the three weeks, mostly in the shelters and the burning districts.

Naval phase (4–12 December)

The icebreakers cut the ice boom on 8 December, and the fleet shelled the city, and the refugee camps on the ice. The waterbenders trapped several ships in ice floes, as they had in 0 AG, but the icebreakers freed them, and the fleet landed troops on 12 December. About 120,000 people died in the shelling.

The landing and the street fighting (12–18 December)

The Special Landing Force came ashore in Arctic Breakers. The defenders' tactic of letting a landing come inland and cutting the ice behind it failed because the Breakers could walk through meltwater and cross the gaps, and because jets strafed the waterbenders who tried to cut it. Rifle bullets did not penetrate the armor. The waterbenders' strongest attacks, which froze the joints, slowed a few of the suits but not the heated ones. The troops fought through the city's gates and canals, clearing the houses and the ice cellars with flamethrowers and napalm, and with their assault rifles at a much higher rate of fire than the defenders. Civilians who would not leave the cellars were burned out or gassed. Those who surrendered were often shot.

The Northern defenders fought just as hard, and took no more prisoners. Waterbenders collapsed the ice streets onto columns, flooded and froze the canals around advancing companies, and froze captured soldiers where they stood. Riflemen picked off the flamethrower crews, whom they regarded as the worst of the attackers, and the Imperial troops who were captured with flamethrowers were not taken alive. Surrendering Imperial columns were ambushed. Both sides committed atrocities, and the Empire's greatly exceeded those of the North in number. About 220,000 people died in the five days of fighting in the streets and cellars.

The fall (18–19 December)

On the night of 18 December most of the Northern leaders, including the Chief, the Council of Elders and about 2,000 others, were evacuated from the western fjord by Qianchan submarines, with a few Northern vessels. The Marshal of the Walls and the rearguard held the city's center for another day. On 19 December the last defenders were overwhelmed, and about 80,000 people were killed in the final assault. The Imperial flag was raised over Agna Qel'a.

The massacre in numbers

Phase Dates Northern dead
Air offensive 13 Nov – 3 Dec about 380,000
Naval phase 4–12 Dec about 120,000
Landing and street fighting 12–18 Dec about 220,000
Final assault 18–19 Dec about 80,000
Total about 800,000

The 800,000 dead were about two thirds of the city's 1.2 million residents, or half the 1.6 million people in the city at the time, counting the refugees. It was among the worst single-city massacres of the war, after the siege of Ba Sing Se. The Empire lost about 14,000 dead, most of them in the street fighting.

The occupation of the North (December 99 – September 100 AG)

The Empire put the North under an Imperial Northern Administration. It applied the methods it had learned in the South: a governor, a collaborationist council, registers of waterbenders and workers, hostage-taking, collective punishment, and forced labor. It also used the new technology it had taken to the North: persistent chemical agents to deny the ice settlements to the population, incendiaries to burn shelters, and air patrols to hunt people on the ice. Waterbenders were hunted, imprisoned or conscripted. The population, which had stood at about 80% of its pre-war number, fell to about 50% by the end of June 100 AG, a few weeks before the death of Ozai. This was about 1,080,000 deaths in six months, from the siege (about 800,000), reprisals and massacres (about 110,000), forced labor and exposure (about 60,000), famine and disease (about 40,000), and deportation and conscription (about 70,000 missing). The Empire's policy, which it applied in both poles, was to scorch the earth: villages, hunting grounds, ice settlements and fishing fleets were destroyed to clear the land for a new Fire Nation colony. An Imperial statistical report dated 17 July 100 AG, the day before Ozai's death, which archivists found after the war, recorded about 1,080,000 Northern dead or missing since 13 November, of whom about 800,000 had died in the siege itself. The Southern figures, compiled separately, ran to several hundred thousand.

After the death of Ozai on 18 July 100 AG, the northern garrisons lost contact with Caldera, and most withdrew or surrendered by September.

Analysis

The Empire won in 99 AG because it had changed. In 0 AG it had relied on zeppelins that the weather defeated, napalm that gelled in the cold, and a landing force of ordinary troops. In 99 AG its jets flew above the weather, its weapons were tested on ice and on people in the South, its armor was proof against rifles, and its troops, many of them veterans of the Southern Pole, had assault rifles and flamethrowers. The Northern Water Tribe, which had no navy or air force and had not modernized, had the same weapons as in 0 AG. Its victory in 0 AG had depended on the environment, and the Empire had learned to counter that. The city's ice cellars, which were its shelters, were the places where most of the people died. The Chief's decision to flee saved the Council and the government, but it left the population to the massacre and the occupation.

Historiography

Imperial accounts give about 100,000 civilian deaths and call the operation a clearing of an armed city. Northern accounts give about 800,000 or more, and describe the siege as the Long Night. Qianchan archives, which include the submarine commanders' reports and photographs of the city, are the most detailed outside record. Both the Imperial statistical report of 17 July 100 AG and the Northern survivors' registers support a figure of about 800,000.

See also

  • First Battle of Agna Qel'a
  • Subjugation of the Water Tribes
  • Southern Uprising (99 AG)
  • Agna Qel'a

soen_strike.title: Sōen strike on Ba Sing Se
soen_strike.html:
The discharge of the forward Sōen array at Qinglan Port on 17 July 100 AG.

Date 17 July 100 AG, 11:40
Fired by Fire Lord Ozai, from Qinglan Port
Target The western Outer Wall and Inner Wall of Ba Sing Se
Dead About 380,000 dead or missing (casualties 300,000–450,000)

The Sōen strike was the first and only discharge of the Sōen. It came without warning, as Earth Kingdom intelligence had not established the array's range. A single white beam, at wide width, atomized the western Outer Wall and everything within about 700 meters, destroyed the Inner Wall and set a firestorm across the districts behind it. Burns reached about 10 kilometers, and people looking toward the flash up to 20 kilometers away were blinded. There was no lasting radiation.

The strike disorganized both armies. In Ba Sing Se, the garrison headquarters in the Inner Ring was destroyed and the command was lost for about 36 hours. The Imperial Western Army Group reorganized first, and advanced on the city that evening, but Ozai's death the next day threw the advance off.

It was the weapon's first full-scale test, and the purpose for which the Sōen Program had been built.

See also

  • Sōen Program
  • Battle of Qinglan Port
