  • Ozai

battle_of_qinglan_port.title: Battle of Qinglan Port
battle_of_qinglan_port.html:
Also known as the Battle of Seiran Harbor (Imperial designation), the Death of the Tentei, and in resistance sources the Silence at Qinglan. Part of the Yanakawan War of Independence.

Date 18 July 100 AG (12:00–19:00), the day after the Sōen strike on Ba Sing Se
Location Qinglan Port (Imperial: Seiran Harbor), Yanakawa (the archipelago and mainland later forming the United Republic of Nations)
Result Allied victory. Forward Sōen array captured and disabled. Death of Fire Lord Ozai. Collapse of Imperial command at Qinglan Port. Onset of the Tajisaki succession crisis.
Belligerents Empire of Tajisaki: Imperial Flame Guard; Ministry of Truth detachment; Breaker Mk II companies; mechanized infantry; IRB Sōen Battery Detachment. Allied forces: Yanakawan Liberation Front (YLF); Earth Kingdom Reformed 2nd Army Corps; Qianchan Republic detachments (3rd Highland Rifle Brigade, Zaofu Iron Guard Detachment).
Commanders Allied: Avatar Aang; Commander Lan Shuyi (YLF); General Fan Dongsheng (Earth Kingdom); Major General Mei Hualan (Qianchan). Tajisaki: Fire Lord and Tentei Ozai (KIA); Governor-General Saitō Raizō (captured); General Nagase Kōji.
Strength Tajisaki: approx. 16,000 (elite, mechanized and Breaker formations, including 14 Breaker Mk II units). Allied: approx. 29,000 (YLF 22,000; Earth Kingdom 4,500; Qianchan 2,500) and the Avatar. No air units took part on either side.
Casualties Battle only (excluding the Ba Sing Se strike): Tajisaki: approx. 3,600 killed, 2,400 captured. Allied: approx. 4,300 killed (YLF 3,300; Earth Kingdom 600; Qianchan 400). Civilians: approx. 6,500 killed or missing. All figures disputed.

The Battle of Qinglan Port was a seven-hour engagement on 18 July 100 AG between elite Imperial formations and an allied force of Yanakawan guerrilla units with Earth Kingdom and Qianchan detachments. It took place one day after the Empire fired the Sōen from a forward array at the port against the Earth Kingdom capital, Ba Sing Se, which was devastated. The scale of the destruction was the reason for the allied attack. Fire Lord Ozai, who had come to the port to oversee the Sōen and had proclaimed himself Tentei (天帝, "Emperor of the Sky") the previous day, was caught off guard by the opening allied bombardment. He was killed by the Avatar, Aang, 23 minutes after the first shells fell, in front of the assembled garrison and attackers. The death was announced on the Imperial high command radio network four minutes later and was heard across the Tajisaki homelands within the hour. It accelerated the Yanakawan War of Independence, which had begun in April, and set off the succession crisis that led to the Fire Nation Civil War.

Background

The Empire and the comet

By 99 AG the Empire of Tajisaki was a totalitarian war state under Ozai, who had taken the throne after the death of Azulon in 97 AG, a poisoning the Court blamed on Qianchan agents and Ozai had in fact arranged. Under the Imperial Constitution, loyalty to the Fire Lord was "the first law, the last law," his authority was without limit, and only he could end a declared emergency (Arts. 1, 46).[1] The Imperial Research Bureau (IRB) had spent decades on the project that became the Sōen, which began as an attempt to harness the destructive power of the comet itself and to build a nuclear weapon on the scale of the comet's destruction. The Empire wanted a weapon of mass destruction for one purpose, the strike on Ba Sing Se. The result was a fire-crystal capacitor array that stores firebending energy and releases it as a directed beam. Charged during the passage of the hundred-year comet, which amplifies firebending output by an estimated factor of five to eight, the main array was projected to store about 9.4 kt-equivalent.[2]

Imperial politics, 97–100 AG

Ozai's reign was marked by polarization. In July 97 AG he pardoned Rear Admiral Yueya and Captain Zhao, who had been convicted of the Jasmine Island Mutiny, and posted them to the Southern Water Tribe insurgency. The Diet and a part of the military lost faith in the Fire Lord, and the opposition gathered around General Iroh. The Diet's bills for veterans' benefits and public provisions passed in 98–99 AG, but the Eastern Colonies Assimilation Bill, which would have given the people of Yanakawa citizenship and representation, was shelved. See the Pardon Crisis of 97 AG.

Yanakawa under Imperial rule

The Yanakawan archipelago and mainland, the province where Fire Lord Sozin had begun his comet-assisted invasion a century earlier, were administered by the Empire as part of the Eastern Territories. Under the Colonial Administration provisions of the Imperial Constitution, local peoples were classified by degree of integration. Laborers not yet integrated could not be issued weapons, and colonial administrators held combined executive, legislative and judicial power, with the authority to request military support without Cabinet approval (Arts. 42–43).[1]

The Yanakawan Rebellion (April–July 100 AG)

In April 100 AG a series of small skirmishes between local irregulars and Imperial garrisons broke out along the coast, beginning with raids on customs posts and supply depots. By June these groups had merged into the Yanakawan Liberation Front (YLF), the successor to the Coastal Resistance Council founded in 97 AG. From May, Earth Kingdom reformist units and Qianchan detachments operated alongside the YLF under "observer" and "volunteer" status. Qianchan, which had been at war with the Empire since 30 AG but had no declared forces in Yanakawa, officially denied any deployment there.

The forward array

In 99–100 AG the IRB completed a forward Sōen array at Qinglan Port, within range of Ba Sing Se. In 99 AG the IRB's report convinced Ozai that the Sōen could break Ba Sing Se, and in December 99 he told his General Staff that a new offensive against the city would begin within the year. The IRB scientists who proposed a fission weapon in 99 AG, and then refused to develop it, were executed, and the Sōen program, the comet-charged array that was the product of the decades-long search for a comet-scale weapon and served as the Empire's nuclear project, went ahead under other staff. The strike on Ba Sing Se was its first full-scale test, and the purpose for which it had been built. Ozai arrived at the port on 16 July. Some Imperial accounts describe his visit as the start of a "comet offensive." The Imperial record shows he came to oversee the discharge, and the Flame Guard present was a security detachment.

Sōen strike on Ba Sing Se (17 July)

Release

The strike came without warning. Earth Kingdom intelligence had not established the range of the forward array, and no alert was issued in Ba Sing Se. By 11:00 on 17 July the IRB's director had reported the array at full charge, and Ozai and about forty members of his staff assembled on the control terrace. At 11:40 Ozai personally supplied the firebending input that released the array. The discharge was a single white beam, configured at wide width and aimed at the western sector of the Earth Kingdom capital. At noon Ozai proclaimed himself Tentei from the terrace.

Effects

Survivors, Earth Kingdom officials and later Qianchan investigators described effects comparable to a nuclear explosion, though the Sōen produced no lasting radiation. The approximate zones, as reconstructed after the event, were:

  • Impact zone (about 700 meters). The western sector of the Outer Wall, then about 60% rebuilt after the 96–97 siege, and everything around it were atomized. Outlines of people and objects remained on surviving stone.
  • Inner zone (to about 3 kilometers). Severe burns, total collapse of buildings, and the destruction of the Inner Wall. Fires combined into a firestorm across the districts behind the wall.
  • Outer zone (to about 10 kilometers). Burns to exposed skin, blast injuries and widespread collapse.
  • Flash zone. Anyone looking toward the flash at long range suffered temporary or permanent blindness. Thousands were blinded at distances of more than 20 kilometers.

The western sector of the Outer Wall had been breached once before, in March 96 AG, with conventional heavy bombs; the Sōen's effect was of a different order. The IRB had projected about 280,000 casualties for a wide-beam strike on the city.[2] In the days that followed, the killed, wounded and missing, civilian and military, were estimated at several hundred thousand (the commonly cited range is 300,000–450,000), and deaths could not be reliably separated from the missing.

Effect on the armies

The strike disorganized both armies. In Ba Sing Se, the Earth Kingdom garrison headquarters in the Inner Ring was destroyed, communications were cut, and central command was lost for about 36 hours. On the Imperial side, forward elements of the Western Army Group, which had been staged to exploit a breach but briefed on a much smaller effect, were also thrown into disorder, and some units that advanced early into the edge of the damaged zone suffered flash and burn casualties. Imperial command was the first to recover. The Western Army Group was reorganized within hours and began advancing on the city that evening.

The strike led Qianchan, already at war with the Empire, to commit regular units to the response. The array required recharging, and the IRB estimated a second discharge in five to six days. The allied commands in Yanakawa decided that night to attack Qinglan Port.

The battle

Allied bombardment and assault (12:00–12:23)

At 12:00 on 18 July the allied artillery, mostly YLF mortars and captured Imperial guns with Earth Kingdom and Qianchan batteries, opened fire on the port. The shells fell on the control terrace, the quays and the Imperial barracks in the first minutes. The Imperial garrison, organized for a ground attack from the north, was caught off guard, and Ozai was on the terrace with his staff. The Flame Guard escorted him toward the inner harbor, where a vessel was ready, either to move him to a safer position or to evacuate him. Accounts differ, and the escort commander, who was killed, left no record.

The YLF's Qinglan Harbor Brigade and Lanxi Militia attacked from the west, and the Earth Kingdom Reformed 2nd Army Corps and the Qianchan 3rd Highland Rifle Brigade attacked from the north. The Zaofu Iron Guard Detachment, fielding Tiejia-III power armor, led the attack on the Imperial armor line. The port's defense rested on elite formations: Breaker Mk II units, mechanized infantry and Flame Guard, with no air support. The Earth Kingdom 1st Highland Earthbender Regiment brought down tenement buildings onto the Breakers, which the IRB later admitted were vulnerable to heavy overhead collapse.[2] Seven were lost within the first twenty minutes.

The Avatar State (12:09–12:23)

At about 12:09 the Avatar entered the port with the allied vanguard and went into the Avatar State. Witnesses described his eyes and tattoos glowing white. Over the next fourteen minutes he went through the port's warehouses, knocking out their walls with earth and air and hunting for Ozai across the quays. Imperial soldiers in his path or in the buildings he brought down were killed, many of them by collapsing masonry and not by intent; the Imperial record counts at least 150 dead. By most accounts he moved "like a beast," without regard for either side's fire.

Death of Ozai (12:23)

At 12:23, 23 minutes after the first shells fell, Aang reached the inner-harbor quay, where Ozai's escort had stopped at the foot of the pier. The quay was full of Imperial soldiers and allied troops who had come up behind the Avatar. Ozai fired at him, and the Avatar State was not stopped. A lance of stone broke up through the quay beneath Ozai and went through his chest under the ribs, piercing both lungs. He died within a minute, drowning in his own blood, according to the nearest witnesses. There was no speech and no ceremony.

A silence fell across the quay. It lasted less than a minute by most accounts, and the resistance record uses the name "the Silence" for it. Then Flame Guard and soldiers nearby opened fire on Aang, and were killed in the next seconds by the Avatar State. Some soldiers on the quay ran. Others dropped their weapons and surrendered on the spot. Aang left the Avatar State a few minutes later and collapsed, and he was carried from the quay. He was unconscious for two days.

Broadcast (12:27)

At 12:27 a signals officer at the Imperial field headquarters transmitted over the high command network: "The Emperor is dead." The officer's identity is not recorded. The message was repeated by the Governor-General's staff, relayed to the General Staff Directorate in Caldera City by 12:46, and was on civilian shortwave by 13:16. State radio was taken off the air at 13:08 on the order of the Ministry of National Enlightenment, but amateur and foreign relays, including Qianchan's, continued to carry it.

Collapse and infighting on the field (12:23–19:00)

The fighting did not end with Ozai's death, and it divided Imperial forces by how committed they were:

  • Fanatical formations. The Flame Guard, Ministry of Truth personnel and the remaining Breaker Mk II crews fell back on the Governor's Citadel and fought until 19:00. Several commanders and officers took their own lives.
  • Stubborn career officers. Some refused to credit the broadcast and held their sectors until the evening, and in several places fired on subordinates who tried to surrender.
  • Opportunists. Other officers used the confusion to withdraw with their units, vehicles and stores toward the ports and to seize ships, preserving their commands for what came next. Some of these later became Regional Emergency Commands.
  • Surrenders. Most professional mechanized infantry, garrison conscripts and local auxiliaries stopped fighting within the hour. Several thousand surrendered to allied units, and many more deserted into the city.
  • Unintegrated colonial laborers. Laborers who had never been issued weapons took them from unattended armories, and in some districts turned on their overseers.

The Imperial position was also divided against itself. Armed clashes took place between Flame Guard and army units at the Citadel gate and on the roads to the harbor. Governor-General Saitō was captured at the Citadel at 19:00, when the last organized resistance ended. IRB demolition teams disabled the forward array before the Citadel fell, and allied technical staff captured part of the crystal stock.

Aftermath

18–25 July 100 AG: the succession

On 18 July the General Staff Directorate ordered all commands to hold their positions. Contact with colonial headquarters was lost within days. On 19 July the Ministry of National Enlightenment announced that the Tentei was "wounded in battle and recovering." The announcement was retracted on 20 July and national mourning was declared.

Under Art. 3 of the Imperial Constitution, a successor designated by the reigning Fire Lord is final; if none was designated, the Privy Council must meet within 72 hours and the claimant must produce fire at a confirmation ceremony within seven days. The Diet has no role in succession, which is reserved to the Imperial prerogative (Art. 25).[1] Nevertheless, on 22 July the Diet's House of Representatives passed a resolution urging the Privy Council to confirm Zuko, who was in the home islands and widely popular, and large demonstrations in Caldera City supported the resolution.

The Privy Council convened on 21 July. The General Staff Directorate produced a sealed designation naming Azula, and troops took control of the chamber. Between 23 and 25 July seven Privy Councillors were arrested, and clashes between soldiers, Ministry of Truth units and demonstrators left approximately 210 dead in Caldera City. A confirmation ceremony was held on 25 July, at which Azula produced fire. The result was certified by the remaining Council.

26 July–August: the Diet confrontation

Newspapers and civilian radio reported the arrests and killings faster than the Ministry of National Enlightenment could close them, and public outrage grew through the end of July. On 2 August the Diet convened in defiance of the Court and declared the confirmation unlawful. Flame Guard and General Staff units surrounded the chamber. On 4 August shooting broke out in the public galleries and 31 people were killed. The Diet was dissolved by Imperial Rescript on 8 August, and many of its members fled. Zuko left Caldera City on 5 August and was joined by his uncle Iroh.

Ba Sing Se: famine and the Imperial advance

The devastation of the western districts destroyed granaries and food distribution and displaced a large part of the city's population. From August a second famine developed in Ba Sing Se, only a few years after the siege famine of 96–99 AG, and was worsened by refugees from the surrounding plains. Tens of thousands more people died of hunger and disease by the end of the year, though no authoritative count exists.

The Imperial Western Army Group, reorganized after the strike, advanced on the disorganized Earth Kingdom defenders from the evening of 17 July and made rapid gains. The death of Ozai the next day threw the advance off. Commanders divided over loyalty to the Court or the Diet, orders from Caldera contradicted one another, and several formations withdrew without orders. The supply lines, stretched across the contested plains, then collapsed, repeating the pattern of the 96–97 AG siege. By mid-August the advance had stalled, and the infighting ended any chance of renewing it.

The Eastern Territories

Regional governors and army group commanders in the Eastern Territories had been invoking martial law (Art. 49) since April.[1] After 18 July they imposed news blackouts, continuing to issue orders "in the name of the Tentei" for several weeks. When the truth leaked they declared themselves Regional Emergency Commands, answering to neither Caldera nor the Diet. By December at least four such commands held ports and garrisons across the Eastern Territories, and they continued to fight the Yanakawan rebels.

The Yanakawan War of Independence

The Yanakawan rebellion, which had started as skirmishes in April, became a full war after 18 July. YLF forces held Qinglan Port and the surrounding coast, while Regional Emergency Commands counterattacked inland and from the south. On 18 September the YLF formed a Provisional Council at Qinglan Port and claimed sovereignty over Yanakawa. The Earth Kingdom reasserted its historic claim to the region. The Qianchan Ministry of Foreign Affairs recognized the Provisional Council's de facto authority and withheld formal recognition, consistent with its long-standing policy of not exporting governance. The war continued until 105 AG, and from 105 to 110 AG it went on as naval skirmishes and landing attempts by the Court faction under Azula, which never retook the coast. It is regarded as one of the causes of the emergence of the United Republic of Nations as a state.

The Fire Nation Civil War

After the Diet's dissolution the Fire Nation split into parties that became the three sides of the Fire Nation Civil War (100–118 AG):

Party Basis Seat
Ozai loyalists (Court Government) Azula; about half the military; General Staff Directorate; Ministry of Truth; Flame Guard; fanatical cultists Caldera City
Royalists (Restoration Government) Zuko and Iroh; surviving Diet members; the other half of the military; popular support Shu Jing
Leftists (Salvationists) War veterans and radicals tired of the war; active as cells from late 100 AG Local councils

The Restoration Government was proclaimed at Shu Jing on 14 September. The first armed clashes between the two main parties took place near the Shu Jing industrial center on 6 October, and by the end of the month both sides had declared the other illegitimate. In November the Imperial Navy split by squadron, and Phoenix Island's military complex changed hands. Iroh was killed in a Salvationist bomb attack in March 101 AG, and Azula was killed by Zuko in a formal duel in 118 AG. See the main article for the later course of the war.

External reaction

Ba Sing Se declared a period of mourning, began repairing its walls, and struggled to manage the famine. Earth Kingdom commands launched limited offensives against the Imperial western garrisons in October, which stalled by November. Qianchan's decision to respond to the strike led to its deployment of regular units into Yanakawa from August. The IRB had assessed that a Qianchan strike capability could be fielded within two to three months of a Sōen strike on Ba Sing Se.[2] No such weapon had been used by the end of 100 AG.

Strategic weapons

The main Sōen array at the Caldera Coastal Battery Complex remained under Court Government control and was not discharged during 100 AG.

Historiography

Three accounts of the battle circulate and diverge in the usual way:

  • The Court Government describes the Tentei as "fallen at the moment of ascension" and Aang as an assassin, and demands the Avatar's surrender.
  • Royalist and later Fire Nation state histories credit Zuko with the defeat of Ozai. This was propaganda, and the Avatar's part at Qinglan Port was played down in Fire Nation schools for decades.
  • The Yanakawan Provisional Council describes the death as the execution of a tyrant before the people he oppressed.
  • The Earth Kingdom's official record gave no casualty or famine figures for the strike.
  • Qianchan intercepts and archives give the most reliable timeline, including the 12:27 broadcast, and are cited by most outside scholarship.

All accounts agree on the Silence and on the shock of the death, which in later retellings was made more orderly than it was.

References

  1. Imperial Constitution of the Empire of Tajisaki, Arts. 1, 3, 25, 42–43, 46–50.
  2. Imperial Research Bureau, Consolidated Technology Status Report, 99 AG, Parts IV–V.

siege_of_caldera.title: Siege of Caldera
siege_of_caldera.html:
The three-sided siege of the Fire Nation capital, 117–118 AG.

Date 117 AG – spring 118 AG
Location Caldera City
Result The Court's defenses collapsed. It ended with the Duel of the Palace on 9 May 118 AG.
Dead About 260,000, mostly civilians

The Siege of Caldera was the last great battle of the Fire Nation Civil War. Royalist, Salvationist and Court forces fought across the capital for about nine months. The Salvationists, who had broken with the Court in 116 AG, closed on the city from the west, and the Royalists took the outer city. The Court's defenses collapsed in the spring of 118 AG, and Azula was left in the Palace district with the Flame Guard, remnants of the Ministry of Truth and the cultists. She challenged Zuko to the Duel of the Palace.

duel_of_the_palace.title: Duel of the Palace
duel_of_the_palace.html:
Also known as the Last Stand of Caldera and, in Royalist usage, the Reckoning. The final engagement of the Fire Nation Civil War.

Date 9 May 118 AG
Location Main courtyard of the Imperial Palace, Caldera City
Result Zuko kills Azula in an Agni Kai to the death under the Way of the Warrior, after she breaks its rules with lightning. The Court Government ends.
Combatants Zuko (Royalists) vs Azula (Court Government)
Witnesses Royalist commanders, the surviving Flame Guard, members of the Diet, and Qianchan observers

The Duel of the Palace was the single combat that ended the Fire Nation Civil War. It took place on 9 May 118 AG in the main courtyard of the Imperial Palace in Caldera City, after the collapse of the Court's defenses in the Siege of Caldera. Azula, the last holder of the Court's throne, blamed her brother Zuko for everything that had befallen the Court and the Empire and called a traditional Agni Kai to the death under the Way of the Warrior. She declared that it would end the matter once and for all, and that whoever lived would be the true inheritor of the lands. Zuko accepted. In the course of the duel Azula broke its rules by using lightning, which Zuko redirected. Zuko then beheaded her with a single stroke of his sword. The Court's remaining forces surrendered the same day, and Zuko was crowned Fire Lord later in 118 AG.

Background

By spring 118 AG the Court Government had been reduced to the Palace district of Caldera City. Most of its field army had passed to the Salvationists in 111–113 AG and had broken with it in 116 AG, and the Court's defenses in the capital gave way in the months after the siege began in 117 AG. Royalist forces held the outer city, and the Salvationists were closing from the west. Azula, who had held the Court's title since the rigged succession of July 100 AG, was left with the Flame Guard, remnants of the Ministry of Truth and the cultists who revered her father.

The Way of the Warrior is the Fire Nation's tradition of honor in combat. Under it, a challenge to a formal duel cannot be refused without dishonor, and the result decides the quarrel. Neither Azula's nor Zuko's supporters disputed that it applied.

The challenge

On 7 May 118 AG, Azula sent a herald under truce to the Royalist command with a challenge. In it she charged Zuko with responsibility for the war and its ruin: for the Diet's defiance in 100 AG, for the division of the army, for the Court's fall, and for the loss of her father's empire. She wrote that the quarrel between them was the only one left to settle, that it should be ended once and for all, and that whoever lived would be the true inheritor of the lands. She asked that her forces and his stand down while it was fought.

Zuko's advisers, including several Diet members, urged him to refuse and to take the Palace by assault, since the Court was nearly beaten. He accepted the next day. He said afterwards that the war had been fought in the name of the throne, and that the throne's holder should answer for it. Royalist officers and later accounts also note that the Salvationists were nearing the city, and that a delay would have given them the Palace.

The duel

The Agni Kai was fought on the morning of 9 May in the Palace's main courtyard, with both sides' forces drawn up at the edges under truce. Qianchan observers and Diet members were admitted as witnesses. Under the old rules of a duel to the death, the fighting is done with firebending only, and each duelist carries a sword for the final stroke. It lasted about twenty minutes, according to the most common account. Witnesses report that before the fight began the two traded insults across the courtyard, Azula raving and talking to people who were not there, and Zuko calm.

Witnesses describe Azula as fighting without restraint and Zuko as giving ground. Several accounts record that the two traded insults throughout, and that she asked him to finish it after the lightning failed. Late in the fight she drew and fired lightning, which the rules do not permit, and which is held to be a sign that a duelist has stopped believing she can win. Zuko, who had been taught the technique by Iroh, redirected it into the Palace's north wall, and was burned in doing so. Azula stood still for a moment. Zuko closed in a flash and beheaded her with a single stroke of his sword, so quickly that those nearest did not see it. By the old rules a duelist who cheats forfeits an honorable death. The courtyard was silent for some time afterwards. Azula's remaining officers stood down, and Court forces in the Palace district surrendered during the day.

Aftermath

Zuko was crowned Fire Lord later in 118 AG. At the coronation an assassin in the crowd aimed a gun at his chest and was shot dead by a loyal guard before he could fire. His reign (118–168 AG) is conventionally dated from the duel. Salvationist forces continued their insurgency until 120 AG.

Historiography

Royalist and most neutral sources treat the killing as lawful and consistent with the Way of the Warrior, and as the only possible end to a war in which the Court would not yield. They point out that Azula chose a duel because it let her die with her honor, and gave her a chance of killing her brother, and that she forfeited the honor by breaking the rules. Court survivors deny that she used lightning. Salvationist accounts condemn it as a family quarrel settled at the cost of millions of lives. Court survivors remember Azula as a martyr, and her challenge is quoted as her final act of defiance. Zuko rarely spoke publicly of the duel.

the_devastation.title: The Devastation (Jasmine Island Mutiny)
the_devastation.html:
Also known as the Jasmine Island Mutiny (Imperial legal designation) and the Night of the New Moon (island usage). Part of the Hundred Year War, western island chain.

Date Night of 7 June 90 AG, the New Moon Celebration (approx. 2100 to 0900 the following day)
Location Jasmine Island, western island chain, Empire of Tajisaki
Result Mutiny suppressed. Rear Admiral Yueya and Captain Zhao arrested by Army and loyal Navy personnel, and sent to the mainland for court-martial. Heavy civilian losses and destruction on the island.
Belligerents Loyal Imperial forces: Jasmine Island garrison ("the protectors"), Army detachment, Navy personnel who refused Yueya's orders, including the imprisoned crew of the battlecruiser. Mutineers: Rear Admiral Yueya's loyalists
Commanders Loyal: Lt. Akataa (garrison, acting commander); Captain Lu Ten (Army liaison); the battlecruiser's captain and executive officer. Mutineers: Rear Admiral Yueya; Captain Zhao
Strength Garrison: approx. 300, about half on leave for the celebration. Army detachment: one company. Squadron: approx. 1,900 personnel, of whom approx. 250 followed Yueya. One battlecruiser (outside the harbor) and two destroyers.
Casualties Garrison: 41 killed. Army detachment: 9 killed. Loyal sailors: 31 killed. Mutineers: approx. 100 killed. Civilians: an estimated 1,900–2,400 killed and 4,500 injured. About 80% of the island's fields and half of its main settlement destroyed. All figures disputed.

The Devastation was the destruction of the harbor town and farmland of Jasmine Island, an Imperial possession in the western island chain, by the loyalists of Rear Admiral Yueya of the Imperial Navy on the night of 7 June 90 AG, the island's New Moon Celebration. It was a mutiny. The island had been part of the Empire for decades and had never rebelled. Yueya, who had petitioned for the garrison command and been refused, took her squadron into the harbor in the absence of the garrison's colonel, declared the island in rebellion, and destroyed it. The killing did not stop at any point in the night: it grew as Yueya seized the squadron's battlecruiser and turned its guns on the hillside where the refugees had gathered. It was stopped by the island's own garrison, led by a junior officer, with the help of Army troops under Captain Lu Ten and Navy sailors who refused to follow her. Those sailors, who had been locked in the battlecruiser's brig, blew their way out and fought to the ship's bridge. Yueya's troops surrendered to Lu Ten at dawn, and she was arrested and sent to the mainland. The event led to her court-martial and, afterwards, to Lu Ten's Address on Conduct.

Background

Jasmine Island

Jasmine Island is a small island with a population of about 25,000, known for its tea and its golden jasmine. It was governed by a three-member island council under Imperial supervision and defended by a garrison of Army troops, mostly recruited locally, who were known as the protectors. The garrison's commander was an Army colonel. The island had no history of resistance, and during the war its main contribution to the Empire was tea. In 90 AG the island's economy was in decline because of the war's effect on shipping.

Yueya's petition

Rear Admiral Yueya commanded a Navy squadron in the western islands. She claimed descent from a man who had been humiliated in an attack on the island in the third century BG, and her family had carried the shame of it for centuries. In early 90 AG she petitioned the Admiralty and the War Council to be made garrison commander of Jasmine Island, which would have given her military authority over it.

The petition was denied. The garrison command was an Army post, the colonel in post had reported no difficulties, and the Directorate saw no operational reason to move it. The refusal was administrative and not personal. Officers who served with her later said that she took it as an insult, that she spoke of the island constantly afterwards, and that she began to prepare a plan to take it by force.

The plan

Yueya told the War Council that the island was a potential base for enemy agents and requested a force to "secure" it, which would be one battlecruiser, two destroyers and some troops. The Council, which believed that it was agreeing to a reinforcement of the garrison, approved. Yueya's real plan was to destroy the island and to describe it afterwards as a suppressed rebellion, in the expectation that her superiors would sanction the result after the fact. She timed it for the New Moon Celebration, when the town would be crowded and a part of the garrison on leave, and for a day when the garrison's colonel was away from the town, on a scheduled visit to the tea estates in the island's interior.

An Army company was embarked with the squadron, as is usual in reinforcement operations. Captain Lu Ten of the Armored Corps, then serving as an Army liaison officer, accompanied it. Yueya briefed him that the island's council had been infiltrated, that the garrison might be compromised, and that the celebration was a cover for an uprising. Lu Ten doubted the account and asked to lead the Army company ashore with the first assault, in order to see for himself.

Course of events

Approach and the first attack (2100–0030)

The squadron arrived at dusk and anchored off the harbor. At about 2100, Yueya transferred her flag from the battlecruiser to a destroyer, so as to command the harbor action herself, and left the battlecruiser under its captain outside the harbor mouth. The captain was told that the ship's main guns would be used only on her order.

At about 2330, Captain Zhao, Yueya's second-in-command, landed with a team of elite firebenders in launches, and placed explosive charges in the market square, under the Monument to Peace. At about midnight the charges were fired. The monument fell onto the council chambers and on the homes of the council members beside the square. Two of the island's three councillors, Shio-Ming and Kai, were killed. The blast and the collapse also killed a large part of the celebration crowd in the square. Yueya's landing parties then spread out through the town and the fields, setting fire to buildings and crops, and shooting at people who tried to put out the fires.

The garrison (0000–0100)

The garrison's commander was out of town, and about half of the garrison was on leave in the crowd. The senior officer present was Lieutenant Akataa, a young officer from the island who had been left in charge for the day. Akataa had a few dozen men in the barracks. He gathered them, organized a response, and sent a group to find the surviving councillor, Yuming, and her son Caishen, and to get them out of the square. The garrison fought in the streets with the rifles and light weapons it had, protected civilians, and was driven back. No one in the garrison knew what was happening beyond the fact that Imperial naval troops were attacking.

Lu Ten meets Akataa (approx. 0100)

Lu Ten had landed with his Army company in the second wave. By about 0100 he had found no rebels and a burning town. At about that hour, near the fish market, his squad met a group of the garrison, Akataa, Aiko, Basalt, Siku and Fu Meili, who had taken a position in a warehouse. The two groups nearly fired on each other. Akataa, who had seen the council chambers collapse, asked who had ordered the attack. Lu Ten told him that the order had come from the Rear Admiral, that he had been briefed on a rebellion, and that he could see no sign of one. Akataa showed him the dead in the square and the garrison's wounded. Lu Ten said that he would go back to Yueya and demand an end to the attack. He warned Akataa that she might not stop.

Lu Ten and Yueya (approx. 0130–0200)

Lu Ten went back to the harbor and confronted Yueya on the quay beside her destroyer. She told him that the rebels were hiding among the civilians. He asked where they were. She did not answer. He told her that he would report to the Western Command by radio if she did not stop, and that the garrison, whose commander would return in the morning, would not take the order to stand down from a Navy officer. Yueya refused to halt. At about 0150 Lu Ten sent his report from the Army company's radio, and Yueya, who learned of it, ordered the attack widened and sent for the battlecruiser's guns.

The battlecruiser (0200–0430)

The battlecruiser's captain, who had learned that no rebellion existed, refused to bring the ship's guns to bear. Yueya sent her flag lieutenant and a party of loyalist marines to the ship. They arrested the captain, the executive officer and about 60 officers and sailors who backed them, and locked them in the brig on the lowest deck. The loyalists then fired the secondary battery on the market district, and at about 0300 the main guns, in two salvos, on the hillside where the refugees had gathered. The shelling lasted until about 0430 and was the greatest single cause of civilian deaths after the explosion in the market square.

On the shore the killing grew through the same hours. Landing parties went through the town street by street and burned the farms in the lower valley, where many farmers were trapped. The garrison, which had lost its commander's authority and a part of its men, held the area around the barracks and the hospital, and Lu Ten's Army company, which had dropped any pretense of taking Yueya's orders, covered the evacuation of the wounded. Navy medical staff from the second destroyer, who had been instructed by their own captain to help, went ashore, and Lu Ten set up an aid station. Yuming took charge of the emergency response. The island's magistrate, Jin Bo, tried to organize the evacuation of the island's library and archive, and the innkeeper Saya took refugees to her inn in the interior.

The brig (approx. 0430–0520)

The imprisoned sailors had listened to the shelling through the hull for two hours. At about 0430, the damage-control ratings among them, using the demolition charges that the brig's compartment shared with the ship's flooding-control stores, blew the brig's door and the bulkhead behind it. About 60 sailors, armed with the loyalist guards' rifles, fought their way up three decks, compartment by compartment, to the bridge. The firefight inside the ship lasted about 50 minutes. They took the bridge at about 0520, at a cost of 31 killed. About 40 loyalists were killed. The battlecruiser's executive officer took command in place of the captain, who had been wounded, and ordered the guns to cease fire and secured the main battery. A signal was sent to the garrison and to the Western Command.

The harbor (approx. 0500–0630)

With the battlecruiser's guns silent, the island's response was prepared. Akataa's garrison, with the Army detachment and a group of sailors who had refused to follow Yueya, took the pier and the harbor boom. The captain of the second destroyer, who had stood down earlier, moved his ship across the harbor mouth, so that Yueya's ship could not leave. The garrison's two coastal guns, which Akataa had manned during the night, hit the destroyer's forward gun mount and steering, and she could not move. Zhao's landing party, cut off in the market area, fell back to the quay and was surrounded there by the garrison and the sailors. The destroyer was boxed in, and by about 0630 she had stopped firing.

Surrender and arrest (0630–0900)

Lu Ten walked onto the quay, with his company behind him, and called on the mutineers to lay down their arms. He did it as an Imperial officer acting under the law against mutiny, and he told them that the Rear Admiral had no authority for what she had done and that those who stopped would be treated as men who had obeyed an unlawful order. The loyalists, who had been fighting for hours against their own comrades, surrendered to him, and Zhao, who was on the quay, surrendered with them. Yueya remained on the destroyer's bridge for some time. She was arrested there by Lu Ten, with the Army detachment and officers of the Navy who had refused to follow her, including the executive officer of the battlecruiser and the captain of the second destroyer.

The garrison's colonel returned to the town at about 0900 and assumed command. Yueya and Zhao were held in the garrison's stockade, and were sent to the mainland under guard the following day, on the second destroyer, with the battlecruiser as escort.

Casualties and damage

Civilians were the largest group of casualties, an estimated 1,900–2,400 killed. The explosion in the market square and the collapse of the council chambers killed an estimated 150–200 people at once. The shelling of the market district and the hillside, mostly by the battlecruiser's main guns, killed about 600. The rest died during the fires, from shooting in the streets, and in the burning of the farms. Fire destroyed about half of the main settlement and about 80% of the island's fields. The garrison lost 41 killed, the Army detachment nine, the loyal sailors 31, and the mutineers about 100. The island's recovery took years.

Aftermath

Yueya and Zhao were court-martialed in the summer of 90 AG. Yueya was convicted of exceeding her orders, deceiving the War Council and the unlawful killing of Imperial subjects, and sentenced to imprisonment. Zhao was convicted on lesser charges and reduced in rank. In July 97 AG, a few days after his coronation, Fire Lord Ozai pardoned both, restored their ranks, and sent them to the south to help suppress the Southern Water Tribe insurgency, which was then a low-level conflict of small-scale skirmishes. The Diet and a part of the military regarded this as a mockery of the court-martial, and Ozai answered that the Empire should concentrate on the insurgency and bury the past (see Pardon Crisis of 97 AG). The sailors of the battlecruiser who had broken out of the brig were commended, and its captain and executive officer were decorated. Jasmine Island was placed under a civilian administrator, and the Directorate granted reconstruction aid. After the trial, Lu Ten submitted the Address on Conduct to Fire Lord Azulon and the Imperial Diet. Lt. Akataa was commended and promoted.

The pardon (97 AG)

After his coronation in 97 AG, Fire Lord Ozai pardoned Yueya and Zhao and sent them to the South Pole, where an insurgency was under way, to pacify it. Lu Ten had been killed the year before, in the siege of Ba Sing Se. The pardon was widely read as a repudiation of the Address on Conduct, since it gave an officer convicted of the unlawful killing of Imperial subjects a command in occupied territory, which was the kind of abuse the Address had warned against.

Historiography

Imperial Navy accounts describe the event as an excess of zeal by one officer, put the number of civilian deaths lower, and do not mention the brig. Army and island records give higher figures, and emphasize the role of the garrison. The sequence of the night, and in particular the shelling and the brig breakout, are known mainly from the court-martial transcripts and from the accounts of Lu Ten, Akataa and the Navy officers and sailors who stood with them.

major_battles.title: Major Battles and Sieges of the Hundred Year War, 0–79 AG
major_battles.html:
The principal battles and sieges of the early war, the Eastern Push and the Desert War, before the Si Wong Offensive. Figures are estimated deaths (Earth Kingdom or other allied dead / Tajisaki dead) and are disputed.

Period 0 AG – 79 AG
Phases covered Early Land War (0–30 AG); Eastern Push (30–50 AG); Desert War (50–79 AG)
Entries 27

The war's first eighty years were fought in three phases. In the Early Land War (0–30 AG) the Empire of Tajisaki occupied the Air Temple chains and the whole west coast, pushed north into the mountains, and cut the southern Omashu front off from the rest of the Earth Kingdom. In the Eastern Push (30–50 AG) it took the western grasslands and reached the Si Wong Desert. In the Desert War (50–79 AG) it tried four times to take the oil fields and was thrown off each time. The following lists the principal engagements, with fuller accounts of those not described elsewhere.

Early Land War (0–30 AG)

# Engagement Date Result Est. dead
1 Assault on the Air Temples Sep 0 AG Imperial victory; the Air Nomads destroyed about 3,400,000
2 First Battle of Agna Qel'a 11–19 Sep 0 AG Northern victory; landing repelled 52,000 / 9,000
3 Occupation of the Western and Southern chains Sep 0 – 1 AG Imperial victory; forward bases built (with no. 1)
4 Yu Dao (Yuhe landing) 3–6 Jan 1 AG Imperial beachhead held; mustard gas 52,000 / 1,100
5 Seiran Bay landing 21–25 Feb 1 AG Second beachhead taken 9,000 / 800

Eastern Push (30–50 AG)

# Engagement Date Result Est. dead
20 Battle of the Hesha Plains 37–38 AG Earth Kingdom army broken by tanks 210,000 / 14,000
21 Siege of Dongping 41–43 AG Central rail junction taken 260,000 / 21,000
22 Battle of the Reed Sea 46 AG Last water line forced 90,000 / 8,000
23 Fall of Chenlu 49 AG Last fortified town before the desert taken 70,000 / 6,000

Desert War (50–79 AG)

# Engagement Date Result Est. dead (Earth Kingdom + Qianchan / Tajisaki)

26 The Wells 71–74 AG Tank counter-attack retakes the fields 110,000 / 60,000
27 Chubulag 77–79 AG Last attempt defeated 130,000 / 70,000

Selected engagements

Battle of Han Tui (12 AG)

The first major battle of the northern push, fought on the river plains at the foot of the northern mountains. The Empire's Northern Army, which had come up from the west coast with armor and artillery, met a provincial levy of about 200,000 men. The levy attacked in mass, as it had in Yanakawa, and the Empire's machine guns and guns destroyed it in two days. Imperial aircraft from the Northern Air Temple base pursued the survivors. It confirmed that the Earth Kingdom's levies could not stand against the Empire in open country.

Destruction of Taku (15 AG)

Taku, a river city in the northern lowlands with about 300,000 people, refused the Empire's leaflets to surrender. The Empire's bombers and heavy artillery destroyed it over three days with fire bombs. About 90,000 people died, most of them civilians, and the city was not rebuilt. Taku was the Empire's first deliberate destruction of a city of this size, and it persuaded several provincial lords to open their gates.

Battle of Garsai (21 AG)

Garsai was a river pass that controlled the road east from the northern plains. The Earth Kingdom's army, which was under a provincial marshal and was the largest it had raised since Yanakawa, tried to hold the pass with entrenchments and earthbender-raised walls. The Empire's armor went around the position by a river ford at night, and encircled the army from the rear. About 150,000 Earth Kingdom soldiers died, and about 9,000 Imperial. Garsai opened the northern plains to the Empire.

Battle of the High Passes (22–25 AG)

When the Empire's attack from the south of Yanakawa toward Omashu and the east was foiled in the lowlands, the General Staff turned its southern army into the high mountains. The Battle of the High Passes was a three-year mountain campaign in which Imperial mountain troops, with aircraft and pack artillery, took the passes one by one. By 25 AG the Empire held the mountains, and the southern Omashu front, a pocket of the kingdom around Omashu, was cut off from the rest of the Earth Kingdom by land. Qianchan supplied it from then on by sea.

Western Air Temple Waters (30 AG)

The first naval engagement between the Imperial Navy and the Qianchan Navy took place in the waters south of the continent, near the Western Air Temple island chain, three years after the sinking of a Qianchan civilian ship there in 27 AG. An Imperial squadron escorting a convoy met a Qianchan squadron that had come to protect the supply route to Omashu. After a day of gunnery, in which each side sank two ships, both withdrew. The battle was a draw, and it brought Qianchan into the war.

Battle of the Hesha Plains (37–38 AG)

The first large tank battle of the war. The Earth Kingdom, which had begun to industrialize in 23 AG with Qianchan's help, put a new army of about 400,000 into the plains with its first tanks and Qianchan-supplied rifles. The Empire's oil-fueled armor, which had been built up for the push since 30 AG, broke the army in a week. The Earth Kingdom lost about 210,000 dead, and the Empire about 14,000.

Siege of Dongping (41–43 AG)

Dongping, a rail junction in the central plains, was the key to the lines of the west. The Earth Kingdom fortified it with its new industry, and held it for two years against the Empire's bombardment. The Empire took it in the spring of 43 AG after cutting the rail line and starving the garrison. About 260,000 died, over half of them civilians, and the fall of Dongping opened the way to the Si Wong.

First Battle of Tongba (56–58 AG)

The first of the Desert War's four captures. The Empire's air force, flying from the desert's edge, destroyed the Coalition's rail and depots, and a small force of tanks and infantry seized the oil fields near Tongba in 56 AG. The Qianchan–Earth Kingdom counter-offensive cut its supply line in 58 AG, and the garrison withdrew. About 65,000 Coalition and 38,000 Imperial soldiers died. The pattern was repeated in 63, 71 and 77 AG, and each time the Empire's gains were too small to hold.

Chubulag (77–79 AG)

The last attempt of the first cycle. The Empire used the largest air raid of the desert war, with about 900 aircraft, and a combined ground attack, and held Tongba for two years before the Coalition retook it. About 130,000 Coalition and 70,000 Imperial soldiers died. The General Staff Directorate concluded that air power alone could not hold the oil and, in 79 AG, adopted Plan Yellow.

pardon_crisis.title: Pardon Crisis of 97 AG
pardon_crisis.html:
Also known as the Coronation Amnesty (Imperial designation). Part of the political polarization of the Empire of Tajisaki, 97–100 AG.

Date July 97 AG – 99 AG
Location Caldera City and the Empire of Tajisaki
Parties Court: Fire Lord Ozai, the General Staff Directorate, the Navy. Opposition: the Imperial Diet's Reform bloc, war veterans, Army reformists, colonial delegates, and General Iroh.
Outcome The pardon stood. The Diet and parts of the military lost faith in the Fire Lord. General Iroh emerged as the leader of the opposition. The Diet passed bills for veterans, for the people and for the eastern colonies, with mixed results.

The Pardon Crisis began in July 97 AG, when Fire Lord Ozai, a few days after his coronation, pardoned Rear Admiral Yueya and Captain Zhao, who had been convicted of the Jasmine Island Mutiny of 90 AG, and posted them to the Southern Water Tribe insurgency, then a low-level conflict of small-scale skirmishes and missing patrol reports. The Imperial Diet and a part of the military regarded the pardon as a mockery of the court-martial and of the people who had died on the island, and they lost faith in the Fire Lord. Ozai replied that the Empire needed every capable officer against the insurgency and that the past should be left in the past. The dispute polarized the Empire for the next three years. It gave General Iroh a political following, led the Diet to a series of bills on veterans' benefits, public provisions and the assimilation of the eastern colonies, and divided the Court and the Diet along lines that reappeared in the succession crisis of 100 AG.

Background

Fire Lord Azulon died on the night of 10 June 97 AG, in what the Court called an assassination by Qianchan agents and Ozai had in fact arranged. Ozai was crowned on 24 June. Three streams of public feeling met his accession. The siege of Ba Sing Se had just ended in failure and had cost the Empire about half a million casualties. Iroh, the siege's commander, had been demoted, and his son Lu Ten, the "People's Prince", had been killed there. And Lu Ten's Address on Conduct of 90 AG, in the wake of the Jasmine Island Devastation, had given the reform movement in the Diet a program: independent military tribunals, civilian protection and the prosecution of abuses of authority regardless of rank.

Yueya had been sentenced to imprisonment in 90 AG for exceeding her orders, deceiving the War Council and the unlawful killing of Imperial subjects. Zhao had been convicted on lesser charges and reduced in rank. The Navy had opposed the Address, and Ozai, then a prince, had praised the court-martial but called the proposed tribunals "an insult to those who command".

The pardon

On 3 July 97 AG, as part of the coronation amnesty, Ozai pardoned Yueya and Zhao by Imperial prerogative, restored their ranks, and assigned them to the Southern Pacification Command to suppress the insurgency of the Southern Water Tribe. They left for the south in August. The Diet had no legal power to review the pardon.

Ozai's stated reasons were practical. The Southern insurgency was still small in 97 AG, a matter of skirmishes and patrols that failed to report in, but he argued that it would spread if it was left alone while the Empire's armies were weakened after Ba Sing Se, and that the Navy officers who knew the southern waters were needed there. He argued that the Empire should focus on the Water Tribe insurgency and bury the past in the past. His opponents pointed out that the pardon freed two officers whose conduct on Jasmine Island had been condemned by a court of the Empire, that it was granted seven years into a sentence, and that it gave Yueya, who had killed thousands of Imperial subjects, a command over more of them.

Reaction

The Diet. On 15 July the House of Representatives passed a motion of censure against the pardon by 214 votes to 161. The motion had no legal effect, but it was the first time in Ozai's reign that the Diet had formally criticized the Fire Lord.

The military. Army officers who had served in the west, the garrison of Jasmine Island under Lieutenant Akataa, and the Navy sailors who had broken out of the battlecruiser's brig and retaken it in 90 AG, were the most bitter. Several of those sailors had been decorated for the act. Their testimony was cited in the Diet, and a number of Army and Navy officers submitted their resignations. The General Staff Directorate and the Navy's senior officers supported the Fire Lord.

The press. The Chronicle and the veterans' papers condemned the pardon as a farce. The Ministry of National Enlightenment banned two of the papers in September.

Polarization

By the end of 97 AG the Empire was divided into two camps. The Court camp consisted of Ozai, the General Staff Directorate, the Navy and the ministries, which regarded the Diet's criticism as disloyalty in wartime. The opposition consisted of the Diet's Reform bloc, war veterans, Army reformists and colonial delegates, who regarded the Court as unaccountable.

The opposition turned to Iroh. He had been demoted after the siege, he had lost his son, and the troops and the public knew that he had opposed the Ash Directive. He was more popular than before. He had not spoken in public in support of Lu Ten's reforms, but in January 98 AG he addressed the Veterans' Assembly in Caldera City for the first time. He said that an army that could not trust its own courts could not win a war, and that the Empire owed its soldiers and their families more than it had given. The speech made him the opposition's leader, though he did not seek the title and did not break with the throne. Later in 98 AG he was forced to retire from the Army. The Court honored him in a public ceremony and gave him a seat in the Diet and a place on its Defense Committee, which kept him in public view and made him the reformists' most visible figure. In the same year Zhao was promoted to Admiral for his service in the south.

The bills (98–99 AG)

From March 98 AG the Reform bloc, with Iroh's backing, introduced three bills:

Bill Provisions Outcome
War Veterans' Benefits Bill Pensions, medical care, housing and land grants, and hiring preference for veterans and the families of the dead Passed the House in 98 AG. Ozai signed a reduced version in 99 AG after the Army's officers made clear they would otherwise support it openly.
People's Provisions Bill Food and fuel relief and reconstruction aid for war-damaged districts, funded in part by the Si Wong oil revenues Passed in 99 AG. Signed in part.
Eastern Colonies Assimilation Bill Citizenship and Diet seats for the people of Yanakawa and the other eastern colonies, and the gradual end of the integration classifications of the Imperial Constitution (Arts. 42–43)[1] Passed the House narrowly in 99 AG. The Privy Council shelved it, and Ozai did not sign.

The failure of the assimilation bill was felt most in the colonies. The colonial delegates had campaigned for it, and its defeat undercut the moderates among them. The Yanakawan Rebellion began in April 100 AG.

Consequences

The pardon and the bills fixed the lines along which the Empire later divided. In July 100 AG, the Diet's resolution urging the confirmation of Zuko, who was popular and associated with Iroh, followed from the opposition that had formed in 97 AG, and the Army reformists and the Navy and General Staff Directorate that split the military in the civil war had taken their positions in the dispute over the pardon. The small-scale insurgency in the south, which Yueya and Zhao were sent to suppress, grew into the full Southern Uprising of 99 AG. Yueya's and Zhao's own record there is not covered here.

  1. Imperial Constitution of the Empire of Tajisaki, Arts. 42–43.

succession_crisis.title: Succession crisis of 100 AG
succession_crisis.html:
The disputed succession after the death of Fire Lord Ozai, July–August 100 AG, and the start of the Fire Nation Civil War.

Date 18 July – 8 August 100 AG
Location Caldera City
Parties The Court: General Staff Directorate, Ministry of Truth, Flame Guard. The Diet and the people: Zuko, Iroh.
Result Azula confirmed by force; the Diet dissolved; the Fire Nation Civil War began

After the death of Ozai at the Battle of Qinglan Port on 18 July 100 AG, the Ministry of National Enlightenment announced on 19 July that he was "wounded and recovering," and retracted it on 20 July. The Imperial Constitution gives succession to the Fire Lord's designation, or, without one, to the Privy Council within 72 hours and a confirmation by firebending within seven days (Art. 3), and excludes the Diet (Art. 25). Nevertheless, on 22 July the Diet's House of Representatives urged the confirmation of the popular Zuko, and large demonstrations in Caldera City supported it.

The General Staff Directorate produced a sealed designation naming Azula, and troops took control of the Privy Council's chamber. Between 23 and 25 July seven councillors were arrested, and about 210 people were killed in clashes. Azula was confirmed on 25 July. The press reported the arrests faster than the Ministry could close it down. On 2 August the Diet convened in defiance and declared the confirmation unlawful, and on 4 August shooting broke out in its galleries, killing 31 people. It was dissolved on 8 August. Zuko left Caldera on 5 August, and was joined by his uncle Iroh. The crisis split the military and began the Fire Nation Civil War.

Rival claims

From 25 July 100 AG two people called themselves Fire Lord, and each had a case. Azula held a right to the throne equal to her brother's: she was Ozai's child, she was named in the sealed designation, and she had been confirmed by the Privy Council, which was the body the Constitution charged with the choice. Zuko had the legitimacy that came from outside the Court: the backing of the people, shown in the demonstrations of 22 July, and the resolution of the Diet, which declared the confirmation of Azula unlawful on 2 August. He was the more favored of the two, and the Court's authority rested on the army alone. Neither side recognized the other, and neither could be removed except by force, so the quarrel over who was Fire Lord became the Civil War.

The Court's seizure of the throne also followed a plan that Ozai's circle had made before his death, and that his death stopped. It was to put the blame for a coming wave of repression on Zuko, and to use Azula and the Kanbukyoku to terrorize the whole country in the Fire Lord's name. Ozai was killed at Qinglan Port before the plan could be carried out, and without him the Court had the army, the police and a claim, but no one to give it direction. The claim was settled on 9 May 118 AG, when Zuko killed Azula in the Duel of the Palace.

dai_li_coup_attempt.title: Dai Li Coup Attempt
dai_li_coup_attempt.html:
Also known as the Night of the Gates (Ba Sing Se usage) and, in Earth Kingdom state records, the Regency Conspiracy of 98 AG. Part of the Hundred Year War, Earth Kingdom home front.

Date Night of 21–22 March 98 AG
Location Ba Sing Se, the Royal Palace and the Inner Ring
Result Coup failed. Dai Li leadership killed or arrested. The Dai Li reformed and largely purged (98–99 AG). King Kuei took direct command of the war.
Parties Crown loyalists: King Kuei, the Council of Five, the Royal Earthbender Guard, the city garrison. Conspirators: the faction of the Dai Li led by Grand Secretariat Long Feng.
Casualties Approx. 1,900 killed: Dai Li approx. 640, Royal Guard and garrison approx. 460, civilians approx. 800.

The Dai Li Coup Attempt was a plot by the Dai Li, the Earth Kingdom's secret police, to seize the Earth King, Kuei, and rule Ba Sing Se through him. It was carried out in the early hours of 22 March 98 AG, about a year after the siege of Ba Sing Se ended. The conspirators, who had grown corrupt over generations of power, feared that Kuei's reforms would end it. They had killed his father, the 51st Earth King, years before for being weak, and they intended to make Kuei a puppet in the same way. The coup failed within fourteen hours, because the Council of Five and the city garrison remained loyal. It led to the purge and reform of the Dai Li in 98–99 AG, and to a centralization of command that allowed Kuei to lead the war himself from Ba Sing Se by 99 AG. There was no successful coup in Ba Sing Se in 100 AG, though a second attempt failed in January.

Background

The Dai Li

The Dai Li were founded in the age of Avatar Kyoshi to protect the monarchy's interests under the constitution. Over the centuries they became a closed and self-serving body, with an unmatched knowledge of the city's people and its secrets, and with the Grand Secretariat, who led them, as the most powerful official in the capital. They kept order in the city by fear and by brainwashing, and they hid the Hundred Year War from the people inside the walls.

The death of the 51st Earth King

The Dai Li and the Grand Secretariat, Long Feng, had murdered the 51st Earth King, who was weak and could not be controlled, and left a four-year-old son, Kuei, as his successor. Long Feng became the boy's regent. Kuei grew up in the palace, shut away from the city and the war, and was given a menagerie and a pet bear, Bosco, as his only interests. He was not told about the war.

The siege and Kuei's reforms

The siege of Ba Sing Se (96–97 AG) ended Kuei's isolation, in its first weeks. In February and March 96 AG the Imperial air force dropped leaflets over the city urging it to surrender, and then bombed it with high explosives and chemical weapons. The Dai Li could not hide a war that was falling on the rings of the city, and Kuei, then nineteen, learned of the Hundred Year War for the first time. He demanded to know why he had not been told. Over the course of the siege, which broke the city open and saw the Palace held by the Empire for a week, he began to ask questions of the Council of Five and General Sung Yaowei, and to read the Dai Li's reports. In late 97 AG he began to centralize the military command, to cut the Dai Li's budget, and to put the Council of Five in charge of the city's security. Long Feng and his officers understood that they were losing control of the king.

The conspiracy

The conspirators planned to seize the Palace's gates, capture the king, and place him under the Dai Li's control with the same methods used to condition prisoners at their base under Lake Laogai. They would rule as regents, in his name, and dissolve the Council of Five. About 900 agents of the Dai Li's 2,400 were in the plot. The plan depended on speed: the king and the Council had to be held before the garrison could act.

The attempt (21–22 March 98 AG)

At about 01:00 on 22 March, Dai Li agents took the Palace's three inner gates and seized the Royal Earthbender Guard's armory. A part of the Guard went over to the conspirators. The Dai Li captured the Council's quarters, and held four of its five members for several hours. Long Feng entered the throne room, but Kuei had left it ten minutes earlier, after a guardsman had warned him, and had been taken by the king's chamberlain to a shelter beneath the Palace.

The Council's fifth member, who had escaped, reached the city garrison's headquarters at 02:30. General Sung Yaowei brought two regiments into the Inner Ring at 04:00, and retook the gates in house-to-house fighting. By 15:00 the coup was over. Long Feng was captured in the Palace's lower galleries, and the Dai Li's base under Lake Laogai was stormed and destroyed that evening.

Aftermath

Purge and reform of the Dai Li

Long Feng was tried by the Council of Five and executed on 9 May 98 AG. In the months that followed, the Crown reviewed every Dai Li agent, in a process called the Great Review (98–99 AG). Of about 2,400 agents, about 1,700 were dismissed, imprisoned or executed, since they had been in the plot, were corrupt, or were not loyal to the Crown's cause. The Grand Secretariat's powers were abolished. The remaining Dai Li, about 700 agents, were reorganized as a security and intelligence service responsible to the king, and their use of brainwashing was ended. They were smaller, loyal, and untried by the end of 99 AG.

Kuei takes command

After the coup attempt Kuei moved against the institutions that had kept him a figurehead. He ended the regency, and made the Council of Five report to him directly. By 99 AG he practically led the war himself from Ba Sing Se, on the Northern Front, the line of fronts from the Taihua Mountains and the Omashu approaches to the Western Lake. He met his generals daily in a war room under the Palace, and visited the walls and the front. His critics said that he was inexperienced and uncompromising, and that the years of lies had made him distrustful. His supporters said that he saved the Earth Kingdom from losing its capital to its own police.

A second attempt (January 100 AG)

A smaller second attempt was made in January 100 AG by Dai Li officers who had escaped the Great Review. They tried to seize the Council of Five's war room while the Coalition was planning a joint offensive by Qianchan and the Earth Kingdom to push north and crush the Empire. The attempt was put down within hours, but it disrupted the planning and the security of the command, and it contributed to the failure of the offensive. The Coalition ended its operation with the Ba Sing Se Treaty (March 100 AG), which placed the Qianchan and Earth Kingdom armies under a single command.

Why there was no coup in 100 AG

In the canon version of these events, the Dai Li, led by Long Feng, were exposed by the Avatar and, in 100 AG, helped Princess Azula take Ba Sing Se. In this history, the exposure came earlier and from inside: the Dai Li's conspiracy was broken in 98 AG, and Azula had no Dai Li to turn in 100 AG. The Fire Nation's attack on Ba Sing Se in 100 AG came instead through the Sōen, and Kuei was in the Palace's command bunker when it struck.

Historiography

Crown histories describe the coup attempt as the final defeat of an old corruption. Dai Li survivors, few of whom talked, said that Long Feng had planned to save the Earth Kingdom from a weak king. Qianchan archives record that Qianchan's intelligence service knew of the plot from a source inside the Dai Li, and did not warn Kuei until it was too late.

soen_program.title: Sōen Program
soen_program.html:
The Empire of Tajisaki's decades-long program to build a comet-scale weapon of mass destruction. 47–100 AG.

Date 47 AG – 17 July 100 AG
Operator Imperial Research Bureau (IRB), under the Fire Lord
Purpose A weapon of mass destruction for the strike on Ba Sing Se
Outcome Fired once, at Ba Sing Se on 17 July 100 AG, which was both its operation and its first full-scale test

The Sōen Program was the Empire of Tajisaki's research effort to harness the destructive power of Sozin's Comet and to build a nuclear weapon on the scale of the comet's destruction. It ran for more than fifty years and produced the Sōen, a fire-crystal capacitor array that stores firebending energy and releases it as a directed beam. The Empire built it for one purpose, the strike on Ba Sing Se, and fired it for the first time on 17 July 100 AG.

Origin

The program was ordered by Fire Lord Azulon in 47 AG. The comet's return in 0 AG had shown the Empire what its firebenders could do under it, and Azulon's staff asked whether that power could be stored and used on demand. The first work was on fire crystals, minerals that hold firebending energy, and on firebender-fed batteries. A second line of research, on fission, was run in parallel from the 70s as a possible alternative.

Development

Year Milestone
47 AG Program founded by Azulon's order
58 AG First charged crystal cell, about one ton of explosive equivalent
72 AG First multi-crystal array, about 100 tons
86 AG The comet's expected return is calculated, and the program is given a date to work toward
95 AG The wall-breaking weapon used at Ba Sing Se (96 AG), a conventional bomb, is a by-product of the program's explosives work
97 AG Ozai's accession brings the program new funding, and the Ba Sing Se strike is named as its purpose
99 AG IRB scientists propose a fission weapon and refuse to develop it, and are executed. The IRB's report to Ozai says the Sōen can break Ba Sing Se
99–100 AG Forward array built at Qinglan Port

According to the IRB's 99 AG report, the main array at the Caldera Coastal Battery Complex was projected to hold about 9.4 kilotons in the comet's window, and about 2–3 kilotons in an ordinary recharge. A portable version, carried by the Koometsu bomber, held about 2.1 kilotons with a range of about 80 kilometers, against about 420 kilometers for the full array. The array was triggered by a firebender, and was charged by a crew of about forty.

The strike

On 17 July 100 AG the forward array at Qinglan Port was fired by Ozai himself, who supplied the trigger input. It destroyed the western Outer Wall and the Inner Wall of Ba Sing Se and killed hundreds of thousands. It was the weapon's first full-scale discharge, and the test that the Empire had built it for. The strike is described in its own article.

Aftermath

Ozai's death the next day left the Empire without anyone with the authority to fire the main array, which was never discharged. Qianchan's fission program, which the IRB had assessed at four to six months, or two to three if accelerated, did not produce a weapon before the war's end. The arrays at Qinglan Port and Caldera were disabled or kept under guard, and the fire-crystal stocks were divided among the factions of the civil war.

Historiography

The Imperial record presents the program as a defensive deterrent. Qianchan intelligence documents, which are the main outside source, describe it as a program for a single purpose and the executions of 99 AG as the moment when the Empire's scientists understood what it was for.

address_on_conduct.title: Address on Conduct
address_on_conduct.html:
The reform document submitted by Captain Lu Ten to Fire Lord Azulon and the Imperial Diet in 90 AG.

Author Lu Ten
Date 90 AG, after the Jasmine Island Mutiny
Called for Independent military tribunals; protection of civilians; prosecution of abuses of authority regardless of rank

The Address on Conduct was written by Lu Ten after the Devastation of Jasmine Island. It called for independent military tribunals, rules protecting civilians, and the prosecution of abuses of authority regardless of rank. The Navy opposed it, and the Diet's reformers adopted it as their program. It made Lu Ten the center of a reform movement, and after his death in 96 AG the movement passed to Iroh. The Pardon Crisis of 97 AG, in which Ozai pardoned Yueya, was a direct challenge to it.

treaty_of_qinglan.title: Treaty of Qinglan
treaty_of_qinglan.html:
The treaty that formally ended the Hundred Year War and recognized the United Republic of Nations, 28 April 105 AG.
Treaty of Qinglan
Signed28 April 105 AG, Qinglan Port
Parties
  • The Restoration Government of the Fire Nation, represented by Zuko
  • The Qianchan Republic, represented by President Zhou Qin
  • The Earth Kingdom, represented by King Kuei
  • The Yanakawan Provisional Council
WitnessThe Avatar, Aang
Not signed byThe Court faction under Azula
Effect
  • The Hundred Year War formally ends (de jure)
  • The United Republic of Nations is recognized as a sovereign state
  • Concessions by all parties

The Treaty of Qinglan was the treaty that formally ended the Hundred Year War and recognized the United Republic of Nations as a legitimate state. The war had ended in fact on 18 July 100 AG with the death of Ozai, but no one had signed anything, and the Empire, the Coalition and the colonies were still at war in law. Five years of civil war, famine and the Yanakawan War of Independence passed before the parties could sign.

Background

The Restoration Government that held the Fire Nation's harbors and half its army under Zuko needed peace with the world to fight its own civil war, and needed the Earth Kingdom and Qianchan to stay out of it. Qianchan, which had supplied the Royalists by sea since 100 AG, wanted its armies home and its trade restored. King Kuei's government, which was losing the Earth Kingdom warlord wars to hunger, needed the Hu Xin Provinces and the garrisons in them out of Imperial hands. The Yanakawan Provisional Council, which had won its war on the ground and held Qinglan Port, wanted recognition and the evacuation of the last Imperial administrators.

The Declaration of Union, made earlier that spring, had founded the United Republic of Nations, and the treaty gave it the standing it lacked.

The conference

The delegations met at Qinglan Port for ten days in April. Zuko came for the Restoration Government, and the Provisional Council received him in the harbor it had taken from his father's navy. President Zhou Qin brought the Qianchan delegation by sea, and King Kuei, who had never left the capital in his reign, traveled to the coast by rail. Aang attended as witness and guarantor, and the Council asked for it. The Court at Caldera was invited and did not come.

Terms and concessions

The treaty ended the state of war between the signatories, set the frontiers of the new republic on the Yanakawan Peninsula and the coast of Seiran Bay, and set out what each party gave up.

PartyGainedConceded
Restoration Government (Fire Nation)Peace on its frontiers; the neutrality of Qianchan and the Earth Kingdom in the civil war; the end of the blockadeWithdrew all garrisons and administrators from Yanakawa within 180 days; gave up its claims to the Hu Xin Provinces and every other colony; disbanded the Regional Commands; handed its chemical weapons stocks and the Sōen records to a joint commission; accepted the Rebuilding Fund, paid from a fixed share of coal and steel exports and customs revenue for forty years; accepted trials of named Imperial officers
Earth Kingdom (Kuei)The return of the occupied provinces; the Rebuilding Fund; the withdrawal of the Imperial remnantsRecognized the United Republic and dropped its claim to Yanakawa; granted the Republic access to its ports and rail; accepted an amnesty for officials and lords who had served the occupation, to be reviewed by a commission
Qianchan (Zhou Qin)Trade, the Republic's neutrality and its harborsGave up the Western Air Temple island chain and its supply route; waived the war loans it had lent the kingdom; promised grain convoys to the northwest; guaranteed the Republic's frontiers
Yanakawan Provisional Council (URN)Recognition as a sovereign state; the evacuation of the Empire; the keys to Qinglan PortPledged neutrality; protected the property and citizenship rights of Fire Nation settlers for ten years; took over the colonial administration's debts; promised to hold a council with representatives of every people on the peninsula
The Avatar (witness)The first formal act of the world order after the warTook custody of the Air Nomad temples and the island chain pending the recovery of an Air Nomad community

What the treaty did not settle

The Court did not sign, and Azula's navy fought the Republic with naval raids until 110 AG, when the Court's fleet was committed to the home islands. The treaty bound the Restoration Government, not the Fire Nation as a whole, and it was only after the Duel of the Palace in 118 AG, when Zuko won, that the Fire Nation as a state inherited its terms. The Rebuilding Fund, and the trials, were the subject of dispute for decades.

Reception

The Fire Nation remembers the treaty as a humiliation that a government fighting for its life had to accept, and many veterans never forgave Zuko for signing it. The kingdom calls it the end of the war and the beginning of its recovery. Qianchan treats it as a sound bargain, and in the Republic it is a birth certificate. Its annual celebration, on 28 April, is one of the Republic's national holidays.

The Qianchan–Earth Kingdom Alliance Treaty of 3 BG, and the war alliance of 30 AG.

Signed 3 BG

War alliance 30 AG, when Qianchan entered the Hundred Year War

The Alliance Treaty of 3 BG united Qianchan and the Earth Kingdom against the Fire Nation's expansion. It was a suspension of tensions, not a reconciliation: Ba Sing Se, which had never recognized the republic's legitimacy, had to revise its language of non-recognition as a condition of Qianchan's signature. Qianchan did not enter the war until 30 AG, after a civilian ship was sunk in 27 AG and a naval battle with the Imperial Navy was a draw. In 100 AG, the Ba Sing Se Treaty put the two armies under a single command.
