homeland_purity_initiative.title: Homeland Purity Initiative
homeland_purity_initiative.html:
The Empire of Tajisaki's policy of aligning territories with Imperial norms through integration, resettlement and removal.

Basis Imperial Constitution, Art. 44
Administered by The Ministry of National Harmony

The Homeland Purity Initiative was formalized after the Air Nomad Genocide. It applied in territories designated by the Cabinet, and brought their "cultural, spiritual, linguistic and population characteristics" into line with Imperial norms by integration, resettlement and, "in cases of irreconcilable resistance," removal. Its classification system divided colonial subjects into Recognized Imperial Persons, Enrolled Colonial Subjects, Unenrolled Populations and Designated Threat Populations. In the Water Tribe subjugation, the Empire used it to justify labor and elimination.

way_of_the_warrior.title: Way of the Warrior
way_of_the_warrior.html:
The Fire Nation's tradition of honor in combat, including the Agni Kai, the formal duel.

Origin Old Fire Nation tradition
Notable duel Duel of the Palace (9 May 118 AG)

The Way of the Warrior is the Fire Nation's code of honor in combat. Under it, a challenge to a formal duel (an Agni Kai) cannot be refused without dishonor, and the result decides the quarrel. A duel to the death is fought with firebending only, and each duelist carries a sword for the final stroke. Lightning is not fire, and its use is held to be a sign that a duelist has stopped believing she can win. A duelist who cheats forfeits an honorable death.

In 118 AG, Azula challenged her brother Zuko to a duel under the Way of the Warrior. She used lightning, he redirected it, and he beheaded her.

breaker_armor.title: Breaker armor
breaker_armor.html:
The Empire's power armor. Breaker Mk II "Hagane no Oni."

Introduced 83 AG (mechanized suit)
Operators About 8,400 (99 AG), after a loss of about 40% at Ba Sing Se
Variants Breaker Mk II; Arctic Breaker (Mk II-N)
Counter Heavy overhead collapse; the Zaofu Iron Guard's Tiejia-III

The Breaker is the Fire Nation's powered armor suit, first invented in 83 AG. The Mk II, which the soldiers called the Hagane no Oni ("iron demon"), has hydraulic legs and a fixed visor, resists rifle fire, and fights in the front line of urban and armored battles. The Imperial Research Bureau admitted that it was vulnerable to heavy overhead collapse, which Ba Sing Se's integrated defense used in the siege, destroying about 40% of the Empire's Breakers.

The Arctic Breaker (Mk II-N), with heated joints and an integral flamethrower, led the landing at Agna Qel'a in 99 AG. The Salvationists later captured Breaker companies and fielded them against both sides.

chemical_weapons.title: Chemical weapons in the Hundred Year War
chemical_weapons.html:
Used by the Empire of Tajisaki alone. The Earth Kingdom never had them.

First use 3 January 1 AG, Yu Dao (mustard gas)
User The Empire of Tajisaki only
Principal agents Mustard gas; phosgene mixes; persistent blister agent (Type 9)

The Empire introduced mustard gas at Yu Dao on 3 January 1 AG, and used chemical weapons for the rest of the war. In the Yanakawan Campaign it gassed levies and villages, and replaced mustard with a heavier phosgene mix by 3 AG, killing about 8,000 men at Liangkou in one morning. The Earth Kingdom never acquired chemical weapons, and its only protection was wet cloth against the Empire's rubber and glass masks. In the Siege of Ba Sing Se, Imperial aircraft dropped chemicals across the rings, which is why civilians were most of the dead. In the Siege of the North, the Empire used persistent blister agents in the ice cellars, where they settled and killed people in the shelters.

demographics.title: Demographics of the Hundred Year War
demographics.html:
An overview of the populations, armed forces and war dead of the Hundred Year War, 0–100 AG. All figures are provisional until the war's campaigns are fully recorded.

Period 0 AG – 100 AG
Population, 0 AG About 501,000,000
Population, 100 AG About 547,600,000 (revised for indirect deaths; see the ledger)
Armed forces, 80 AG About 20,000,000 (before the Si Wong Offensive)
War dead before 80 AG About 30,000,000
War dead, 0–100 AG About 41,000,000 (provisional; about 8% of the 0 AG population)
All casualties, 0–100 AG About 75–80,000,000 (dead, wounded and missing)

Revision. The figures on this page count direct deaths only. Including indirect deaths (famine, epidemic, displacement, medical collapse), the war killed about 81 million people (range 75–90 million), and the populations in 100 AG below are the revised figures. See Demographic ledger of the Hundred Year War.

The Hundred Year War killed about 41 million people by 100 AG by violence, about 8% of the world's population in 0 AG. About 30 million of them died before the Si Wong Offensive began in 80 AG. The deaths were heavily lopsided: for every Fire Nation death there were about eight in the Earth Kingdom, where the Empire used genocide, engineered famine and chemical weapons across the occupied lands from the first week of the war. The war destroyed one nation, the Air Nomads, almost entirely, and took about half of the Water Tribes.

Population in 0 AG

Nation Population, 0 AG
Earth Kingdom 230,000,000
Qianchan Republic 140,000,000
Empire of Tajisaki (Fire Nation) 120,000,000
Water Tribes 8,000,000 in all (about 6,000,000 at the poles: North approx. 3,600,000, South approx. 2,400,000; about 2,000,000 elsewhere)
Air Nomads 3,000,000
Total 501,000,000

Scale

The world is about the size of Earth, with continents of the same order. At 501 million people, it is thinly settled: about four people per square kilometer of land, against about eleven on Earth in 1900. The density is uneven. The Earth Kingdom averages about 14 per square kilometer, and the Fire Nation's islands are among the densest places in the world. The poles, the Si Wong Desert, the Foggy Swamp and the Yanakawan frontier are nearly empty.

Growth

Growth before and during the war depended on the nation:

Nation Growth rate Reason
Empire of Tajisaki 0.4% a year Industrial economy, compulsory service; the war's dead were mostly soldiers
Qianchan Republic 0.4% a year Industrial economy and a distant war
Water Tribes 0.25% a year Pre-industrial, then crushed by occupation
Earth Kingdom none Genocide, famine and chemical weapons across the occupied lands from 0 AG suppressed births and killed non-combatants, cancelling any natural growth

Without the war, these rates would have taken the Fire Nation to about 179 million by 100 AG, Qianchan to about 209 million and the Water Tribes to about 10 million, and the Earth Kingdom would have been about 295 million at the world average of 0.25%.

Armed forces before the Si Wong Offensive (80 AG)

Before 80 AG, the Fire Nation and its opponents together had about 20 million people under arms.

Nation Armed forces, 80 AG Share of population
Empire of Tajisaki 8,000,000 about 6%
Earth Kingdom 7,000,000 about 3%
Qianchan Republic 4,500,000 about 3%
Water Tribes and irregulars 500,000 about 6%
Total 20,000,000

The great campaigns used a part of these totals: the Si Wong Offensive about 2 million per side, the siege of Ba Sing Se about 1 million Imperial and 2 million Coalition troops, and the Battle of Qinglan Port about 16,000 and 29,000.

War dead

The Earth Kingdom

The Earth Kingdom lost about 29.6 million people, about 13% of its 0 AG population. From the first week of the war the Empire used chemical weapons against cities and strongholds, practiced extermination policies against the people of the occupied northwest, and starved districts that resisted. These policies killed far more people than the battles did. Chemical weapons were used by the Empire alone, throughout the war: the Earth Kingdom never had them. The siege of Ba Sing Se added famine and the Sōen strike.

Tally by front

Front Years Dead Notes
Earth Kingdom land war (the Yanakawan Campaign, genocide and famine in the northwest, chemical weapons, Hu Xin, Taku, Garsai and unlisted campaigns) 0–79 AG about 24,000,000 Earth Kingdom about 22,000,000; Fire Nation about 2,000,000. The Yanakawan Campaign (1–10 AG) accounts for about 3,950,000 of this (Earth Kingdom about 3,500,000; Fire Nation about 450,000)
Air Nomad Genocide 0–20 AG about 3,400,000 Air Nomads about 3,000,000; Water Tribe collateral about 400,000
Subjugation of the Water Tribes 0–79 AG about 1,680,000 South about 960,000; North about 720,000
Naval war 30–79 AG about 1,200,000 Fire Nation about 600,000; Qianchan about 600,000
Subtotal before the Si Wong Offensive about 30,300,000
Si Wong Offensive 80–88 AG about 880,000 Earth Kingdom about 430,000; Fire Nation about 300,000; Qianchan about 150,000
Siege of Ba Sing Se 96–97 AG about 3,500,000 Earth Kingdom about 3,250,000 (civilians about 2,700,000); Fire Nation about 210,000; Qianchan about 40,000
Southern Uprising 99 AG about 480,000 Southern Water Tribe
Siege of the North and occupation 13 Nov 99 – 17 Jul 100 AG about 1,080,000 Northern Water Tribe
Sōen strike on Ba Sing Se 17 Jul 100 AG about 380,000 Earth Kingdom, dead or missing
Occupation, famine and unlisted campaigns 80–100 AG about 4,200,000 Earth Kingdom about 3,500,000; Fire Nation about 400,000; Qianchan about 300,000
Subtotal, 80–100 AG about 10,500,000
Total, 0–100 AG about 40,800,000

By nation

Nation Dead, 0–100 AG Share of 0 AG population
Earth Kingdom about 29,600,000 about 13%
Water Tribes about 3,640,000 about 45%
Fire Nation about 3,510,000 about 3%
Air Nomads about 3,000,000 about 100%
Qianchan about 1,090,000 under 1%
Total about 40,800,000

The Earth Kingdom lost about eight people for every one the Fire Nation lost, both before 80 AG and over the whole war. Qianchan's losses were about one third of the Fire Nation's.

Counting the wounded, maimed and missing, the war produced an estimated 75–80 million casualties.

Why the Earth Kingdom's death ratio was so high

The Earth Kingdom lost about eight people for every one the Fire Nation lost. Historians give several reasons, and agree that no single one explains the whole figure. The ratio counts civilians. Counting only soldiers, the Earth Kingdom lost about four for every one the Empire lost in the early campaigns, and about two and a half over the whole war.

  1. Industrial gap. In 0 AG the Empire had the world's largest industrial base, built since the Fire Nation's industrial revolution of 300–100 BG. It could mass-produce machine guns, artillery, coal-powered warships and zeppelins. The Earth Kingdom, a large agrarian state with an economy centered on its provinces, had none of this at scale, and the Earth Kingdom's own governments had seized or restricted new technology for generations.
  2. Opposed doctrines. The Empire's Harvest Plan relied on firepower, entrenchment and attrition. The Earth Kingdom's provincial levies relied on the mountain rush, a charge in mass numbers that had worked against swords and muskets and was suicidal against machine guns and wire. The two doctrines were nearly perfectly mismatched.
  3. Fragmented command. The Earth King's authority did not extend beyond the walls of Ba Sing Se, and the war was fought by provincial lords and local levies, each with its own supply, plans and rivalries. The Empire could concentrate its forces against one province at a time. This changed only after the Dai Li coup attempt of 98 AG, when King Kuei centralized the command.
  4. Untrained levies and poor medicine. Levies were raised from peasants with little or no training, with no veteran core, and were thrown into battle in days. The Empire had professional non-commissioned officers and army medical services. Many Earth Kingdom wounded died of wounds that Imperial soldiers survived.
  5. Chemical weapons. Only the Empire had them. It introduced mustard gas at Yu Dao in 1 AG, and the Earth Kingdom, which never acquired chemical weapons of its own, had neither the means to reply in kind nor the masks to survive them: its protection was wet cloth against the Empire's rubber and glass.
  6. Air and sea control. The Empire's zeppelin wing and fleet gave it freedom to bombard cities, blockade ports and cut off sieges, as at Hengli and Taigu, and, at Ba Sing Se, to drop leaflets demanding surrender and then bombs and chemicals across all the rings of the city. The Earth Kingdom had no air force and almost no navy.
  7. Occupation policy. The Empire killed civilians as a matter of policy in the occupied lands: genocide in the northwest, famine used as a weapon, and forced labor. These deaths were not battle deaths and made up the largest share of the Earth Kingdom's dead. The Earth Kingdom's civilians had no comparable exposure on the Imperial side.
  8. Late adoption of firearms and doctrine. The Earth Kingdom, like the other nations, had been slow to adopt firearms, because of its older military traditions and the value placed on bending, and had also been slow to change its tactics. Imperial firebenders were integrated with riflemen and machine guns, which gave the Empire a combined-arms advantage that the levies lacked.

How the ratio changed

The ratio narrowed as the war went on. After Qianchan entered the war in 30 AG, it supplied the Earth Kingdom with rifles, machine guns and doctrine. By the 80s the Coalition had trained armies, gas protection and entrenched positions of its own, and the Si Wong Offensive and the siege of Ba Sing Se were fought at far closer odds.

Period Earth Kingdom : Fire Nation dead (all) Soldiers only
1–10 AG (Yanakawan Campaign) about 8 : 1 about 4 : 1
0–79 AG (whole land war) about 8 : 1 about 3.5 : 1
80–88 AG (Si Wong Offensive) about 1.4 : 1 (Coalition about 1.9 : 1) about 1.9 : 1
96–97 AG (Siege of Ba Sing Se) about 15 : 1 about 2.8 : 1
0–100 AG about 8 : 1 about 2.5 : 1

The siege of Ba Sing Se shows both effects at once. The soldiers' ratio was close, because the defense was well organized and well supplied, while the overall ratio was extreme, because the city's civilians died in numbers that the Empire's own did not.

Population in 100 AG

Nation Expected without the war After war dead, 100 AG
Empire of Tajisaki 178,800,000 about 172,100,000
Qianchan Republic 208,600,000 about 206,700,000
Earth Kingdom 230,000,000 (no growth) about 165,350,000
Water Tribes 8,000,000 (without growth) about 3,410,000
Air Nomads 3,000,000 about 400 (the airbending remnant)
Total about 547,600,000

The world's population in 100 AG was about 9% larger than in 0 AG. The Earth Kingdom, which was the largest nation in 0 AG, was smaller than Qianchan by about 41 million, and the Fire Nation had grown by almost half, with the share of the world population shifting toward the two industrial states.

The Post-War Conflicts (100–120 AG), the Fire Nation Civil War, the Earth Kingdom's warlord wars and famine, and the Yanakawan War of Independence, then killed an estimated 19 million more, and are the third most deadly war in history. The Fire Nation Civil War alone killed about 3.5 million, about 2% of the Empire's population, and displaced 7–10 million.

chronicle_address.title: The Chronicle: The Prince Who Asked Why
chronicle_address.html:
Caldera City · Autumn, 90 AG · Opinion & Analysis

The Prince Who Asked Why

Lu Ten's Address on Conduct is a rebuke to the Navy, an embarrassment to the Admiralty, and the first honest question put to the Directorate in years

By the Chronicle's Political Correspondent

For ninety years the Imperial military has answered to itself. On Tuesday, a captain of the Armored Corps, who happens also to be the Fire Lord's grandson, stood before the Diet's Committee on Military Affairs and asked it a question nobody has asked in a generation: why?

Captain Lu Ten read his Address on Conduct to a full committee room and a public gallery that overflowed into the corridor. It had already been submitted in writing to Fire Lord Azulon. Its subject is the destruction of Jasmine Island by Rear Admiral Yueya, which the Chronicle has covered since the first reports. Its target is wider: the habit of the services, and of the Navy in particular, of treating the Empire's own territory and subjects as the property of whoever commands the nearest ship.

What the Address asks for

The Address makes five proposals, which the Chronicle has read in full:

  • Independent military tribunals, answerable to neither the Army nor the Navy chiefs.
  • A requirement that any declaration of martial law or emergency be reported to the Directorate and the Diet within days, and that operations beyond their approved orders be halted.
  • Legal protection for civilians in Imperial and occupied territory.
  • Prosecution of abuse of authority regardless of rank.
  • A clearer division between Army and Navy in garrison appointments.

The Address says that "savages" must not be allowed to taint the image of the Imperial military. The word has already been quoted in every paper in the capital, and the Chronicle will return to it below.

The question the Admiralty cannot answer

The facts of the case are not in dispute, and they are worth stating plainly. Jasmine Island has been an Imperial possession for decades. It has a council, a small garrison commanded by an Army officer, and a local constabulary. It has never rebelled. Yueya, who commanded a squadron in the western islands, applied for the garrison command, and was refused. Within weeks she had taken her ships into the harbor, declared the island in rebellion, and killed two of its three councillors.

The Admiralty's position, put to the Chronicle by a spokesman, is that island chains are naval territory in the first place, that garrison commands there have in the past gone to naval officers, and that Yueya's petition was therefore not unreasonable. The Chronicle does not doubt that. What the Admiralty cannot explain, and what Lu Ten pressed on in the committee, is why the Directorate should have granted it.

"The island had a garrison," he told the committee, according to the transcript. "The garrison had a commander. The commander told me himself that he had no complaint, that the island council worked with him, that the tea was delivered and the harbor was quiet. I ask the Admiralty what problem it was trying to solve. Whether an operation is civilian or military, it needs a reason. I have looked for the reason in the Navy's petition and I cannot find one."

He then addressed the personal ground of Yueya's claim directly. The transcript records a pause here, and then:

"The Admiral's family lost a fight on that island three centuries ago. That is the whole of her case. I have read it twice. There is no logical reason why anyone should want to command a garrison because an ancestor was embarrassed there. There is no logical reason why anyone should destroy it for that reason. I would like the committee to consider the kind of person who can hold a grievance for three hundred years and call it a strategic assessment."

"Petition politely"

The sharpest part of the speech concerns the refusal itself. Yueya's petition was denied. The Chronicle understands that the Directorate saw no reason to move an Army post to the Navy, and that nothing in the denial was personal.

"A petition was refused," Lu Ten said. "That is what happens to petitions. The reasonable response is to petition again, to appeal, to ask politely and to ask a second time. The Admiral did not do any of that. She was angry, and so she took ships and firebenders into a harbor and burned a town. I do not know how anyone can describe this as the conduct of an officer."

He then added the line that has been quoted in the capital's cafés ever since. Both Yueya and her second-in-command, Captain Zhao, had served in the southern waters campaign before their posting to the western islands. "I have wondered," Lu Ten said, "whether the southern waters did this to them. Whether they looked at that much white and blue for that many months, and something in them went. I have wondered because I cannot think of another explanation."

The gallery laughed. The chairman called for order. The remark was not struck from the transcript, and it has been repeated in the press with enthusiasm. It has also been criticized: several veterans of the southern campaign have written to the Chronicle to say that it was a cheap thing to say about men and women who had spent two years on the ice, and that a prince who wished to demand conduct from the Navy might begin by showing some. The Chronicle thinks the criticism is fair, and that the remark was unworthy of the rest of the speech.

The arrest, and the Navy that did not follow

The Army–Navy divide is the center of the story, and the Chronicle's reporting suggests that it is not as clean as either service would like.

It was Lu Ten, not the Directorate and not the Admiralty, who arrested Yueya. He did so with the Army detachment he had led on the island, and with a group of her own Navy officers who had refused to follow her and who stood with him in the harbor. According to several accounts, these included the executive officer of her battlecruiser and the captains of both destroyers. The Chronicle was told by an officer who was present that "at least half the squadron knew by midnight that it was wrong, and by dawn they were looking for someone to follow instead."

This matters because the Admiralty's defense depends on the claim that Yueya's conduct was an excess of zeal, a mistake of one officer in a hard war. The facts suggest that her own officers knew better and acted on it, and that the Navy's institutional reflex was to defend her anyway.

Lu Ten made this point in the committee. "I did not arrest a Navy," he said. "I arrested one officer, and I did it with her own comrades beside me, because they saw what I saw. I ask the people and the military to try this barbarian, and I ask the Navy to remember that its own officers were not in favor of her idea. The logical thing for any officer to do is to petition, and to wait. The logical thing for any officer who cannot wait is to resign. There is no logical case for what she did."

The word "savages"

The Address's sharpest word is also its most vulnerable. Lu Ten uses "savages" for officers and soldiers who use the Empire's uniform for private revenge or for cruelty. He means, and says, that the army that burns its own subjects has lost the purpose for which it fights.

The Chronicle sympathizes with the intention. But the word will be used against him. It lends itself to a reading in which a prince in a clean uniform is lecturing enlisted men, and the court's hardliners will be glad of the chance. Prince Ozai, who has praised the court-martial but called the proposed tribunals "an insult to those who command," has been quick to use the framing.

What the Directorate should do

There is a larger risk. Lu Ten's strongest argument is not about the Navy, and it is not about Yueya. It is that the Empire has no mechanism for stopping an officer who decides on her own authority to declare martial law, and that Yueya was stopped by an accident: an Army captain who happened to be on the island. The Navy's hostility to the Address, however, gives the Directorate an easy way to dispose of it, by presenting it as a quarrel between the services and not a question about the law.

The Directorate should not take that way. The question of who commands Imperial garrisons is a small one. The question of who may be stopped, and by whom, when they burn an Imperial town, is not. Captain Lu Ten has asked it clearly, in front of the Diet and the people, and it should be answered the same way.

Fire Lord Azulon has not commented on the Address. General Iroh, Captain Lu Ten's father and the Directorate's Planning Director, declined to speak to the Chronicle.

cinders_courtyard.title: Cinders in the Furnace
cinders_courtyard.html:
118 AG: The Courtyard

I remember the laughing before I remember her face.

It came across the stones ahead of her, high and dry and a little too long, the sound of someone who has heard a joke so many times she's forgotten what it was. Four hundred soldiers stood on three sides of the courtyard, Flame Guard in black, my own officers in grey, Diet members in their ridiculous ceremonial robes, two Qianchan observers who had asked politely where to stand. Nobody told them. Nobody tells you where to stand at a killing.

Smoke on the east wing. Salvationist guns to the west, close enough that the windows hummed.

Then she walked out of the shadow of the gate, and the laughing stopped being the strangest thing.

She had cut her own hair. Badly, with something that wasn't scissors. Her armor was still the Court's red, scraped bright in places and black in others, and under it she was thin in a way that had nothing to do with hunger. Her eyes went everywhere. The roofline, the sky, the men behind me. Once, a place just over my shoulder, where nobody was standing.

"Father's here," she said, to no one, quite warmly. "He wanted to watch."

"Father's dead, Azula," I said.

"Is he?" She grinned at the empty air. "Funny. He told me you'd say that."

The arbiter was an old judge from the Diet, a man who'd spent forty years writing the laws we were about to break the spirit of. His voice shook. He read the rules anyway. Agni Kai to the death. Fire against fire. Each duelist carries a sword for the final stroke, and for nothing else. No other art is permitted. No lightning. He said that last one twice, looking at her.

"No lightning," Azula repeated, in a little sing-song. "No lightning, Zuzu. What a quaint little world you live in."

"Don't call me that."

"Why? Does it hurt?" She tilted her head, looking at my face, the half of it that never healed right. "Look at you. Half a face and all of Uncle's sermons. You look like a candle somebody forgot to put out."

"You look tired."

It was true, and I said it without any edge. I think that was what made her flinch.

"Tired." She laughed again, shorter, uglier. "I held this empire together with my teeth while you hid behind the Diet's skirts and wrote letters to the Qianchan. Eighteen years. Eighteen years of mud and smoke and burying people, and you want to tell me I look tired."

"You held it together," I said. "There are towns in the south that don't have names anymore. You can ask them how well."

"Mine was an empire." Her voice cracked on it. "Yours is a funeral."

"Then I'll bury you in it."

I hadn't meant to say that. It came out calm, which was worse. The courtyard breathed in.

Azula stopped smiling. For half a second I saw somebody I used to know, a girl in a doorway who'd just been told something she didn't want to hear. Then it passed, and something that wasn't her pushed back to the front.

"Everyone who died in this war," she whispered, "has your face, brother. Every one. Did you know that? I counted."

"Then look at it," I said. "And tell me which one was mine."

We bowed.

She was still the best I'd ever seen. People forget that. You carry the child in your head, the grinning girl with her hands behind her back, and then she comes at you with twenty years of Father's lessons and nothing left to protect. The first pass took the skin off my forearm. The second drove me back three steps.

She talked the whole time.

"Come on! Fight me, Zuzu! Is that all you've got? Uncle taught you to dance and Father taught you to kneel, and now you just stand there like a fucking monk—"

I gave ground. Parried. Gave ground again. I wasn't trying to win yet. I was trying to hear her breathing.

"You think they love you? The Diet? They love that you're convenient. You think the army follows you? They follow whoever's still standing—"

"They're following something," I said. "I don't think it's me."

"Liar!"

I saw her stance change a half-second before.

Weight shifted back. Two fingers, then the others. The long, slow draw of the arm that every firebender in that courtyard knew, and that not one of them had ever seen done at a duel.

The arbiter said, quite clearly, "That is forbidden."

"Don't," I said.

I said it softly. I want that on the record. I had hoped, right to the last, that there was something in her still above this.

"Rules," Azula said, and her whole face broke open with delight. "Father never kept a single rule in his life."

The lightning came across the courtyard like the sky had split.

I did not decide. That is the honest account. Seventeen years since Uncle put his hands over mine in the dirt behind a tea shop, and the body remembered what the mind had been afraid to. Breath. Spine. Take it in at the fingertips, let it come down and across, turn it at the stomach, throw it away.

It burned. It burned all the way through me, a white sound with no end, and for a moment there was no courtyard and no sister. Then it left my other hand and went wide, and the north wall of the Palace came apart in a long gout of stone.

I was on one knee. My chest was on fire. My hand didn't feel like my hand.

Silence.

Azula stood in the middle of the courtyard with her arm still out and her mouth a little open. She looked, for the first time all morning, exactly her age.

"No," she said. "No, that's, that was Uncle's, you can't—"

"I told you there was one rule."

I don't remember getting up. I don't remember the twelve steps. The sword was out, and there was a sound like a single clean breath, and the world went white at the edges and came back.

When I could see again she was standing, still.

Her head wasn't.

It was the quickest thing I have ever done. No one saw it happen. The Flame Guard sergeant nearest told me later that he'd blinked, and that when he opened his eyes it was over, and he hadn't understood yet what he was looking at. The Qianchan officer by the gate had taken off his cap.

Then her body remembered it was dead, and folded, and the courtyard let out a breath it had held for eighteen years.

I didn't feel anything. That frightened me, later. Not then. Then, I wiped the blade, because the old rules require it, and I stood in the smoke and I waited to feel something.

A cloth. Someone gave me a cloth. I did not know what to do with it.

An old sergeant of the Flame Guard crossed the stones, a man older than my uncle, and laid his sword down at my feet. Then another. Then the rest, one by one, until the stones rang with it.

Whoever lives is the true inheritor of the lands.

I'd read the line twice when the herald brought it. I read it a third time then, standing in all that quiet. She'd put it at the end of her letter, after the page of everything I'd done, and I'd thought it was a threat.

It wasn't. It was the only question she had left.

I stood.

sozin_rearmament.title: The Sozin Rearmament (37 BG – 0 AG)
sozin_rearmament.html:
The thirty-seven years in which the Fire Nation was converted from the world's leading industrial economy into a state able to wage a global war: the Diet, the opposition, procurement, diplomacy and mobilization, 37 BG – 0 AG.

For the long background, see History of the Fire Nation. For what the other nations saw and did, see Prewar diplomacy. For the forces that resulted, see Prewar military balance.
Period37 BG – 0 AG (the "Sozin Rearmament")
Directed byFire Lord Sozin, with the General Staff Directorate and the Imperial Research Bureau
PhasesI (37–30 BG), II (30–20 BG), III (20–12 BG), IV (12 BG – 0 AG)
Military budgetNavy 70%, Army 30% (see Imperial military budget)
CoverIndustrial modernization, protection of commerce, colonial security
TriggerRoku's check on Sozin (37 BG); the energy forecast; the Qianchan race (from 26 BG); Roku's death (12 BG)
CulminationThe Air Nomad Genocide, 0 AG

The Sozin Rearmament was the process by which Fire Lord Sozin changed the Fire Nation's institutions, economy, military and public imagination until a war of conquest became possible. It was not an open preparation for invasion. The Fire Nation in 37 BG already had the world's largest economy and its most advanced industry, with Qianchan in second place, and Sozin did not have to industrialize a backward country. He had to take an already prosperous industrial society and make it serve the throne's ambitions. Factories, railways, shipyards and research institutions existed for civilian reasons before they were adapted for military ones, and most of the rearmament was carried out under the names of modernization, commerce and colonial security.

The result was a thirty-seven-year political transformation as much as a military one. The state that could have used its lead to build a system of international cooperation built instead the institutions that allowed a single ruler to turn prosperity into war.

The strategic problem

Three pressures shaped the program, and later historians disagree on how much weight each deserves.

  • Energy. The Empire's engineers and planners projected that accessible domestic oil would fall short of demand within about a century if industry, shipping and aviation kept growing. The discovery of oil in the Si Wong Desert in 28 BG showed where the largest field within reach lay: inside the Earth Kingdom. The forecast was a projection, not a proof, and it rested on assumptions about population, consumption and the availability of imports. Sozin treated it as a deadline.
  • A peer rival. From 26 BG the Fire Nation and Qianchan were in a technology race. The Fire Nation's lead in mechanical engineering narrowed, and the General Staff concluded that its advantage would not survive another generation of Qianchan growth.
  • The Avatar. In 37 BG Avatar Roku checked Sozin's expansion along the Earth Kingdom coast and spared him. Sozin learned that open expansion could be stopped by a diplomatic and spiritual authority outside his control, and began to pursue national strength through institutions that Roku could not challenge directly.

Beneath these lay an ideology. Sozin believed that the world's separate political systems were obstacles to the coordination of its resources, and that Fire Nation prosperity should be "shared" with the world. At first this could be read as a universalist program of roads, factories and medicine. The authoritarian turn came when he concluded that those who refused it were obstructing progress and that their sovereignty could be overridden. The oil forecast did not create that belief. It gave it a timetable.

The political foundation (37–12 BG)

A court that Sozin could control

The Fire Nation Sozin inherited had already undergone centuries of royal centralization. Zoryu's successors had weakened the great clans, and General Oraso Eiko's defeat of the last warring houses early in Sozin's reign removed the final armed check on the crown. Yet the clans, senior officers, industrialists, senior bureaucrats and religious institutions still held influence he could not ignore. His first problem was political: how to mobilize an entire country without letting its power brokers decide what the mobilization was for.

The Imperial Diet

His answer was to reorganize the relationship between the court and the rest of society. The Imperial Diet met for the first time in about 29 BG as a modernization of government, not an abolition of monarchy. Its two houses brought together the heads of the great houses, the commercial and industrial elite and selected commoners, and it had real influence over ordinary domestic policy: tariffs, infrastructure, commercial law, labor disputes. Its members were told that they were partners in national development.

Group in the DietPublic purposeEffect under Sozin
Clan delegatesGive the old houses a recognized role in national policyDrew clan leaders into a state institution the Fire Lord could dominate
Industrial and commercial delegatesRepresent those funding factories, railways and tradeSecured the loyalty of economic elites through contracts and access
Commoner delegatesGive workers, professionals and provincial towns a voiceMade the regime appear representative without giving ordinary people equal power
Royal ministersCoordinate national policyConcentrated executive authority in the Fire Lord's government
Military and naval advisersExpert advice on defense and modernizationNormalized military spending as national development

The Diet's character changed with each phase of the rearmament. Early on it helped Sozin govern a complicated industrial society. Later it became the institution through which he legitimized decisions that its members could not examine. The Empire's constitution of 12 BG, which made the realm formally an empire, wrote the final limits into law: the Diet kept the budget, but under Article 28 it could not investigate the Fire Lord, the military or the Ministry of Truth. Before that, the same limits had been applied by standing orders and by classification. See Political institutions of the Empire.

The four phases

Phase I: consolidation and industrial mobilization (37–30 BG)

Roku had checked Sozin but let the colonists stay, and the Fire Nation retained its coastal colonies on the Earth Kingdom's western shore. Sozin concluded that his expansion needed to be built into institutions that could not be stopped by the refusal of a single clan, province or supplier.

  • Coal-powered shipping, ironworks, rail infrastructure and government-backed engineering were expanded.
  • Long-term procurement contracts were signed with private manufacturers and clan-owned enterprises.
  • Strategic ports, mines and industrial districts came under tighter central control.
  • Military supplies and officer training began to be standardized.
  • The Zeisan affair of 37 BG (below) allowed the court to take control of the Fire & Air Center of Learning and to restrict religious networks.
  • The Diet was drafted as a "modernization of government", with a dependable majority among clan and industrial delegates built in advance.

The fast ship that engineer Nyn Chei had designed with the Water Tribe boatwright Massak as a trade vessel was turned into the model of a fleet. The fleet created hundreds of jobs for the poorest workers and made the shipyards a constituency for continued spending. From the start the Navy was the favored service: under Sozin the military budget was split roughly 70 percent Navy and 30 percent Army.

Phase II: the military-industrial state (30–20 BG)

The technology race with Qianchan made it impossible for Sozin to assume that economic supremacy guaranteed military superiority. This was the phase in which the Fire Nation built the capacity for sustained war, not merely a large fleet.

  • Naval construction, military engineering, metallurgy and weapons research were enlarged under the Imperial Research Bureau.
  • Standardized ammunition, improved breech-loaders and more reliable bolt-action rifles went into production. A self-loading pistol appeared in 29 BG.
  • Oil was found in the Si Wong in 28 BG. The first aircraft flew in 27 BG, and armored land vehicles, protected with meteorite metal in theory and with plate in practice, were tested.
  • Military academies, technical schools and the officer corps were expanded.
  • Strategic stockpiles of metals, coal, fuel, spare parts and ammunition were laid down, and contingency plans for blockade were written.

Military contracts were officially justified as protection of commerce, maritime trade and the colonies. Most of the new capacity could be used for civilian purposes, which gave the buildup plausible cover.

Phase III: strategic competition and acceleration (20–12 BG)

As the race with Qianchan intensified, research concentrated on capabilities that could win a short, decisive campaign.

  • A first-generation military aviation program followed the first flight of 27 BG, and experiments began with airships, reconnaissance and the delivery of incendiary weapons.
  • Naval artillery, ship protection, signals and coordinated fleet operations were improved.
  • Military intelligence mapped potential routes into neighboring territory.
  • Planning began for simultaneous operations across several distant theaters.
  • The Diet's powers over security were narrowed, and the Ministry of Truth took control of the press.

These were research programs and not mature weapons. Early aircraft were limited by reliability, payload, range and training, and the first tank would not enter service until 2 AG. Their importance lay in the direction of development.

Phase IV: mobilization after Roku's death (12 BG – 0 AG)

Roku's death on Island Jezhi in 12 BG, which Sozin could have prevented, removed the person who had most directly restrained him. The final twelve years were not the beginning of the buildup but the period in which existing preparations were converted into a war plan.

YearsStageContent
12–10 BGConsolidationThe court presented Roku's death as a tragedy and not a political turning point. Central control over military planning, strategic industry and intelligence was strengthened. The Empire was proclaimed under the new constitution.
10–7 BGMobilizationShipyards expanded, fuel reserves were established, military contracts grew and transport networks received strategic investment. Procurement was standardized, and plans were drawn for moving troops and supplies across the archipelago. Aviation moved from experiment toward operational use.
7–4 BGPreparationThe future enemy was defined. Planners began to treat the Air Nomad temples as strategic targets, studied their geography, transport requirements and timing, and the possibility of simultaneous attack. Anti-Air Nomad propaganda was intensified.
4–1 BGFinal readinessPreparations were completed behind routine state activity. Security around sensitive programs tightened, and commanders were authorized to act without a further political debate once the chosen moment arrived. Exercises were held under the cover of defensive maneuvers and colonial security.
0 AGThe cometThe plan was executed as the Air Nomad Genocide, followed a week later by the order to subjugate the Water Tribes.

Access to the invasion plan was limited to a small circle of trusted officials in the General Staff, the Fire Lord's household and the Research Bureau. Even members of the Cabinet learned of the final operation late.

What was being built

Not every Fire Nation invention was a secret weapon. The industrial lead came from a combination of civilian technology, military research and the capacity to manufacture at scale. The program's public explanations and its real purposes diverged as follows.

ProgramPublic explanationMilitary purpose
Naval expansionProtect shipping and overseas commerceSecure sea lanes, blockade opponents, transport forces
Rail and port modernizationImprove trade and link industrial centersMove troops, weapons, coal and supplies quickly
Standardized firearmsReplace unreliable equipmentSimplify mass production, ammunition supply and training
Armored vehicle prototypesIndustrial engineering experimentsExplore protected mobility and breakthrough warfare
Aircraft and airshipsExploration, observation, commercial aviationReconnaissance, transport, strategic surprise, aerial attack
Communications researchCoordinate the growing economyCoordinate fleets, armies and distant commands
Fuel and mineral surveysSecure long-term energy suppliesIdentify strategic resources and reduce dependence on foreign suppliers
Military mappingImprove colonial administration and navigationPrepare invasion routes, landing sites and target lists
Chemical researchIndustrial and agricultural chemistryAgents later used from 1 AG at Yu Dao (Chemical weapons)

The opposition and its suppression

The regime did not face a society neatly divided between patriotic imperialists and foreign sympathizers. Its opponents were several groups with conflicting interests.

GroupArgumentFate
Diplomatic officialsTrade, resources and access can be had by treaty; a war would provoke a coalitionMarginalized; their positions recast as naive
Commercial interestsWar closes markets, destroys shipping, exposes investment to retaliationCo-opted by contracts; the unwilling lost opportunities
Some clan leadersThe concentration of contracts and power in the royal government is unjustDivided by patronage; rivals disadvantaged
Religious and cultural institutionsObject to the political use of traditionThe Sages were weakened and the Fire & Air Center seized
Commoner representativesWorried about taxation, conscription and labor conditionsOutvoted; later restricted from security debates
Zeisan and the Guiding WindProsperity gives no right to rule othersSee below
Naval officers and merchantsThe fleet is not ready; oil can be boughtReassigned or silenced

How repression developed

Sozin did not need to begin with mass arrests. He made opposition less effective by stages:

  1. Marginalization. Diplomats who opposed expansion lost influence over strategic policy.
  2. Patronage. Clans and industrialists who supported the crown received prestige, contracts and access.
  3. Classification. Military research, resource forecasts and colonial planning became secret. Officials who questioned the buildup could be accused of disclosing sensitive information.
  4. Political framing. Critics were portrayed as undermining national unity or helping rivals exploit Fire Nation prosperity.
  5. Institutional capture. The Diet continued to sit, but its membership, committees and agenda were shaped by the government.
  6. Targeted repression. The most organized opponents faced surveillance, dismissal, prosecution or detention. The regime avoided treating every dissenter as an enemy at first, since it still needed administrators and industrial specialists.

This let the Empire keep the appearance of a modern state with deliberative institutions while reducing the ability of those institutions to stop the Fire Lord.

The Zeisan affair (37 BG)

Princess Zeisan, Sozin's sister, had given up her royal title for the ideas of the Guiding Wind and proposed a political marriage to its leader, Khandro. She is evidence that the Fire Nation's political future was contested from within: her rejection of royal privilege challenged the idea that the monarchy was the highest expression of Fire Nation identity.

On 10 June 37 BG a bombing at a public event killed Zeisan and her fiancé. The deaths were real and so was the security failure. The government used them at once to portray the Guiding Wind as extremist, to isolate Zeisan's allies, to bring the Fire & Air Center of Learning under state control and to justify monitoring religious networks and public gatherings. The official investigation reached its conclusions suspiciously fast, evidence was lost, and later historians cannot establish whether the bombing was the work of extremists, a botched operation or an event manipulated from within the government. Sozin's direct involvement is unproven. His political responsibility is not in doubt: the bombing turned a disputed program into an emergency in which extraordinary measures seemed justified.

The Diet becomes an instrument of rearmament

Sozin did not abolish the Diet. He changed what it did. In its early years it could genuinely debate domestic policy. Over time the balance shifted:

  • The royal executive gained greater control over defense spending.
  • Military procurement committees were closed to ordinary scrutiny.
  • Emergency and security provisions restricted the Diet's ability to examine strategic programs.
  • Opposition delegates could debate appropriations but could not look at the war plans behind them.
  • Government-aligned delegates described military expansion as protection of the country's industrial achievements.
  • National exhibitions, ceremonies and demonstrations linked the Fire Lord personally to progress.

The result was neither a democratic legislature nor an empty one from the start. It was an institution whose original purpose was gradually hollowed out, and that is why the regime could claim to be modernizing government while narrowing the public's choice.

Diplomacy and concealment

The Empire's diplomacy was designed to delay a response. It offered commercial agreements, assurances about the colonies and invitations to inspect exhibition fleets, while keeping the purpose and timing of its plans from its neighbors. It spread the impression that the Fire Nation was preoccupied with resources and the Avatar's patience, and that any quarrel would be settled by arbitration. Its opponents could recognize a threat without knowing its timetable. The details are in Prewar diplomacy.

The economic and social side

The rearmament rode on an economy that was already the world's largest. It also changed that economy: procurement made certain industries dependent on state contracts, naval construction put the poorest to work, and propaganda taught those workers to see hardship as national sacrifice. See Fire Nation economy and society.

Why the others did not stop it

By 0 AG the Empire had the institutions, production capacity, stockpiles and command structure to launch its opening attack. The other powers had no collective-security system. The Alliance Treaty of 3 BG created no joint command and no joint plan, the Earth Kingdom's provincial armies could not be mobilized under one authority, the Water Tribes were distant and divided, and the Air Nomads had no army. Recognizing a threat was not the same as knowing its timetable, its plans or the extent of its capabilities.

Historiography

ViewHeld byArgument
NecessityImperial loyalistsThe Empire faced a real energy and security problem, and acted before the world could organize against it.
ChoiceQianchan and United Republic historiansA resource problem proved nothing about conquest. The Empire never tested the alternatives: purchase, treaties, substitution.
IdeologyMany modern historiansThe forecast was a pretext. Sozin's belief in a Fire Nation-led world came first, and the forecast gave it a deadline.
Institutional driftConstitutional historiansNo single decision started the war. A chain of reasonable-looking steps removed every institution that could have said no.

The irony that United Republic historians stress is that Sozin was right about where the world was going and wrong about how to get there.

Timeline

DateEvent
37 BGColonies on the Earth Kingdom coast; Roku spares Sozin; Zeisan and her fiancé are killed (10 June)
c. 35–30 BGPhase I: procurement contracts, the Nyn Chei fleet, the Center of Learning seized
c. 29 BGThe Imperial Diet first meets; the self-loading pistol
28 BGOil discovered in the Si Wong
27 BGFirst flight of a plane
26 BGTechnology race with Qianchan begins
20 BGPhase III begins; the Diet's powers over security are narrowed
12 BGRoku dies; the constitution of the Empire; Phase IV
10–7 BGIndustrial and logistical mobilization
7–4 BGThe Air Nomad temples become targets
3 BGAlliance Treaty between Qianchan and the Earth Kingdom
4–1 BGFinal readiness behind defensive exercises
0 AGThe comet; the Air Nomad Genocide

prewar_diplomacy.title: Prewar diplomacy (37 BG – 0 AG)
prewar_diplomacy.html:
The treaties, disputes and negotiations of the last thirty-seven years of peace: Roku's attempts to restrain Sozin, the Earth Kingdom's and Qianchan's responses, and why the world's diplomacy failed to deter the war of 0 AG.

For the Fire Nation's side of the same years, see The Sozin Rearmament. For the forces involved, see Prewar military balance.
Period37 BG – 0 AG
Principal actorsSozin; the Avatar Roku (to 12 BG); the Earth King and court of Ba Sing Se; the Presidents and Parliament of Qianchan; the Northern and Southern Water Tribes; the Air Nomad temples
Key instrumentsThe 37 BG settlement; the Natsuo exercises; the Alliance Treaty of 3 BG
MissingA joint command, a shared threat estimate, a common mobilization plan
OutcomeNo deterrent in place when the comet returned

The world of the last decades before the war had no machinery for collective security. Its disputes were settled by bilateral bargaining, by occasional conferences and, when these failed, by the Avatar. For four centuries the system had worked tolerably well because the strongest states preferred a settlement to a general war and because the Avatar was willing and able to enforce one. The diplomacy of 37 BG – 0 AG is the story of how that system was tested by a ruler who no longer wanted a settlement, and of how each of the other powers misjudged him in a different way.

The old system

By the time of Roku and Sozin the world's order rested on three things. The first was the Avatar's authority, which was moral, spiritual and, in the last resort, personal. The second was a rough balance of power in which the Fire Nation's industry was offset by the Earth Kingdom's size and, since 255 BG, by Qianchan. The third was habit: the four nations had not fought a general war in living memory, and the Platinum Affair of 530 BG, the Chenbao incidents of 56–54 BG and a long series of lesser disputes had all been settled without one.

What the system lacked was any means of acting before a crisis. No treaty bound the great powers to consult. No combined staff existed. The Earth Kingdom and Qianchan did not recognize one another's legitimacy. The Water Tribes were a kingdom of two poles whose northern chief could not commit the South to war. The Air Nomads had no state at all. When a power chose to make war, the only institution able to stop it was one person.

The 37 BG crisis

The coastal colonies

In 37 BG Sozin established the first Fire Nation colonies on the western coast of the Earth Kingdom, in the land that would become the province of Yanakawa. It was an escalation: for the first time a major power had planted settlements in another's territory. The colonies, which needed governors, police and defense, quickly became local industrial centers.

Roku intervened. He stopped the expansion, spared Sozin, and let the colonists stay. It was a settlement of the kind the old system produced, and it had a fatal consequence. Ba Sing Se, unable to agree on a response and with no army that could retake the coast, learned that persistence paid: a determined state might keep its gains in spite of the Avatar. Sozin learned something else, that open expansion could be stopped by a figure outside his control, and that an alternative had to be found.

Natsuo and the Earth King's exercises

Two further disputes belong to the same years. The Fire Nation claimed Natsuo Island, one of its easternmost possessions, after a large cache of ore was found there. The calculating Earth King Jialun sent ships on exercises near it in the hope of goading Sozin into a quarrel that would bring the Avatar down on the Fire Nation's side of the argument. The attempt backfired. Sozin presented the exercises as a provocation, and the incident joined the file of grievances that his press used.

Crescent Island

The Crescent Island disaster, in which Roku destroyed the upper half of the island's temple and set off its volcano, left homeless people on the Fire Nation's side who blamed the Earth Kingdom for failing to help them. The Fire Nation's propaganda made it a symbol of Earth Kingdom indifference and of the limits of the Avatar's protection.

Roku's attempts to restrain Sozin

Roku and Sozin were friends, and that complicated the diplomacy. Roku understood power through the responsibilities that came with it; he believed that the Fire Nation's strength obliged it to accept limits. Sozin believed that limits were obstacles to a national mission. Their disagreement was never a contest between progress and stagnation. Roku recognized the Fire Nation's technical achievements and thought other nations might benefit from them. What he rejected was Sozin's assumption that progress gave the Fire Lord a right to rule everyone.

QuestionSozinRoku
What is progress?A coordinated world using the Fire Nation's industrial and political modelBetter conditions for people without abolishing their right to govern themselves
What causes conflict?Rival nations competing for resources and resisting integrationCompetition and injustice, to be addressed without erasing sovereignty
Who decides the world's future?The state able to unify and modernize itNo single nation has the right to impose its will on the others

Roku's attempts to restrain him took four forms.

  1. Private argument. He argued with Sozin as a friend, in letters and in person. He told him that the four nations were meant to remain four, a statement that was less a prophecy that their peoples must never mix than a refusal of any claim to erase the independence of the others.
  2. Arbitration. He settled disputes that might have become wars, in the manner of the Chenbao settlement of 56–54 BG, and he used the 37 BG settlement to freeze the colonial question.
  3. Visits and warnings. He visited the courts of the other nations and warned Ba Sing Se and the Water Tribes of the direction of Fire Nation policy. He was believed in outline, but not in detail.
  4. The threat of force. His own power was the one sanction no state could ignore. It was exercised sparingly, and each time Sozin took note of how far it reached.

The limits of these attempts were structural. The Avatar had no army, no treasury and no jurisdiction beyond the force of his character. He could stop an expansion in progress, but he could not compel a state to change its institutions or abandon a plan he did not know about. And he did not know, before his death, how far Sozin would go once he was no longer there to oppose him. In the years after 37 BG, as the rearmament was disguised as modernization, Roku found less to act upon.

The Earth Kingdom's response

The court at Ba Sing Se saw colonies, a coal-fired fleet and a nationalist press. It did not see the scale or timing of the rearmament. Its secret police, the Dai Li, had been founded to hunt republicans, not to read the Fire Nation's procurement. The Earth Kingdom's response was shaped by four weaknesses.

  • Command. The kingdom had provincial armies, and the lords who commanded them would not send their troops across the continent to defend a coast that was not theirs.
  • Intelligence. Qianchan's information was better than Ba Sing Se's, and the allies disagreed over the severity of the threat.
  • Politics. A kingdom that had fallen twice from within was reluctant to arm its provinces.
  • The assumption of the Avatar. For four centuries the old order had relied on the Avatar to settle crises. No state had a plan for a world without him.

See History of the Earth Kingdom for the full account.

Qianchan's response

Qianchan read the Fire Nation more carefully than anyone. Its Academy of Gaoling printed freely, and the Empire's own journals and exhibitions told its engineers a great deal; its merchants had agents in every Fire Nation port; and from 26 BG the technology race made the two powers' patents, launches and exhibitions each other's best intelligence. Qianchan's leaders concluded that the Fire Nation was building the largest army and fleet in its history. They disagreed with Ba Sing Se about what that meant.

DateQianchan initiativeResult
Late 20s BGOffer to discuss an oil-sharing arrangement through neutral brokers, after the discovery of the Si Wong fieldUnanswered by the Empire
20s–10s BGProposal for rules on maritime disputes and technological competitionNot taken up
Before 10 BGProposal for a standing combined staff with the Earth KingdomRefused: Ba Sing Se would not accept a body that implied the republic's legitimacy
Before 10 BGStandard railway gauge to the border, to move troopsRefused or delayed by provincial lords
Before 5 BGNaval convention with the Northern Water TribeNot concluded
3 BGThe Alliance TreatySigned, without a joint command

Qianchan's own problem was how to preserve the balance without provoking a war it was not yet prepared to fight. Its governments, a coalition of veterans, merchants and agrarian assemblies, fell regularly over the question of how much to spend on rearmament, and its fragmented politics made it slow. It also feared that visible preparation would give the Empire's hawks the argument that the republic was encircling them.

The Alliance Treaty of 3 BG

The treaty was a response to the Fire Nation's expansion, and it was a pact of mutual defense between Qianchan and the Earth Kingdom Confederation. It was the first document in which Ba Sing Se named the republic. Qianchan signed it only on condition that the kingdom revise its language of non-recognition. The negotiation took much of two years, and most of it was spent on that one clause.

What the treaty did not do is the point. It promised support and a common cause. It did not create a joint command, a shared intelligence service, a common mobilization plan, an agreed estimate of the threat or a commitment to a preventive war, and it did not station a single soldier on the other's soil. The two powers could not agree on any of these without implicitly recognizing each other's authority. The Empire's General Staff read the text, found the gaps and concluded that it could defeat its enemies one at a time. The treaty is better understood as a suspension of tensions than as a reconciliation. In 100 AG, the Ba Sing Se Treaty finally put the two armies under a single command, which is the thing the Alliance Treaty omitted.

The Water Tribes and the Air Nomads

The Water Tribes were consulted late and by individuals. The Kingdom of Two Poles gave the South a veto over a Northern war, and the North's navy was the strongest in the polar seas, but the two tribes' divergent cultures and thousands of kilometers of ocean prevented joint planning. Modernizers such as Chief Qanitt of Whale Harbor and the merchant Tiqriganiannig had begun to build links with the other nations, and the Unity expedition carried the four nations' studies and technologies around the world. The governments suspected it of being a spy mission. In 0 AG both poles lacked sea defenses against an industrial fleet.

The Air Nomads noticed the political tension around the Guiding Wind and Sozin's growing hostility to Air Nomad ideas, and the four temples had supported the Fire & Air Center of Learning. They had no army, no intelligence service and no tradition of preparing for a deliberate extermination campaign. Their spiritual neutrality was real, and they misjudged how little it would protect them.

What each side believed

PartyWhat it could seeWhat it risked misunderstanding
Fire Nation leadershipResource insecurity, industrial competition, the value of overseas positions, the Avatar as an obstacleThat conquest was necessary, that opposition proved disloyalty and that a short-term advantage guaranteed long-term success
Earth Kingdom leadershipExpansion and a threat to the coastThe scale of the transformation and the danger of fragmented provincial responses
Qianchan leadershipA rising rival and the importance of the Earth Kingdom allianceWhether deterrence could work against a state ready to act before its opponents coordinated
Water Tribe leadersMaritime assertiveness and threats to their territoryHow far the Fire Nation would go against distant, isolated communities
Air Nomad leadershipPolitical tension around the Guiding WindThat neutrality and the lack of an army would not protect them from extermination
RokuSozin's expansionism and the threat to the balance among nationsBefore his death, how far Sozin would go once the Avatar was gone

These are historians' reconstructions and not a claim that every leader held exactly these views.

What Roku's death changed

Roku died on Island Jezhi in 12 BG. Sozin, who could have helped him, left him to die. His death removed the most personal restraint on Sozin and the one sanction no state could ignore. It also changed what the others knew: the next Avatar would be born among the Air Nomads, and no one outside the Fire Nation court had thought through what that would mean. The Empire's court presented the death as a tragedy, and its diplomats took advantage of the world's mourning to press commercial agreements and assurances. For the last twelve years of peace, there was no Avatar, no arbitrator and no plan.

Why deterrence failed

  • No joint command. The only alliance in the world lacked a common staff, a threat estimate or a plan.
  • A delayed alliance. It came in 3 BG, after twenty-five years of rearmament.
  • Disagreement about the threat. Ba Sing Se and Qianchan read the same warnings and drew different conclusions.
  • Concealment. The Empire's offers, assurances and defensive exercises gave each neighbor a reason to doubt its own estimate.
  • The wrong target. No power expected the first blow to fall on a people with no army.
  • The missing Avatar. The system's only enforcer was gone.

Not every government was incompetent. Some had incomplete intelligence, domestic crises or incompatible priorities. Others had no credible way to intervene before the attack. The failure was of institutions, and the world paid for it for a century.

Timeline

28 BGOil discovered; Qianchan offers to discuss sharing

5 BGNaval convention with the North not concluded
3 BGAlliance Treaty
0 AGThe comet; the war begins

fire_nation_economy_and_society.title: Fire Nation economy and society
fire_nation_economy_and_society.html:
The industrial economy, class structure, workers, conscription, propaganda and public opinion of the Fire Nation, before and during the Hundred Year War.

For the political side, see Political institutions of the Empire. For the budget, see Imperial military budget. Figures on this page are estimates reconstructed after the war.
PopulationAbout {{stat:pop_fn_0|n}} (0 AG); about {{stat:pop_fn_100|n}} (100 AG, after the revised ledger)
Economic rank (0 AG)First in the world; Qianchan second
Industrial revolutionFrom about 290 BG
Energy baseCoal, iron, natural gas, volcanic heat; Si Wong oil from 28 BG (about 140,000 barrels a day by 90 AG)
ConscriptionThree years of service for all adult men; service is a precondition for the vote
Military budgetNavy 70 / Army 30 (Sozin); Army 60 / Navy 40 (Azulon, Ozai); plus 30% of the civilian budget for superweapons under Ozai
Information controlMinistry of National Enlightenment (press, schools); Ministry of Truth (security)

The Fire Nation that went to war in 0 AG was not a poor nation seeking a way out of poverty. It was the richest and most industrialized country in the world, and it was also a country in which the benefits of that wealth were unevenly shared, in which rural communities remained poorer than the industrial cities, and in which the government had learned to explain hardship as sacrifice. The economy supplied the war machine, and the war machine in turn reshaped the economy.

The industrial base

From the revolution to the eve of war

The islands lacked arable land, but they had coal, iron, natural gas and volcanic energy, and they overcame their limits earlier than any other nation. The first steam engine (Zenshin) dates to 500 BG, the industrial revolution to about 290 BG, the first train to 260 BG. By the century before the war the Fire Nation had railways, coal-fired shipping, ironworks, a steel industry, a financial system and a coinage standardized by Szeto's reforms. See Technology timeline and History of the Fire Nation.

SectorPosition at 0 AG (estimates)
Coal and ironThe largest output in the world; the base of rail, shipbuilding and steel
Steel and machineryFirst in the world, centered on the northern and eastern island ironworks
ShipbuildingThe largest yards of any nation, with steam-driven, steel-hulled ships
RailDense island networks and port connections; limited by geography to short lines
ChemicalsAdvanced, with large dye, fertilizer and explosives industries
OilDomestic production on the way to decline; Si Wong oil not yet in Imperial hands
AviationThe world's first aircraft (27 BG); zeppelins in service
AgricultureIntensive, but unable to feed the islands without imports in poor years

A dense industrial network lay behind these headline figures: trained workers, engineers, ports, financial institutions and centralized procurement. The Fire Nation's advantage over its rivals was not a better weapon, but its ability to turn scientific advances into equipment and equipment into sustained operations.

Who owned what

Ownership was mixed and changed over the thirty-seven years of rearmament.

  • Clan and noble enterprises. The great houses held mines, shipyards and estates, and many had turned from rule to commerce after Zoryu's reforms ended their armies. Patronage from the crown increasingly decided which of them prospered.
  • Private industrial houses. Merchant and manufacturing families owned most factories and the larger railways, and their long-term military contracts after 37 BG made them dependent on the state.
  • The state. The crown controlled strategic ports, coalfields and industrial districts, and ran arsenals and the Research Bureau directly. A public rail authority and the mint were state bodies.
  • Colonial enterprises. The coastal colonies of 37 BG supplied raw materials and small manufactures, and made their governors and the firms they favored rich.

The combination created what historians call a feedback loop: industrialization increased the state's resources, the state invested in modernizing the military, procurement stimulated particular industries, and those industries became constituencies for continued spending.

Classes and workers

GroupPositionStake in the war
The thirteen houses and nobilityLand, mines, shipping, seats in the House of Lords; close to the NavyPrestige and patronage; some feared the loss of independence
Industrial and merchant familiesFactories, railways, banksContracts and markets; some feared retaliation and closed trade
Salaried professionals, engineers, officialsThe expanding urban middle classCareers in a growing state; strongly tied to the regime's success
Industrial workersMills, mines, yards and railways in the citiesWages and jobs; also the first to bear shortages and conscription
Rural poor and fishing communitiesFarm labor, small tenancy, coastal fishingLittle; the largest source of conscripts
Colonial settlersFarmers, traders and officials in the coastal coloniesProtection of their holdings; a loud constituency for expansion

Labor conditions

Industrial work was dangerous and long. Coal mines, rolling mills and shipyards had high accident rates, and wages in the poorest districts lagged behind the cities. The naval construction programs created hundreds of jobs for the poorest workers, which gave the state a political base among those who had the least to lose. There were strikes at the coal ports and in the mills, and unrest over housing and prices. They were typically settled by concessions, by arrests or, in the late years of the rearmament, by invoking security regulations that placed whole industries under military supervision.

Mechanization displaced craft workers and small farmers, who moved to the cities. The government's answer was to offer them places in the new factories and, increasingly, in the armed forces.

Wealth and its distribution

The benefits of growth flowed to the court and its allies, and the social costs of militarization fell on the poor. Nationalist propaganda directed discontent outward: resentment of inequality was turned toward the Earth Kingdom, the Water Tribes and the Air Nomads, and workers in hard conditions were invited to see their hardships as sacrifices for national greatness.

Conscription and the army of the people

Every adult man owed three years of military service, a condition of voting under Articles 20–22. The Army expanded by conscription, and its rank and file came from every part of the Empire. Its non-commissioned officers were predominantly commoners, and its officer corps mixed academy graduates from ordinary backgrounds with members of the old military houses. It was the one institution in which a commoner and an aristocrat served in the same chain of command.

The Navy, by contrast, recruited from coastal families and drew its officers disproportionately from aristocrats and their clients. Service therefore divided the population by class as well as by geography: the Army was the rural and urban poor in uniform, while the Navy was an elite, well-funded service. See The Army–Navy divide.

Conscription turned the franchise into a veterans' franchise. It also meant that the generation that fought the Hundred Year War had been educated, drilled and told what to think by the state for years before the first shot.

Propaganda and the press

The government used propaganda to win the poorest to the cause. It presented the Fire Nation as industrious and innovative and the other nations as obstacles to progress or as beneficiaries of Fire Nation leadership. It concealed the central contradiction of Sozin's program, that the nation which claimed to share its prosperity denied others the right to decide whether they wanted it. Its methods included:

  • National exhibitions, parades and military demonstrations that linked the Fire Lord to progress.
  • The dragon hunts, a spectacle that won back noble support and weakened competing cultural institutions.
  • Schoolbooks rewritten to fit the official past. Sozin sealed the Dragonbone Catacombs, and the Empire's history of itself took shape in classrooms.
  • A press controlled by the Ministry of National Enlightenment, which communicated the government's interpretation of events and maintained the official narrative.
  • Anti-Earth Kingdom feeling stoked through repeated disputes over scarce materials, Natsuo, and the Crescent Island refugees.
  • After 20 BG, a campaign against the Air Nomads' influence that portrayed the Guiding Wind's methods as typical of the whole tradition.

The Ministry of Truth handled dissent. It ran political policing and censorship enforcement, stood outside judicial review (Art. 33) and enforced "The Truth", the state ideology of the Fire Lord's sacred authority and national purity.

Public opinion before the war

GroupView of the buildup (estimated)
Urban working classSupported jobs and growth; resented prices and long hours. Responded to patriotic appeals.
Rural communitiesDivided; poorer and less exposed to propaganda, but a large share of conscripts
VeteransRespected and generally loyal; the future base of reform and of the Salvationists
MerchantsDivided between those with military contracts and those who relied on trade with the other nations
SettlersStrongly in favor of expansion
Intellectuals and religious traditionalistsThe most skeptical, and the most closely watched

Few in the Fire Nation expected a world war. The government spoke of prosperity, national defense and the need to protect the country's future, and most citizens interpreted the military buildup as a sign of strength, not an invitation to invade.

The war economy (0–100 AG)

Mobilization

The war was fought by an economy that was already half mobilized. Armed forces grew from about 1.4 million in 0 AG to about 8 million by 80 AG, about 6 percent of the population. The Army took the largest share: from the 20s AG the budget was divided 60 percent to the Army and 40 percent to the Navy, and under Ozai a further 30 percent of the civilian budget was set aside for the superweapon program. See Imperial military budget.

Oil

The Si Wong field was the Empire's strategic prize. After the Si Wong Offensive (80–88 AG) production reached about 140,000 barrels a day by 90 AG, and it paid for the Army's mechanization. Because this income came from outside the annual appropriations, it let the Army grow without winning the budget fight, and it became a source of friction with the Navy.

Labor from the occupied lands

The Empire used forced labor in the occupied territories. In the South Pole the laborers built harbors, dry docks and rail lines across the ice. Deportees from the Water Tribes and the Earth Kingdom worked in the Eastern Territories. See Occupation and resistance.

The home front

The civilian economy bore the costs of the conventional war, and from 97 AG of the superweapon program. Civilian infrastructure and public services grew more slowly, scientific and industrial institutions were redirected, and ministries competed for a shrinking pool of resources. Rationing, controls on information and a steady flow of casualty lists shaped daily life. The Fire Nation lost about 3,510,000 people to violence and, by the revised accounting, about 3,200,000 more to disease, shortage and medical collapse. See Demographic ledger of the Hundred Year War.

By the 90s AG opinion had hardened in the other direction. The Siege of Ba Sing Se, the Jasmine Island scandal, the Pardon Crisis and the poisoning of Azulon revealed divisions at the top, and the Army's reform movement under Lu Ten and Iroh gave voice to grievances that the Ministry of Truth could not entirely suppress. The collapse of 100 AG followed.

Historiography

Imperial historians present the economy as proof of a national mission; Qianchan's historians as proof that prosperity can be turned into aggression by a government that needs a war to hold together; and modern scholars as a case study in how an industrial state's institutions, contracts and interests can commit it to a path that no one planned in full.
